reading.why: adamw defaults (including weight decay), how state dtypes follow params, and MultiSteps for gradient accumulation.

chapters.title: Preference learning with DPO
chapters.subtitle: Derive DPO from the KL-regularized reward objective, build verifier-labeled pairs on MBPP, and test it against a chosen-only control that isolates the contrastive signal.
chapters.why:
Week 1 trained the model to imitate passing code. The verifier tells you more than that: it also says which of the model's own samples fail. Preference learning uses both halves of that signal. DPO is the cheapest way to do it. It is one supervised-looking loss, roughly 15 lines on top of the week-1 masked log-prob function, and it needs no sampler in the loop and no reward model. It also starts from the same KL-regularized objective that GRPO optimizes in weeks 4 to 6. Once you have derived it by hand, the beta, the reference policy and the implicit reward in later weeks will already be familiar.

For a research-engineer job the derivation is only half the skill. The other half is experimental hygiene. A DPO gain means little until you have run a control that gets the same extra verified data without the contrast. You also need to read the curves well enough to catch the usual failure modes: a falling chosen log-prob, a margin that grows only by pushing rejected samples down, and length drift. You need to trust a step-0 sanity value before you trust any curve. And you need to say exactly what a single-seed, paired-CI comparison supports. This week's three-arm table is the first entry in the scorecard and the non-RL baseline that week-5 RL has to beat.
prereqs: Ch 0: unbiased pass@k, bootstrap CIs over items, and the noise floor (basic 0.17 pts, bar 0.35 pts)
Ch 0: per-item scored JSONL from harness/score.py and status counts
Ch 1: masked per-token log-prob with EOS included and prompt/pad excluded, fp32 upcast
Ch 1: LoRA-filtered NNX train step (nnx.Optimizer wrt=nnx.LoRAParam, nnx.DiffState) and fp32 LoRA state
Ch 1: paired bootstrap over shared item IDs and when McNemar applies
Ch 1: merged SFT checkpoint and Orbax SFT adapter

sections.heading: What a preference loss is for on this spine
sections.md:
SFT maximizes $\log \pi_\theta(y|x)$ on passing code. It never sees a failure. Yet the verifier labels every sample, and the failures carry information too. A failing sample often differs from a passing one at one spot: a wrong boundary, a renamed function, a missed edge case. A preference loss says: for this prompt, make the passing completion $y_w$ more likely *relative to* the failing one $y_l$.

The classic route to that is RLHF. You fit a reward model on pairs, then run RL against it with a KL penalty that keeps the policy near a reference. DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023) shows that both steps collapse into one loss on pairs. The policy itself acts as the reward model. Here no reward model has to be learned at all, since the verifier is the reward. So DPO matters on this spine for two reasons:

- It is a cheap, off-policy, non-RL baseline. Week-5 GRPO must beat it to justify its cost.
- Its derivation is the cleanest place to learn the KL-regularized objective, the reference policy and beta. All three come back in week 4.

The experiment has three arms, all evaluated on frozen test and dev:

1. **SFT**: the week-1 adapter, unchanged.
2. **SFT + chosen-only**: continue SFT on the $y_w$ of each pair. Same steps, same LR schedule.
3. **SFT + DPO**: continue the SFT adapter with the DPO loss, $\beta = 0.1$, reference = SFT.

Arm 2 gets the same new verified data as arm 3 but no contrast. The question is not "does DPO help?" but "does pushing failures down add anything beyond the new passing samples?"

sections.heading: The KL-regularized objective and its optimal policy
sections.md:
Fix a prompt $x$. We want a policy that earns high reward without drifting far from the reference:

$$
\max_{\pi} \; J(\pi) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi(\cdot|x)}[r(x,y)] - \beta\, \mathrm{KL}(\pi(\cdot|x) \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot|x))
$$

Treat $\pi(\cdot|x)$ as a distribution over whole completions. Write both terms as one sum over $y$:

$$
J(\pi) = \sum_y \pi(y|x)\Big[r(x,y) - \beta \log \frac{\pi(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}\Big]
= -\beta \sum_y \pi(y|x)\Big[\log \pi(y|x) - \log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x) - \frac{r(x,y)}{\beta}\Big]
$$

The last two terms combine into $-\log\big(\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)\, e^{r(x,y)/\beta}\big)$. The thing inside the log is not a normalized distribution. Normalize it with the partition function

$$
Z(x) = \sum_y \pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)\, e^{r(x,y)/\beta}, \qquad \pi^*(y|x) = \frac{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)\, e^{r(x,y)/\beta}}{Z(x)}
$$

Then $\log(\pi_{\text{ref}} e^{r/\beta}) = \log \pi^* + \log Z(x)$. Substitute, and use $\sum_y \pi(y|x) = 1$ to pull out the constant:

$$
J(\pi) = -\beta \sum_y \pi(y|x) \log \frac{\pi(y|x)}{\pi^*(y|x)} + \beta \log Z(x) = -\beta\, \mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \pi^*) + \beta \log Z(x)
$$

$Z(x)$ does not depend on $\pi$. KL is nonnegative and zero only when the two distributions match. So the unique maximizer is $\pi = \pi^*$. The optimal policy is the reference tilted by $e^{r/\beta}$. Small $\beta$ means a sharp tilt toward high reward. Large $\beta$ keeps it near $\pi_{\text{ref}}$.

Now invert. Take logs of $\pi^*$ and solve for $r$:

$$
r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)} + \beta \log Z(x)
$$

This is the key move. Any reward can be written through its own optimal policy, plus a term that depends only on the prompt. You cannot compute $Z(x)$: it is a sum over every possible completion, on the order of $V^T = 151936^T$ terms for completions up to length $T$. The next step makes it disappear.

sections.heading: Bradley-Terry, the cancellation, and the DPO loss
sections.md:
Bradley-Terry models a preference between two completions of the same prompt as a logistic function of their reward difference:

$$
P(y_w \succ y_l \mid x) = \sigma\big(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l)\big), \qquad \sigma(u) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-u}}
$$

Substitute the inverted reward for both completions:

$$
r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l) = \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)} + \underbrace{\beta \log Z(x) - \beta \log Z(x)}_{=\,0}
$$

$Z(x)$ cancels because both completions share the same $x$. It would not cancel for a pair across two prompts $x \neq x'$, because $\beta(\log Z(x) - \log Z(x'))$ is an unknown, intractable constant that would sit inside the sigmoid. Pairs must therefore be formed within a prompt. The same fact explains why this works at all: Bradley-Terry only sees reward differences, so a reward is identified only up to a per-prompt shift. The $\beta \log Z(x)$ term is exactly such a shift.

Now parameterize $\pi^*$ by $\pi_\theta$ and maximize the Bradley-Terry log-likelihood of the observed pairs. Define the log-ratios and the scaled margin:

$$
\Delta_w = \log \pi_\theta(y_w|x) - \log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x), \quad \Delta_l = \log \pi_\theta(y_l|x) - \log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x), \quad u = \beta(\Delta_w - \Delta_l)
$$

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(\theta) = -\mathbb{E}_{(x, y_w, y_l)}\big[\log \sigma(u)\big]
$$

The implicit reward of a completion is $\hat r(x,y) = \beta \Delta$. Each $\log \pi(y|x) = \sum_t \log \pi(y_t | x, y_{<t})$ is a **sum over completion tokens only, EOS included**. The derivation needs the probability of the whole sequence, and EOS is part of it: without it you score a prefix, not a finished program. Prompt tokens are not part of $y$. Padding is not part of anything.

Why not average per token? On base-model samples from MBPP train prompts with mixed outcomes, passing completions have a median of 217 tokens and failing ones about 229. A per-token mean divides each log-ratio by its own length. The loss is still bounded, and it still equals $\log 2$ at step 0. But it is no longer $\log \pi_\theta/\pi_{\text{ref}}$, so the link to the KL objective is gone. The derivation no longer describes what you train, and the implicit reward means something different. That is a different method (length-normalized variants exist). If you use one, give it its own name.

sections.heading: The gradient, the per-pair weight, and beta
sections.md:
Differentiate with the chain rule. For $f(u) = -\log \sigma(u)$, using $\sigma'(u) = \sigma(u)(1-\sigma(u))$:

$$
f'(u) = -\frac{\sigma(u)(1-\sigma(u))}{\sigma(u)} = -(1 - \sigma(u)) = -\sigma(-u)
$$

The reference terms are constants, so $\nabla_\theta u = \beta\big(\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y_w|x) - \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y_l|x)\big)$. Therefore, per pair,

$$
\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} = -\beta\, \sigma(-u)\, \big(\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y_w|x) - \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y_l|x)\big)
$$

A descent step raises $\log \pi_\theta(y_w|x)$ and lowers $\log \pi_\theta(y_l|x)$, scaled by the weight $\sigma(-u) = \sigma(\hat r_l - \hat r_w)$. The weight is near 1 when the implicit reward ranks the pair the wrong way. It decays toward 0 as the margin grows, so pairs that are already ranked correctly contribute less and less. This is the difference from SFT, which keeps pushing every example with the same weight forever.

**Step 0.** The DPO arm starts from the SFT adapter, and the reference is the SFT model. So $\pi_\theta = \pi_{\text{ref}}$, $\Delta_w = \Delta_l = 0$, and $u = 0$. The loss is $-\log \sigma(0) = \log 2 \approx 0.6931$, and every pair has weight $\sigma(0) = 0.5$. This value does not depend on the data. That makes it a strong test.

**A worked pair.** Under the SFT model, $\log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x) = -38.0$ and $\log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x) = -52.0$. After some steps, $\log \pi_\theta(y_w|x) = -40.0$ and $\log \pi_\theta(y_l|x) = -60.0$. Then:

- $\Delta_w = -2.0$, $\Delta_l = -8.0$, raw log-ratio margin $\Delta_w - \Delta_l = 6.0$ nats
- $u = 0.1 \times 6.0 = 0.6$, loss $= \log(1 + e^{-0.6}) = \log 1.5488 = 0.4375$, weight $= \sigma(-0.6) = 0.354$
- implicit rewards $\hat r_w = -0.2$, $\hat r_l = -0.8$

The loss fell from 0.693 to 0.438 while the chosen sequence became *less* likely. Section 7 returns to this.

**What beta does.** The loss saturates once $u$ is a few units. A loss of 0.05 needs $\sigma(u) = e^{-0.05} = 0.951$, so $u = \log(0.951/0.049) \approx 2.97$. The raw log-ratio gap needed is $2.97/\beta$: about 30 nats at $\beta = 0.1$, 300 nats at $\beta = 0.01$, and 3 nats at $\beta = 1$. Small $\beta$ lets the policy drift much further from $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ before the weights decay. That is a weaker KL constraint, as section 2 predicts.

The explicit $\beta$ factor in front of the gradient matters much less. Adam's update is roughly $\eta\, \hat m / (\sqrt{\hat v} + \epsilon)$, which is invariant to a constant rescaling of the gradient as long as $\epsilon$ is negligible (AdamW's decoupled weight decay is not rescaled either). The behavioral effect of $\beta$ comes through *where* $\sigma(-u)$ decays, not through the step size.

Log the margin two ways. The $\beta$-scaled margin $\hat r_w - \hat r_l = u$ is what the loss sees. The raw gap $u / \beta$ measures drift from the reference in nats, and it is comparable across runs with different $\beta$.

> With deterministic verifier labels, the Bradley-Terry maximum-likelihood margin is infinite. Only finite steps and the decaying weight stop it. Over many epochs on a few dozen pairs, DPO will overfit. IPO (Azar et al. 2023) was designed partly to address this. Watch the dev curves, not the train loss.

sections.heading: On-policy pairs from a verifier, and which prompts carry signal
sections.md:
The recipe: draw 4 samples per MBPP train prompt from the SFT model, verify each, and pair one pass with one non-pass. Here "fail" means any basic status other than `pass` (`fail`, `error` such as a NameError from a renamed function, or `timeout`). A prompt where all 4 pass or none pass yields no pair. If a prompt's pass probability is $p$ and samples are independent:

$$
P(\text{skip}) = p^4 + (1-p)^4
$$

- $p = 0.1$: $0.0001 + 0.6561 = 0.656$
- $p = 0.3$: $0.0081 + 0.2401 = 0.248$, and $p = 0.7$ gives the same by symmetry
- $p = 0.5$: $2/16 = 0.125$, the minimum

The train-set skip fraction is the average of this over each prompt's own $p$. Averages hide bimodality, so use the real distribution. In week 0 the *base* model was sampled 16 times per train prompt (`runs/week0_sftpool_train_qwen3-1_7b`). By basic tests, 90 of 274 prompts passed 0 of 16 and 116 passed 16 of 16. Only 68 had mixed outcomes. Drawing 4 of the 16 samples without replacement, with $c_i$ passes for prompt $i$, the expected all-pass-or-all-fail probability is

$$
\frac{1}{274}\sum_i \frac{\binom{c_i}{4} + \binom{16-c_i}{4}}{\binom{16}{4}} = 0.852
$$

So about 85% of prompts are skipped, and about **41 pairs** survive out of 274 prompts. The SFT model will likely do worse here. Its training pool contained all 274 train references plus verified self-samples for these same prompts, so its train pass rates move toward 1 and more prompts become all-pass. Write that prediction down before you run.

Signal comes only from prompts of intermediate difficulty for the SFT model. The kept pairs are a biased sample: neither the hardest prompts (no on-policy winner exists) nor the easiest. If too few pairs survive, you have two options:

- **8 samples per prompt.** On the base-model rates this keeps about 55 prompts (skip 0.80).
- **Several pass/fail pairs per prompt.** With $c$ passes out of $m$ samples there are $c(m-c)$ pairs. On the base-model rates the expected totals are 134 at $m=4$ and 624 at $m=8$. They are strongly correlated within a prompt, so cap them (for example at 4 per prompt) and keep item-level statistics keyed by prompt ID.

Two practical details. First, "on-policy" here means sampled from the SFT model at the week-0 decoding config (T = 0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20). DPO does not need sampler log-probs, because the loss recomputes every log-prob with the trainer, so a truncated sampling distribution is acceptable here, unlike in week 4. Second, keep only `finish_reason=stop` samples. Otherwise a truncated completion becomes a "rejected" sample and DPO learns to stop early. (Truncation is rare at 768 max tokens: 13 of 4384 base samples.) Log the pass-count histogram of the kept prompts next to the skip fraction.

sections.heading: The code: log-probs, reference cache, loss, step, step-0 test
sections.md:
Batch chosen and rejected rows together, `[2B, L]`, chosen first. One forward then serves both. The week-1 function, restated so the shapes are explicit (the model call is the Tunix Qwen3 signature `model(tokens, positions, cache, attention_mask)`):

```python
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp, optax
from flax import nnx

def seq_logprob(model, ids, positions, attn, loss_mask):
    """Sum of log pi(y_t | x, y_<t) over completion tokens, fp32, shape [rows].
    loss_mask [rows, L-1] marks targets ids[:, 1:] that are completion tokens
    (EOS included, prompt and pad excluded)."""
    logits, _ = model(ids, positions, None, attn)               # [rows, L, V] bf16
    logp = jax.nn.log_softmax(logits[:, :-1].astype(jnp.float32), axis=-1)
    tok = jnp.take_along_axis(logp, ids[:, 1:, None], axis=-1)[..., 0]
    return jnp.where(loss_mask, tok, 0.0).sum(-1)

@nnx.jit
def ref_forward(model, batch):
    return seq_logprob(model, batch["ids"], batch["positions"], batch["attn"], batch["loss_mask"])
```

If you are handed per-token log-probs `[B, T]` and a completion mask instead, the sequence value is `(tok_logp * mask).sum(-1)` in fp32. Sum, never mean over $T$ (section 3).

Run `ref_forward` once over all pairs with the SFT model before training. Store the values in a JSON keyed `"<item_id>:w"` and `"<item_id>:l"`, along with the git SHA, chat template and `enable_thinking=False`. Precomputing saves a second model's forward pass, and its activations, at every step.

The loss and its metrics:

```python
def dpo_loss(lp_w, lp_l, ref_w, ref_l, beta=0.1):
    ref_w, ref_l = jax.lax.stop_gradient(ref_w), jax.lax.stop_gradient(ref_l)  # documents intent
    d_w, d_l = lp_w - ref_w, lp_l - ref_l          # log-ratios, fp32, [B]
    u = beta * (d_w - d_l)
    loss = -jax.nn.log_sigmoid(u).mean()           # stable; never log(sigmoid(u))
    metrics = dict(
        loss=loss, margin_raw=(d_w - d_l).mean(),
        reward_w=(beta * d_w).mean(), reward_l=(beta * d_l).mean(),
        acc=(u > 0).mean(), weight=jax.nn.sigmoid(-u).mean(),
        lp_w=lp_w.mean(), lp_l=lp_l.mean())
    return loss, metrics
```

The step reuses the week-1 filtering. Model, optimizer, batch and cached references are all `nnx.jit` arguments, so it compiles once per length bucket:

```python
@nnx.jit
def dpo_step(model, opt, batch, ref_w, ref_l):
    B = ref_w.shape[0]                             # static under jit
    def loss_fn(m):
        lp = seq_logprob(m, batch["ids"], batch["positions"], batch["attn"], batch["loss_mask"])
        return dpo_loss(lp[:B], lp[B:], ref_w, ref_l, beta=0.1)
    (_, metrics), grads = nnx.value_and_grad(
        loss_fn, argnums=nnx.DiffState(0, nnx.LoRAParam), has_aux=True)(model)
    opt.update(model, grads)
    return metrics

opt = nnx.Optimizer(model, optax.adamw(1e-5), wrt=nnx.LoRAParam)  # model = base + SFT adapter
```

These three pieces were run on CPU against a toy NNX model with `nnx.LoRA` layers under Flax 0.12: the step-0 loss is 0.6931 with weight 0.5, the hand pair below gives 0.4375 and 0.354, non-LoRA parameters stay bit-identical after training, and right-padding a batch leaves the sums unchanged.

The step-0 test feeds the *same padded batch* to a fresh forward and to the cache, so the values agree to within float noise:

```python
def test_step0_loss_is_log2(sft_model, pair_batch, ref_cache):
    lp = ref_forward(sft_model, pair_batch["arrays"])
    ref = jnp.array([ref_cache[k] for k in pair_batch["row_keys"]])
    assert float(jnp.max(jnp.abs(lp - ref))) < 1e-3     # cache reproduces
    B = lp.shape[0] // 2
    loss, m = dpo_loss(lp[:B], lp[B:], ref[:B], ref[B:])
    assert abs(float(loss) - float(jnp.log(2.0))) < 1e-3
    assert abs(float(m["weight"]) - 0.5) < 1e-3
```

**Reading a wrong step-0 value.** Suppose the first logged loss is 0.58. $f(u) = -\log\sigma(u)$ is convex, so by Jensen $f(\bar u) \le \overline{f(u)} = 0.58$, which forces the batch-mean $\bar u \ge \log(1/(e^{0.58}-1)) \approx 0.24$: a systematic log-ratio advantage for chosen of at least 2.4 nats on average at $\beta = 0.1$. Zero-mean random mismatch cannot produce that. With $f''(0) = \sigma(0)\sigma(0) = 1/4$, zero-mean noise in $u$ with variance $s^2$ gives $\mathbb{E}f \approx \log 2 + s^2/8$, which is *above* $\log 2$. A loss below $\log 2$ means the policy already prefers chosen relative to the reference. Check these causes in order:

1. The policy and reference are not the same model. A classic case is reference = base and policy = SFT: SFT learned passing code, so $\Delta_w > \Delta_l$ and the loss starts below $\log 2$. The reverse mistake (policy = base or a fresh zero-init LoRA, reference = SFT) pushes it above.
2. The reference was computed on different inputs: another chat template, `enable_thinking`, tokenization, or EOS present in one sum only.
3. Mask mismatch: prompt or pad tokens counted on one side.
4. Numerics: no fp32 upcast in one path, or a different LoRA scale $\alpha/r$.

To diagnose, recompute the references online for one batch and diff them per sequence against the cache. The diff should be about 0, up to bf16 noise.

**Memory.** One pair is 2 sequences. At $L = 1024$, a single fp32 logits copy is $2 \cdot 1024 \cdot 151936 \cdot 4 \approx 1.24$ GB per pair. The loss path holds several such copies (chapter 0). So use 1-2 pairs per microbatch with gradient accumulation, and length buckets. Most rows here are a few hundred tokens, not 1024.

sections.heading: Reading the curves: falling chosen log-prob, margins, length
sections.md:
Log per step: loss, `acc`, `weight`, both implicit rewards, the raw margin, and the mean `lp_w` and `lp_l`. The loss depends only on $\Delta_w - \Delta_l$. Nothing in it says $\Delta_w$ must rise. Three patterns to recognize:

- **Healthy:** $\Delta_w$ flat or rising, $\Delta_l$ falling, `acc` rising, dev pass rate rising.
- **Margin by push-down:** both fall, $\Delta_l$ faster. The loss improves while chosen becomes less likely, as in the section 4 example. Probability mass is moving to sequences that are neither $y_w$ nor $y_l$.
- **Length drift:** mean completion length moves steadily. In the base data, failures were slightly longer (median about 229 vs 217 tokens), so DPO can partly learn "shorter" rather than "correct".

**Why chosen cannot fall in a tabular toy.** Take $y_w = (a, b)$ and $y_l = (a, c)$, sharing the first token. In a *tabular* policy with separate logits per context, $\log\pi(y_w) - \log\pi(y_l) = \log p(b|a) - \log p(c|a) = z_b - z_c$, because the $\log p(a)$ terms and the log-sum-exp over the context $a$ cancel. The gradient raises $z_b$, lowers $z_c$, and touches nothing else. Both moves raise $p(b|a)$, so chosen can only rise. In the tabular world the failure mode cannot happen.

**Why it does happen in a network.** A real network shares parameters. Code pairs from one model are near-duplicates: same signature, same imports, often the same suffix after a one-token divergence. The suffix tokens after $b$ and after $c$ sit in different contexts, but the network gives them nearly identical hidden states, so to first order they share one logit vector. Look at one such shared token $t$, with probability $p_w$ in the chosen context and $p_l$ in the rejected one. Since $\partial \log p_t / \partial z_t = 1 - p_t$, the DPO direction on the shared logit $z_t$ is

$$
(1 - p_w) - (1 - p_l) = p_l - p_w
$$

The pushes cancel only when $p_w = p_l$. After a mistake the model is often less confident, so $p_l < p_w$ and the net push on the shared token is *down*, which lowers its probability in $y_w$ too. Summed over hundreds of shared tokens, and over other pairs whose rejected sequences contain chosen-like idioms, $\log\pi_\theta(y_w|x)$ can fall while the margin grows. Razin et al. (2024) study this under the name likelihood displacement. Pal et al. (2024, DPOP) observe it on pairs with small edit distance, which is exactly the situation for code pairs sampled from one model.

This can be harmless for greedy or low-temperature pass rate. It can also produce off-distribution output at T = 0.7. That is why the plan requires plotting the chosen log-prob trend. A common fix adds an NLL term on $y_w$ to the DPO loss, as in iterative RPO (Pang et al. 2024) or DPOP. The chosen-only arm is the pure version of that NLL term.

**beta predictions.** At $\beta = 0.01$, expect a much larger raw margin before saturation (about 300 nats), more drift, a higher risk of a collapsing chosen log-prob and length drift, and a step size set by the LR rather than by $\beta$. At $\beta = 1$, expect saturation after about 3 nats and a policy that stays near SFT. Compare runs by raw margin and by drift, not by loss.

sections.heading: The control, the statistics, and scorecard row 1
sections.md:
**Why chosen-only.** The DPO arm sees new on-policy, verifier-checked passing solutions. That alone could help, through ordinary SFT. SFT + chosen-only trains on the same $y_w$, from the same SFT adapter, with matched steps and LR schedule. It separates "more verified data" from "pushing failures down". Read the outcomes like this:

- DPO > chosen-only > SFT, with the paired DPO-minus-chosen-only CI excluding 0: the contrast adds something (exploratory, one seed).
- DPO and chosen-only both beat SFT, and DPO-minus-chosen-only straddles 0: the gain came from the data, not the preference signal.
- DPO beats SFT only together with a length change: suspect a format or truncation effect. Check `finish_reason` counts and the status breakdown.

**Which test.** Each arm's per-item score is pass@1 estimated from $n = 4$ samples on 500 test items, so it is a rate in $\{0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1\}$, not a binary outcome. Use `stats.paired_bootstrap` over shared item IDs (or Wilcoxon signed-rank). Note the direction: `paired_bootstrap(a, b)` reports mean(b - a), so call `paired_bootstrap(sft, dpo)` for DPO minus SFT. McNemar needs one binary outcome per item, such as greedy pass@1.

Predict the width before you run. In week 0 the between-item SD of per-item pass@1 on test was 0.47, so one arm's CI half-width is about $1.96 \times 0.47/\sqrt{500} \approx 4.1$ pts. Pairing removes most of that. The SD of the per-item difference is $0.47\sqrt{2(1-\rho)}$, where $\rho$ is the item-level correlation between arms. Two adapters on the same base will be highly correlated. At $\rho = 0.9$ the SD is 0.21, the SE is $0.21/\sqrt{500} = 0.94$ pts, and the half-width is about 1.8 pts. At $\rho = 0.8$ it is about 2.6 pts. The paired CI half-width is still 5-7x the 0.35-pt noise-floor bar, so the CI is the binding criterion. Measure $\rho$ from your scored files and compare with this prediction.

Three comparisons (DPO vs SFT, chosen-only vs SFT, DPO vs chosen-only) stay under the roughly 5-comparison Holm threshold. One training seed means the CI covers item and sampling noise, but not seed variance: pair order, LoRA init effects, and which pass and fail got paired. So label everything exploratory. The 3-seed re-run happens on week-4 nights.

**Scorecard row 1 (post-training).** Score each criterion 1-5:

| Criterion | Weight |
|---|---|
| Surprise from your data | 3 |
| Iteration speed | 2 |
| Follow-up feasibility | 2 |
| Enjoyment | 2 |
| Relevance | 2 |
| JAX/TPU leverage | 1 |
| Public signal | 1 |

The weights sum to 13, so the maximum is $5 \times 13 = 65$. Every score links to a plot or table in the repo. An unlinked score counts as 1. Iteration speed should come from measured wall clock, such as launch to scored row for one arm, and feasibility from a sized next experiment, not from impressions. Surprise of 4 or more needs a result that contradicts a prediction you committed *before* the run. For example: "DPO will beat chosen-only by more than 2 pts on test basic", followed by a CI straddling 0. Without the written prediction, any result can be read as expected. This row feeds the week-10 top-2 selection and the week-13 rule that the chosen area must have a Surprise of 4 or more from your own data.

chapters.lab:
Do these in order. Light week (5-7 h): evening 1 covers steps 1-3, evening 2 covers steps 4-6, and the weekend block covers steps 7-11. Run evaluations overnight.

**1. Derivation on paper (about 1 h).** From the KL objective to $\pi^*$, the inverted reward, Bradley-Terry, the loss, the gradient with weight $\sigma(-u)$, and the step-0 values (loss $\log 2$, weight 0.5). Commit a photo or LaTeX as `docs/week2_dpo_derivation.md`. Check: you can say in one sentence why $Z(x)$ does not cancel across prompts.

**2. Pre-run predictions.** Commit `docs/week2_prereg.md` before generating anything. Include the predicted skip fraction (base-model estimate 0.85 at 4 samples, higher for SFT), the predicted DPO-minus-chosen-only difference, the predicted paired CI half-width (about 1.8-2.6 pts), and the predicted chosen log-prob trend. Surprise in the scorecard is scored against this file.

**3. Sample train prompts from the SFT model** (torch env, GPU free of JAX). Make sure the week-1 merged export directory also holds the tokenizer and config files.
```bash
uv run --project envs/torch python scripts/gen_vllm.py --model ckpt/sft_merged --split train --n 4 --seed 0 --out runs/week2_pairs_gen
uv run --project envs/jax python -m harness.score runs/week2_pairs_gen/completions.jsonl
```
Check: `summary.json` exists, `meta.json` shows the same chat template and decoding config as week 0 (T 0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20, 768 max tokens), and the status counts look like week 0 (no extraction regression).

**4. Build pairs: `scripts/week2_build_pairs.py`.** Group the scored rows by `id`. Keep only `finish_reason == "stop"`. Choose one basic pass and one basic non-pass with a seeded RNG, then write `data/week2_pairs.jsonl` with `{id, prompt, chosen, rejected, chosen_sample, rejected_sample}`. Print the skip fraction, the all-pass and all-fail counts, and the pass-count histogram of kept prompts. Check: pairs exist only for train IDs (assert none fall in dev, test or ood from `data/splits.json`). If fewer than about 30 pairs survive, re-run step 3 with `--n 8` and record why.

**5. DPO module and tests.** Add `dpo_loss` and `ref_forward` next to your week-1 log-prob module (outside `harness/`, which stays jax-free). Write `tests/test_dpo.py` with these tests:
- the step-0 loss equals log 2 and the weight equals 0.5 on a real pair batch from the SFT model
- the cache reproduces from a fresh forward to within 1e-3 on the same padded batch
- appending extra padding leaves the sequence log-prob unchanged
- a row whose loss mask covers only prompt positions gives 0
- `dpo_loss` on hand values (lp_w=-40, lp_l=-60, ref_w=-38, ref_l=-52) returns 0.4375 and weight 0.354

The last three can run on CPU with a toy NNX model (an `nnx.Embed` plus an `nnx.LoRA` head with the same `(ids, positions, cache, attn)` call signature), so they stay fast. Run `uv run --project envs/jax pytest tests/ -q`.

**6. Precompute reference log-probs once.** Use the SFT adapter model and the same template, `enable_thinking=False` and masks. Save them to `runs/week2_ref_logps.json` with the git SHA and adapter path. Check: one-batch online-vs-cache diff below 1e-3.

**7. Train two arms from the SFT adapter.** Use `scripts/week2_train.py --arm chosen_only|dpo`. Both arms get the same pairs, the same number of optimizer steps (for example 2 epochs), the same LR and schedule, and the same microbatch of 1-2 pairs with accumulation. Use the week-1 loss for chosen-only. Run with `JAX_LOG_COMPILES=1` for the first steps and confirm one compile per length bucket. Log every step to `runs/week2_<arm>/train_log.jsonl`: loss, acc, weight, reward_w, reward_l, margin_raw, lp_w, lp_l (chosen-only logs lp_w and lp_l too, computed without gradient). Check: the DPO step-0 loss prints 0.6931.

**8. Export and evaluate.** Merge each arm in fp32, cast to bf16, and re-check parity against the adapter model. Then generate on test (n=4, seed 0, week-0 decoding) and dev, and score with `harness.score`. Also re-score the SFT arm with the same extractor if the harness changed.

**9. Statistics and results rows.** Build per-item pass@1 dicts (c/n per item from `harness.stats.per_item_counts`) from each `scored.jsonl`. Call `harness.stats.paired_bootstrap(sft, dpo)`, `paired_bootstrap(sft, chosen_only)` and `paired_bootstrap(chosen_only, dpo)`; each returns mean(second minus first). Do this on test basic, then on the 165 plus-compatible test IDs. Report per arm: test pass@1 with 95% CI, mean length, `finish_reason` and status counts, final margin, and the chosen log-prob delta from step 0. Compute the item-level correlation between arms and compare with your predicted CI width. Append rows to `runs/results.jsonl` from a clean tree with every 3.2.8 field (git SHA, config hash, chat template, decoding config, sampler version, seed, allocator settings, accelerator_hours, cost_usd, per-item JSONL path), labeled exploratory.

**10. Plots.** Plot margin_raw, lp_w, lp_l and mean length vs step for the DPO arm, and lp_w for the chosen-only arm, into `runs/week2_plots/`. Check: you can state which section-7 pattern you see.

**11. Scorecard row 1.** Score each of the 7 criteria, link a plot or table for each, compute the weighted total out of 65, and cite `docs/week2_prereg.md` for Surprise.
takeaways: The KL-regularized objective has the closed-form optimum pi* = pi_ref exp(r/beta)/Z(x), so any reward can be rewritten as beta log(pi*/pi_ref) plus a per-prompt constant.
Z(x) cancels in Bradley-Terry only because both completions share the prompt, so pairs must be formed within a prompt and log-probs must be summed over completion tokens including EOS.
The DPO gradient is the difference of chosen and rejected log-prob gradients, weighted by sigmoid(-u), which is 0.5 at step 0 and decays once a pair is ranked correctly.

Step-0 loss must equal log 2; because the loss is convex, zero-mean mismatch pushes it above log 2, and a value below log 2 means a systematic reference error such as reference = base with policy = SFT.
Beta mainly sets where the loss saturates (a raw margin of about 3/beta nats), not the step size, which Adam normalizes away.
With 4 samples, the bimodal MBPP train pass rates leave only about 15% of prompts with a pass/fail pair, so DPO learns from a small, intermediate-difficulty subset.

A growing margin can come from pushing both log-probs down, because shared tokens in near-duplicate code pairs get a net push of p_l - p_w, so always plot the chosen log-prob and length next to the loss.
Only the paired comparison against SFT + chosen-only can credit a gain to the contrastive signal, and one training seed makes that result exploratory.
