chapters.title: Build your JAX LLM stack
chapters.subtitle: Write and verify your own Qwen3-1.7B model, KV-cache sampler, LoRA, chunked log-probs and checkpointing, because every later week runs on them.
chapters.why:
Weeks 0 to 2 used Tunix and qwix as black boxes. From week 4 on, every number you report depends on four contracts: the model computes the same function as the published weights, the sampler's log-probs are the trainer's log-probs, the reference policy is exactly the SFT policy, and a resumed run is the same run. If any of them is broken, RL still produces curves. They are just wrong, and nothing in the curve tells you so. This week you build each piece yourself and pin each contract down with a test.

For a research-engineer job this is the most portable week in the plan. Labs that train frontier models run their own model code, samplers and training loops. To be trusted with that code you need three skills. You can derive the memory and precision budget from a config file. You can write static-shape JAX that compiles once. And you can tell a numerical floor from a bug. The same skills carry over to MaxText-scale code on TPUs in week 11.
prereqs: Ch 0: unbiased pass@k, bootstrap CI over items, noise floor across sampling seeds (basic 0.17 pts, predicted ~0.42 pts)
Ch 0: Qwen3-1.7B memory arithmetic (1.72B params, 3.44 GB bf16, 112 KiB KV per token) and jit cache keys / recompiles
Ch 1: masked per-token log-prob, LoRA parameter count (17.43M at r=16 all-linear), optimizer filtered to nnx.LoRAParam, fp32 LoRA state
Ch 1: paired bootstrap over shared item IDs
Ch 2: sequence log-prob log pi(y|x) as a sum of token log-probs, reference policy precompute

sections.heading: What you are building and why it is gated
sections.md:
You will replace four borrowed components with your own: the model, the sampler, LoRA and the log-prob path. You also add checkpointing and a stronger bootstrap. Each component has one **acceptance test** and a timebox. The order matters, because each one is the oracle for the next.

1. **Model + loader** (Mon PM to Tue, 1.5 days). Oracle: HF PyTorch in fp32, exchanged through saved files from `envs/torch`.
2. **Sampler MVP** (by Wed evening, 2 days). Oracle: your own model's teacher-forced forward pass.
3. **LoRA** (half a day). Oracles: `nnx.LoRA`, the unmerged forward, and HF loading your merged export.
4. **Chunked log-prob** (part of a day). Oracles: the naive full-vocab log-softmax for values, and `memory_analysis()` for memory.
5. **Orbax resume.** Oracle: an uninterrupted run.

Everything else (length buckets, top-k/top-p, early exit) is polish. Polish overflows into week 4 Mon to Tue AM. A gate more than about a day over its timebox falls back to the off-the-shelf path, and you record why. The sampler is the exception. Its fallback is the MVP, not vLLM, because vLLM lives in a different process and framework and cannot hand log-probs and fresh weights to a single-process JAX RL loop.

Monday morning is statistics. The OOD split (HumanEval+, 163 IDs) is already frozen in `data/splits.json`, so you only confirm that it has not changed. Then you add the two-level bootstrap to `harness/stats.py`. Section 9 explains why it is needed before any multi-seed comparison.

> Do not start top-k/top-p, buckets or speed work before the MVP passes its log-prob test. A fast sampler with the wrong log-probs is worse than a slow correct one, because it fails silently in week 5.

sections.heading: Freezing the OOD slice
sections.md:
Test tells you whether training helped on the distribution you trained on. It cannot tell you whether the model got better at *code* or just better at *MBPP*: the short imperative prompts, the single `assert` shown as an example, the habit of naming functions after the task. The out-of-distribution (OOD) slice is there to make that difference measurable. Chapter 6 evaluates every final checkpoint on it at $n=16$. Chapter 13 reads a flat OOD result as a reason to *narrow* the claim ("RLVR improves MBPP-style tasks") rather than as a failed experiment. Both readings depend on the set being chosen once, cleaned once and never touched again. This section does that on Monday of week 3.

**Choosing the source.** A good OOD set for this spine has to meet four conditions. (1) It is the same task type, so the same verifier and prompt builder apply: write one Python function and check it with tests. (2) It differs in surface form, so a format habit learned on MBPP does not transfer for free. (3) It has strong tests, so a pass means something. (4) It has an established reference point. HumanEval+ meets all four. Its prompts are a signature plus a docstring with doctests, not a one-line English request. Its EvalPlus tests are much stricter than the original HumanEval checks. `harness/prompts.py` already has a `humaneval` branch that asks the model to complete the function and puts the prompt back in front of a body-only answer. One consequence follows: OOD items have no MBPP-style `tests`, only `plus_test`, so **the OOD metric is the `plus` verifier field** in `summary.json`, and `basic` is empty for these items.

**Checking the references.** A test set whose canonical solutions fail its own tests measures noise. `harness/build_data.py` runs every HumanEval+ reference through the same sandboxed verifier the models face (60 s timeout for `plus`) and drops any item whose reference does not pass. On this machine one item fails: `humaneval/32` (`find_zero`, a float root-finding task whose tolerance check is fragile). That leaves 163 of 164 items. Write the dropped ID and the reason in the chapter notes. A reader comparing your numbers with a leaderboard needs to know the denominator is 163.

**Deduplicating and decontaminating.** Two questions matter here. Are any OOD items duplicates of each other? That would double-count them in the bootstrap. Does any OOD item leak into data you *tune on*? Here that means train and dev, because dev drives early stopping and hyperparameters. Test is held out too, but overlap with test does not inflate anything you fit. A cheap, honest check normalizes and tokenizes the text, then measures the fraction of an OOD item's word 10-grams that also appear anywhere in the tuning data. It also flags function-name collisions. For item $i$ with n-gram set $G_i$ and tuning n-gram set $G_{\text{tune}}$:

$$
\text{overlap}_i = \frac{|G_i \cap G_{\text{tune}}|}{|G_i|}, \qquad \text{flag if } \text{overlap}_i > 0.2 \text{ or the entry point is defined in tuning data.}
$$

I ran this over the 163 items against MBPP train and dev, using both the prompt and the solution body (with the docstring stripped so the shared prompt does not count twice). There are no duplicate prompts. The highest overlap is $0.12$ (`humaneval/59`, a largest-prime-factor task, where some MBPP code is similar). The only flags are name collisions: `humaneval/45` and `humaneval/71` are both called `triangle_area`, and MBPP train item `mbpp/626` defines `triangle_area` for a different problem (the largest triangle inscribed in a semicircle). A shared name with no shared text is not contamination, so both items stay. Record the rule, the threshold and the three flagged pairs. The judgement is part of the result.

This check does *not* rule out pretraining contamination. HumanEval has been public since 2021, and Qwen3 has almost certainly seen it. That is acceptable for this use: what you measure is a *change* between checkpoints of one base model. Contamination shifts the base and SFT levels but is the same for every arm. Do not report the absolute OOD number as a clean capability estimate.

**Freezing the IDs.** The OOD list lives in `data/splits.json["ood"]` next to train/dev/test. `build_data.py` refuses to overwrite a `splits.json` that differs. Add a test that pins the list's hash, so an accidental edit fails CI instead of silently changing the denominator:

```python
import hashlib, json
from pathlib import Path

OOD_SHA256 = "1a81c921ef421b4eb2f61743ef135c19185387a3ae7ccb3d41864e16e3ea76c8"

def test_ood_frozen_and_disjoint():
    s = json.loads(Path("data/splits.json").read_text())
    assert hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(s["ood"]).encode()).hexdigest() == OOD_SHA256
    assert len(s["ood"]) == 163 and "humaneval/32" not in s["ood"]
    assert not (set(s["train"]) | set(s["dev"])) & set(s["ood"])
```

**Never tune on it.** Each time you look at OOD to pick a learning rate, a checkpoint or a reward variant, information leaks from it into your choices. After a few such peeks the slice is a second dev set, and it no longer measures transfer. The rule is mechanical: OOD runs only on final checkpoints whose configs are already fixed, and they are scored once. Dev does all the selecting.

**Recording baselines.** Before any RL, generate $n=16$ samples per item from the base model and from your SFT checkpoint at the training temperature (`scripts/gen_vllm.py --split ood --n 16`, then `python -m harness.score`). Report pass@1 as the mean of $\hat p_i = c_i / n$ over items, with an item-bootstrap 95% CI (`harness/stats.summarize`). Expect the CI to be wide. In the worst case every item is all-pass or all-fail, and then

$$
\text{half-width} \approx 1.96\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{163}} \approx 0.077 \quad (p = 0.5),
$$

so the OOD slice detects changes of roughly 8 points or more. Smaller effects need the paired bootstrap against the SFT baseline (same items, so per-item difficulty cancels), which is why the base and SFT per-item JSONL files must be saved now and kept.

sections.heading: Qwen3-1.7B from config.json
sections.md:
Read the architecture straight off `config.json` in the HF cache: `hidden_size` 2048, `num_hidden_layers` 28, `num_attention_heads` 16, `num_key_value_heads` 8, `head_dim` 128, `intermediate_size` 6144, `vocab_size` 151936, `rope_theta` 1000000, `rms_norm_eps` 1e-6, `attention_bias` false, `tie_word_embeddings` true, `rope_scaling` null.

**The forward pass.** With token embeddings $E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d_{model}}$, each of the $N_L = 28$ layers is a pre-norm residual block:

$$
h = x + \mathrm{Attn}(\mathrm{RMSNorm}_1(x)), \qquad x' = h + \mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{RMSNorm}_2(h))
$$

$$
\mathrm{MLP}(u) = W_{down}\,\big(\mathrm{silu}(W_{gate} u) \odot W_{up} u\big), \qquad \mathrm{RMSNorm}(u) = w \odot \frac{u}{\sqrt{\mathrm{mean}(u^2) + \epsilon}}
$$

After the last layer comes a final RMSNorm, then logits $z = E\,\mathrm{RMSNorm}_f(x_{N_L}) \in \mathbb{R}^V$. That is the tied embedding: there is no separate output matrix. There is also no $\sqrt{d_{model}}$ scale on the input embedding (Gemma has one, Qwen does not).

**Attention with QK-norm and GQA.** Project $q = W_q u$ into $H = 16$ heads of $d_h = 128$, and $k, v$ into $H_{kv} = 8$ heads. Qwen3 applies an RMSNorm over the 128 dims of each q head and each k head (separate weights `q_norm`, `k_norm`, shape [128]). The order is projection, then QK-norm, then RoPE. Each KV head serves $H/H_{kv} = 2$ query heads. HF's `repeat_kv` maps query head $h$ to KV head $\lfloor h/2 \rfloor$, so KV head $j$ serves query heads $2j$ and $2j+1$. Reshaping q to `[B, T, H_kv, 2, d_h]` reproduces exactly that grouping.

**RoPE, derived.** Split each head vector into halves $x = (x^{(1)}, x^{(2)})$ of 64 dims (HF's `rotate_half` convention, not interleaved pairs). For dimension $i < 64$ use frequency $\omega_i = \theta^{-i/64}$ with $\theta = 10^6$. This is HF's `1 / theta**(arange(0, 128, 2) / 128)`. At position $p$ rotate each pair $(x^{(1)}_i, x^{(2)}_i)$ by angle $p\,\omega_i$:

$$
R_p x = \big(x^{(1)} \cos p\omega - x^{(2)} \sin p\omega,\; x^{(2)} \cos p\omega + x^{(1)} \sin p\omega\big)
$$

Rotations compose, $R_p^\top R_{p'} = R_{p'-p}$, so the score between a query at $p$ and a key at $p'$ is

$$
(R_p q)^\top (R_{p'} k) = q^\top R_p^\top R_{p'} k = q^\top R_{p'-p}\,k
$$

It depends only on the offset $p' - p$. Keep this fact. It explains why adding a constant to every position in a row is harmless, and why mixing two position conventions in one row is not (section 5). On CPU, shifting all positions by 5 changed the fp32 scores by at most 1.5e-5, which is trig rounding at larger angles.

**Parameter count** (from week 0, now from your own module): attention $2 \cdot 2048^2 + 2 \cdot 2048 \cdot 1024 = 12.58$M, MLP $3 \cdot 2048 \cdot 6144 = 37.75$M, so 50.33M per layer and 1.409B for 28 layers. The embedding adds $151936 \cdot 2048 = 311.2$M, counted once. The total is 1.720B (the loaded tensors sum to 1,720,574,976 with the norms), or **3.44 GB in bf16**.

The core pieces in NNX. On CPU in fp32 they match an HF-style reference (`rotate_half` RoPE, `repeat_kv` attention): `attend` exactly, `rope` to 1.2e-6.

```python
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp
from flax import nnx

class RMSNorm(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, eps=1e-6, dtype=jnp.bfloat16):
        self.w = nnx.Param(jnp.ones((dim,), dtype))
        self.eps = eps
    def __call__(self, x):
        x32 = x.astype(jnp.float32)                 # variance in fp32, as HF does
        y = x32 * jax.lax.rsqrt(jnp.mean(x32 * x32, -1, keepdims=True) + self.eps)
        return self.w[...] * y.astype(x.dtype)       # cast back, then scale

def rope(x, pos, theta=1e6):                         # x [B,L,heads,d_h], pos [B,L]
    half = x.shape[-1] // 2
    inv = theta ** (-jnp.arange(half, dtype=jnp.float32) / half)
    ang = pos[..., None].astype(jnp.float32) * inv   # [B,L,half]
    cos, sin = jnp.cos(ang)[:, :, None], jnp.sin(ang)[:, :, None]
    x1, x2 = x[..., :half].astype(jnp.float32), x[..., half:].astype(jnp.float32)
    return jnp.concatenate([x1 * cos - x2 * sin, x2 * cos + x1 * sin], -1).astype(x.dtype)

def attend(q, k, v, mask):          # q [B,T,H,d], k/v [B,S,H_kv,d], mask [B,T,S] bool
    B, T, H, d = q.shape
    q = q.reshape(B, T, k.shape[2], H // k.shape[2], d)          # head h -> kv h//2
    s = jnp.einsum("btgrd,bsgd->bgrts", q, k).astype(jnp.float32) / jnp.sqrt(d)
    s = jnp.where(mask[:, None, None], s, -1e30)                  # finite, and replaces NaN
    p = jax.nn.softmax(s, axis=-1).astype(v.dtype)
    return jnp.einsum("bgrts,bsgd->btgrd", p, v).reshape(B, T, H * d)
```

The attention module is then `q_norm(q_proj(x).reshape(B, L, 16, 128))`, the same for k with 8 heads, `rope` on both, `attend`, and `o_proj`. Use `nnx.Linear(..., use_bias=False)` for all seven projections. One small known difference: HF casts cos and sin to the activation dtype and rotates in bf16, while this `rope` rotates in fp32. In fp32 parity the two agree. In bf16 the difference is at rounding level and falls inside the bf16 tolerance.

**The parity checklist, with the symptom of each mistake.** Learn the symptoms. When parity fails, they tell you where to look.

- *QK-norm missing, or applied after RoPE.* The error is large from layer 0. Omitting it changes the scale of every score. Applying it after RoPE is a different function, because RMSNorm commutes with the rotation only if the norm weight is equal on each rotated pair $(i, i+64)$, and trained weights are not.
- *QKV bias added* (a Qwen2.5 habit). The loader asks for `q_proj.bias` keys that do not exist. That is a good reason to make missing keys an error.
- *Wrong GQA grouping* (`jnp.tile` instead of `jnp.repeat`, so head $h \to h \bmod 8$). Layer 0 is already wrong at every position, including position 0. On random inputs the two groupings differed by about 5 at position 0.
- *Interleaved RoPE or wrong theta.* Position 0 matches, because the rotation is the identity there, and the error grows with position. Theta 1e4 instead of 1e6 shows the same growth pattern.
- *Swapped gate and up.* The output is garbage from layer 0, because silu is applied to the wrong branch.
- *RMSNorm variance in bf16, or eps 1e-5.* The errors are small, concentrated in rows where the normalization is sensitive, and easy to confuse with a precision problem. Rule them out by reading the HF code, not by tuning tolerances.
- *Embedding scaled by $\sqrt{2048} \approx 45$.* Activations are 45 times too large, and the logits are nonsense.
- *lm_head handled as a separate matrix that is never loaded.* With a random or zero output matrix, logits are garbage at every position. Section 3 shows how to load the tie explicitly.

sections.heading: Loading weights and proving parity
sections.md:
**The loader is a table, not a guess.** The two safetensors shards in your cache hold **311 keys**: `model.embed_tokens.weight`, then 11 per layer x 28 (four projections, two QK-norms, three MLP projections, two layer norms), then `model.norm.weight`, and also `lm_head.weight`. The last one is a surprise. Even though `tie_word_embeddings` is true, the checkpoint stores `lm_head.weight` as a separate key, and it is bit-identical to the embedding. A loader that silently ignores unknown keys would hide a real untied model. Map the key explicitly instead: assert that it equals the embedding, then drop it.

Two transforms matter. HF `Linear.weight` has shape `[d_out, d_in]`, while `nnx.Linear.kernel` is `[d_in, d_out]`, so every projection is transposed. Norm weights and the embedding are copied as they are. The function below ran against the cached checkpoint on CPU. It produced 310 arrays (311 keys minus the tied head) with `k_proj` at `(2048, 1024)`.

```python
import re, jax.numpy as jnp
from safetensors import safe_open

RULES = [  # (HF regex, NNX path template, transform)
    (r"model\.embed_tokens\.weight", "embed.embedding", None),
    (r"model\.norm\.weight", "final_norm.w", None),
    (r"model\.layers\.(\d+)\.self_attn\.([qkvo])_proj\.weight", "layers.{0}.attn.{1}_proj.kernel", "T"),
    (r"model\.layers\.(\d+)\.self_attn\.([qk])_norm\.weight", "layers.{0}.attn.{1}_norm.w", None),
    (r"model\.layers\.(\d+)\.mlp\.(gate|up|down)_proj\.weight", "layers.{0}.mlp.{1}_proj.kernel", "T"),
    (r"model\.layers\.(\d+)\.(input|post_attention)_layernorm\.weight", "layers.{0}.{1}_norm.w", None),
    (r"lm_head\.weight", "TIED", None),
]

def load(files, expected_paths):            # expected_paths: set of NNX paths in your model
    out, head = {}, None
    for f in files:
        with safe_open(f, framework="flax") as g:
            for key in g.keys():
                m = next(((re.fullmatch(p, key), t, x) for p, t, x in RULES if re.fullmatch(p, key)), None)
                if m is None:
                    raise KeyError(f"unmapped HF key {key}")
                match, tmpl, tf = m
                w = g.get_tensor(key)
                if tmpl == "TIED":
                    head = w; continue
                out[tmpl.format(*match.groups())] = w.T if tf == "T" else w
    if head is not None and not bool(jnp.array_equal(head, out["embed.embedding"])):
        raise ValueError("lm_head differs from embedding: model is not tied")
    if missing := expected_paths - set(out):
        raise KeyError(f"model params not loaded: {sorted(missing)[:5]}")
    if extra := set(out) - expected_paths:
        raise KeyError(f"HF keys with no model param: {sorted(extra)[:5]}")
    return out
```

Then write the arrays into the module, for example by building a nested dict and calling `nnx.update(model, state)`. Check one shape per rule as you go. A transposed `q_proj` or `o_proj` is square (2048 x 2048), so it loads without a shape error and produces garbage. Only a parity test catches it.

**Why fp32 parity needs 'highest' precision.** Floating-point formats differ in the number of significand bits $m$ (including the implicit leading bit). Round-to-nearest has unit roundoff $u = 2^{-m}$, the largest relative error of one rounding:

- fp32: $m = 24$, so $u \approx 6 \times 10^{-8}$
- TF32: $m = 11$ (10 stored bits), so $u \approx 4.9 \times 10^{-4}$
- bf16: $m = 8$ (7 stored bits), so $u \approx 3.9 \times 10^{-3}$

On Ada GPUs such as the 4090, XLA may run fp32 matmuls on tensor cores in TF32. Each input is then rounded to 11 bits before the multiply. Torch has its own TF32 switch. So "fp32 vs fp32" can really be TF32 vs fp32, or TF32 vs TF32 with different rounding. The fingerprint is an error of about 1e-3 to 1e-2 in the logits that is roughly **uniform across positions** and already visible after layer 0. A RoPE bug grows with position. A mask bug shows up next to pads. Neither of those is uniform. So before touching model code, set both sides to full precision and rerun:

```python
jax.config.update("jax_default_matmul_precision", "highest")   # before any tracing
# torch env: torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False
#            torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("highest")      # verify for your version
```

If the gap persists at 'highest', save the hidden state after each layer on both sides and find the first layer whose max abs diff jumps. Then bisect inside that layer: after the norm, after q_proj, after QK-norm, after RoPE.

**The acceptance criteria, and why each has its shape.**

- *fp32 logits within about 1e-4 to 1e-3 max abs on 20 prompts.* With full precision on both sides, the remaining differences come from summation order across 28 layers. That is small, but it is not zero.
- *fp32 greedy identical for 64 tokens on at least 95% of 50 prompts.* A divergence counts as a bug only if the top-2 logit gap at the first divergent position exceeds about 1e-3. If two candidate tokens differ by 2e-5, a 1e-4 numerical difference can legally flip the argmax. After one flip the continuations share nothing, so you judge only the first divergence.
- *bf16: top-1 agreement of at least 99% on teacher-forced positions, plus a log-prob tolerance.* There is no greedy-identity test in bf16. Here is why, in numbers. Logits for a confident token are often between 8 and 16. In that range, adjacent bf16 values are $2^{3} \cdot 2^{-7} = 0.0625$ apart. Two candidates within about 0.06 of each other can swap order through rounding alone. Across 64 tokens, the chance that at least one step has such a near-tie is large, and one flip changes everything after it. So greedy divergence on 30% of prompts in bf16 is not by itself evidence of a bug. Teacher forcing feeds both models the same token IDs at every position, so one flip cannot cascade, and top-1 agreement measures what you care about.

sections.heading: The memory budget from first principles
sections.md:
Write this budget before you write the sampler. It tells you which batch sizes are possible at all. GB here means $10^9$ bytes.

**Weights:** 1.720B x 2 bytes = **3.44 GB** (bf16). For the RL reference policy you reuse the same weights with LoRA scale 0 (section 7), so there is no second copy.

**LoRA + Adam at r=16, all 7 projections:** each adapted map adds $r(d_{in} + d_{out})$ params. Per layer that is $16 \cdot (4096 + 3072 + 3072 + 4096 + 3 \cdot 8192) = 622{,}592$, so 17.43M for 28 layers. In fp32 that is 70 MB for the params, 70 MB for the grads, and 139 MB for Adam's $m$ and $v$, about **280 MB** in total.

**KV cache per token.** Each layer stores K and V. Each is $H_{kv} \times d_h$ values per token:

$$
\text{bytes/token} = 2_{(K,V)} \times N_L \times H_{kv} \times d_h \times 2_{\text{bf16}} = 2 \cdot 28 \cdot 8 \cdot 128 \cdot 2 = 114{,}688 \text{ B} = 112 \text{ KiB}
$$

A preallocated cache of 256 sequences x 768 tokens holds 196,608 token slots, so 196,608 x 114,688 B = **22.5 GB**. With the 3.44 GB of weights, that is already more than the 4090's 24 GB before any activations. At 64 x 768 the cache is 49,152 slots, **5.6 GB**. The realistic rollout range is 64 to 96 sequences at 768 (96 x 768 is 8.5 GB).

The plan's older estimate of "256 x 768 is about 5-6 GB" came from Qwen2.5-1.5B, which has 2 KV heads. That gives $2 \cdot 28 \cdot 2 \cdot 128 \cdot 2 = 28{,}672$ B, 28 KiB per token. Qwen3-1.7B has 8 KV heads, so its cache is **4x larger** per token. The fallback Qwen3-0.6B also has 28 layers x 8 KV heads x 128, so switching models does not shrink the cache. Never copy a memory number from a different config.

**Logits.** A full $[B, L, V]$ tensor at 256 x 768 has $256 \cdot 768 \cdot 151936 = 2.99 \times 10^{10}$ elements. That is **59.7 GB in bf16 and 119.5 GB in fp32**, and the backward pass needs a softmax of the same size. Two consequences follow:

- In **prefill**, compute logits only at the last prompt position, $[B, V]$, which is 39 MB in fp32 at B=64. Computing them at every prompt position wastes $[B, P, V]$ memory for nothing.
- In **training**, never materialize them. Section 8 builds the chunked path.

**Activations.** With per-layer remat, the saved state per layer is the layer input $[B, L, d_{model}]$ in bf16. For a microbatch of 8 x 768 that is 25 MB per layer, or 0.7 GB for 28 layers. One layer's internals are recomputed in the backward pass. The largest of them is the MLP hidden $[B, L, d_{ff}]$, 75 MB at the same shape (and there are three of that size: gate, up, and their product).

**Decode speed, a roofline estimate.** One decode step must read all the weights plus each sequence's KV cache from GPU memory. The 4090 moves about 1 TB/s, so 3.44 GB of weights alone cost at least 3.4 ms per step. At B=64 with an average context of 400 tokens, the cache adds $64 \cdot 400 \cdot 114{,}688 \approx 2.9$ GB, about 6.4 GB per step in total. That is roughly 6.4 ms per step, or about 10k tokens/s at best. For comparison, vLLM recorded 12,727 tokens/s on the week-0 noise run (`gen_tokens_per_s` in `runs/week0_noise_test_qwen3-1_7b_s0/meta.json`). It beats this estimate because it batches more sequences per step. An MVP at a few thousand tokens/s is acceptable. That run produced 2,000 completions averaging 215 tokens (p95 393), about 430k tokens, so one noise seed takes about 2 to 3 minutes at 3k tokens/s.

sections.heading: A KV-cache sampler with static shapes
sections.md:
JAX compiles one program per combination of input shapes, dtypes and static values. A sampler that appends a token to an array of growing length therefore compiles a new program at every step. The design rule is that **every shape is fixed before the first token**, and progress lives in traced integers.

**State.** The cache is `[N_L, B, max_len, H_kv, d_h]` for K and the same for V, allocated once. There is also a boolean `kv_valid [B, max_len]` that says which slots hold real tokens. A prompt bucket has fixed length $P$. Each prompt is **left-padded** to $P$, so all prompts end at slot $P-1$ and every row writes its $i$-th new token at the same slot $P + i$. One shared write index lets you use `lax.dynamic_update_slice` at a traced index. Left padding also makes prefill's "last position" the same index $P-1$ for every row.

**Positions.** For a row with $n$ real tokens and $P - n$ pads, use `pos = cumsum(mask) - 1`, clipped at 0. The real tokens then get positions $0 \ldots n-1$. At decode step $i$, that row's position is $n + i$, while its slot is $P + i$. Example with $P = 8$: a 5-token prompt has positions [0,0,0,0,1,2,3,4] and its first new token gets position 5. An 8-token prompt gets position 8.

There is a second correct convention: use the slot index as the position everywhere, prompt and decode alike. The short row then has its real tokens at positions 3 to 7 and its first new token at 8. By the RoPE identity in section 2 only offsets matter, so a constant per-row shift is harmless. The bug is **mixing** the two: cumsum positions in prefill and slot positions in decode. The short row then puts its first new token at position 8 when its last prompt token was at 4. The distance is 4 instead of 1, an error of 3, which is the row's pad count. This is why batch-1 runs look perfect (no pads) and the shortest prompts in a padded batch produce garbage.

**Masks.** In prefill, query $t$ may attend to key $s$ only if $s \le t$ and slot $s$ is real. In decode, the single new query attends to every slot with `kv_valid` true, and that includes the slot just written. Forgetting the pad mask in decode, after applying it in prefill, lets real tokens attend to pad slots. Again only short rows break.

**NaNs from padding.** A pad query row in prefill has every key masked. With an additive $-\infty$ mask, its softmax is $0/0 =$ NaN. That pad position's hidden state becomes NaN, so from layer 1 on the K/V computed there and written into the cache are NaN. Later, a real query gives that slot weight $p = 0$, but $0 \times \text{NaN} = \text{NaN}$, so the real row goes NaN too. Anything that reduces across rows, such as a mean loss or a global gradient norm, then spreads it to the whole batch. On CPU, one fully masked query row gave NaN with `-inf` and finite values with `jnp.where(mask, s, -1e30)`. Use all three defenses:

1. Use `jnp.where(mask, s, -1e30)`. A finite value keeps the softmax finite, and `where` also replaces a NaN score, which an additive mask cannot.
2. Zero the K/V written at pad positions.
3. Keep `kv_valid` false for those slots.

**The decode loop.** `lax.while_loop` compiles the loop body once and runs it on device. A per-sequence `done` mask freezes finished rows, and the loop condition gives early exit when all rows are done. This code ran on CPU with a stub model that provides `decode_step`. Two seeds and two rows gave different tokens, and a second call with new seed and temperature did not recompile.

```python
from functools import partial

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("graphdef", "max_new"))
def decode(graphdef, state, cache, kv_valid, logits, pos, slot, key, temp, eos_id, max_new):
    model = nnx.merge(graphdef, state)        # params arrive as traced arguments
    B = logits.shape[0]
    toks = jnp.zeros((B, max_new), jnp.int32)
    lps = jnp.zeros((B, max_new), jnp.float32)
    done = jnp.zeros((B,), bool)

    def cond(c):
        i, *_, done = c
        return (i < max_new) & ~jnp.all(done)              # early exit

    def body(c):
        i, cache, kv_valid, logits, pos, toks, lps, done = c
        logp = jax.nn.log_softmax(logits.astype(jnp.float32) / temp, axis=-1)
        t = jax.random.categorical(jax.random.fold_in(key, i), logp)   # [B], rows differ
        lp = jnp.take_along_axis(logp, t[:, None], axis=-1)[:, 0]
        t, lp = jnp.where(done, eos_id, t), jnp.where(done, 0.0, lp)  # freeze finished rows
        toks, lps = toks.at[:, i].set(t), lps.at[:, i].set(lp)
        done = done | (t == eos_id)
        kv_valid = kv_valid.at[:, slot + i].set(True)
        logits, cache = model.decode_step(t, pos, slot + i, cache, kv_valid)
        return i + 1, cache, kv_valid, logits, pos + 1, toks, lps, done

    c = (jnp.int32(0), cache, kv_valid, logits, pos, toks, lps, done)
    i, *_, toks, lps, done = jax.lax.while_loop(cond, body, c)
    return toks, lps, done, i
```

Note what is static and what is traced. `max_new` and the graph definition are static. They fix shapes and code. The step `i`, the temperature, the slot, the positions and the key are traced, so changing them never recompiles. The `state` from `nnx.split(model)` is an argument, not a closure. If a jitted function closes over the parameters, they are captured as constants at trace time. That does not recompile, but the executable keeps using the old values after the weights change, which in RL means sampling from a stale policy. A greedy mode needs `jnp.where(temp > 0, sampled, argmax)` with a safe divisor, not a Python `if`.

Early exit helps less than you might hope. In week 0, 17 of 2,000 completions hit the 768-token cap (`finish_reason` "length"). With B=64, the chance that a batch holds at least one such row is $1 - (1 - 17/2000)^{64} \approx 0.42$, so 42% of batches run to the cap anyway. Length buckets and sorting by expected length help more.

**PRNG discipline.** Derive `key = fold_in(base_key, seed)` once per sampling seed, then `fold_in(key, i)` per decode step. A single `categorical` call over `[B, V]` draws independent noise per row, so duplicated prompts in a batch still get different samples. The classic bug is reusing one key across seeds, or across steps. Then all seeds produce identical samples. The noise floor across seeds drops to nearly 0 and looks like good news. It is a bug.

**Recompiles and the zero-recompile assertion.** If `jax_log_compiles` shows a compile at every decode step, there are three usual causes:

1. A Python loop that grows an array. Fix it with the preallocated cache and the while loop.
2. The step index, or another changing value, passed as a static argument. Make it a traced `jnp` scalar.
3. The jitted function rebuilt inside the loop, for example `jax.jit(lambda ...)` per call. Build it once at module level and pass params through `nnx.split`.

There is a subtler fourth cause. A Python `2.0` and `jnp.float32(2.0)` hash differently, because the Python float is weakly typed. On CPU, after warming up with `jnp.float32` scales, one call with a Python float scale triggered one extra compile. To turn "zero recompiles" into a test, count backend compiles with a monitoring listener. This works in the installed JAX (0.8):

```python
from jax import monitoring
compiles = [0]
def _count(event, duration, **kw):
    if event == "/jax/core/compile/backend_compile_duration":
        compiles[0] += 1
monitoring.register_event_duration_secs_listener(_count)

def test_zero_recompiles(sampler, batches):
    for b in batches: sampler(b, temp=jnp.float32(1.0), scale=jnp.float32(2.0))   # warm every bucket
    before = compiles[0]
    for b in batches:
        sampler(b, temp=jnp.float32(0.7), scale=jnp.float32(0.0))  # new values, same types
    assert compiles[0] == before
```

**Tests for the MVP.** Each batched row must equal its own batch-1 run, at temperature 0 in fp32 or on the log-probs of fixed tokens, and the batch must include one prompt that is mostly padding. Rows must stop at their own EOS and emit EOS with log-prob 0 afterwards. And the sampler's log-probs must match teacher forcing, which the next section explains.

sections.heading: The persistent compilation cache
sections.md:
Chapter 0 covered the in-process jit cache: a function is traced and compiled the first time it sees a given set of shapes, dtypes, static arguments and shardings, and later calls in the *same process* reuse the executable. That cache dies with the process. Every seed you launch, every resume after preemption and every eval job starts with empty caches, and XLA recompiles the prefill, every decode bucket and the train step. For a 1.7B model with scanned layers this can take tens of seconds to minutes per program. On the 4090 that is an annoyance. On a rented H100 billed by the hour, across 9 runs and 3 seeds, it costs real money. The persistent compilation cache writes compiled executables to disk, so the next process can load them instead of running XLA again.

**Turning it on.** Three settings matter, and all three must be set before the first `jit` call:

```python
import jax
jax.config.update("jax_compilation_cache_dir", "/path/to/jax_cache")
jax.config.update("jax_persistent_cache_min_compile_time_secs", 1.0)  # default 1.0
jax.config.update("jax_persistent_cache_min_entry_size_bytes", 0)     # default 0
```

The two thresholds decide what is worth writing. A program is cached only if compiling it took at least `min_compile_time_secs` and its serialized executable is at least `min_entry_size_bytes`. The defaults are right for real runs: the model programs take seconds to compile and get cached, while the many tiny `jit_add` and `jit_convert_element_type` programs JAX builds while initializing parameters do not clutter the directory. For a CPU demo, or to check that caching works at all, set the time threshold to `0.0`. Put these lines in the one entry module every script imports, next to the memory settings from week 0, and log the cache directory into `meta.json`.

**What the key contains.** Each entry's file name is `<program name>-<sha256>`. The hash covers everything that could make a stored executable wrong to reuse:

$$
\text{key} = H\big(\text{HLO module},\ \text{JAX / jaxlib / XLA version},\ \text{backend and device kind},\ \text{compile options and XLA flags},\ \text{device assignment}\big).
$$

The HLO already includes shapes, dtypes, shardings, donation and precision attributes. Setting `jax_default_matmul_precision` to `"highest"` in code adds `HIGHEST` to every `dot`, so the parity runs and the bf16 runs have separate entries. That is correct behavior, not a bug. Changing `XLA_FLAGS` also changes the key. I checked this on CPU: the same NNX MLP hit the cache on a second run, then missed and wrote a new entry when `XLA_FLAGS=--xla_cpu_use_thunk_runtime=false` was set.

**Confirming a hit.** Do not assume the cache works because the directory exists. Two logs tell you what happened. `jax_log_compiles=True` (or `JAX_LOG_COMPILES=1`) prints a line every time the in-process cache misses, that is, every time JAX traces and lowers. With the persistent cache on, the compiler logger also reports either `PERSISTENT COMPILATION CACHE MISS for 'jit_logits_fn' ...` followed by `Writing ... to persistent compilation cache`, or `Persistent compilation cache hit for 'jit_logits_fn' ...`. On a hit, the line `Finished XLA compilation` that follows reports almost no time. Tracing and lowering still happen on a hit, because the key is a hash of the lowered HLO and there is no other way to compute it. The cache saves XLA's time, not Python's. For a quieter check, set `jax_explain_cache_misses=True` once and grep the logs for `MISS` on the second launch of a job. After warm-up there should be none.

**Why a rented GPU or a TPU misses on the first run.** Device kind is part of the key. A cache filled on the 4090 (`sm_89`) holds nothing an H100 (`sm_90`) can use, and a TPU backend shares nothing with either. A different jaxlib build on the cloud image also changes the key, even when your own code is identical. So you cannot prewarm a cloud cache from home. The first job on new hardware always pays the full compile. The aim is to pay it **once per hardware type**, not once per seed. This is what Chapter 6's warning about device-kind misses refers to.

**Warming in a burst.** Compile every program the run will need ahead of time (AOT) from abstract shapes, before any real job starts. Then point every seed at the same cache directory, on the instance's persistent disk or in a GCS bucket (a `gs://` path works). With NNX, split once and lower a pure function from `jax.ShapeDtypeStruct`s, one per bucket:

```python
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp
from flax import nnx

graphdef, state = nnx.split(model)

@jax.jit
def logits_fn(state, ids):
    return nnx.merge(graphdef, state)(ids)

abstract = jax.tree.map(lambda a: jax.ShapeDtypeStruct(a.shape, a.dtype), state)
for L in (128, 256, 512):  # every sampler/trainer bucket
    logits_fn.lower(abstract, jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((4, L), jnp.int32)).compile()
```

No weights are loaded and no data is touched, so this runs in a few minutes at the start of the burst. Then run it on CPU with a small model, as I did: the warm process logs three `MISS` and `Writing` lines, and a fresh process that calls `logits_fn` with real arrays logs three hits and no compilation. Two caveats apply. First, the abstract structs must match the real call exactly, including sharding on multi-device runs and `donate_argnums`. Otherwise the real call gets a different key, and the warm-up was wasted. Second, the zero-recompile assertion from section 5 still matters: the persistent cache makes a recompile cheaper but does not prevent one, and an unexpected shape still costs tracing, lowering and a disk lookup on every occurrence.

sections.heading: The sampler-trainer log-prob contract
sections.md:
Policy-gradient RL with stale samples uses the per-token importance ratio

$$
\rho_t = \frac{\pi_\theta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})}{\pi_{old}(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})}
$$

where $\pi_{old}$ must be **the distribution the tokens were actually drawn from**. The trainer computes the numerator by teacher forcing. The sampler supplies the denominator. Write the sampling temperature as $\tau$. The contract:

> For every sampled token, the sampler returns $\log \mathrm{softmax}(z/\tau)[y_t]$ over the **full, untruncated** vocabulary. The trainer computes the same quantity with the same $\tau$, chat template, token IDs and masks. Tokens after EOS are masked on both sides.

**Why truncation breaks it.** Top-p or top-k sampling draws from a renormalized distribution $q(y) = \pi(y)/Z_t$ on a kept set $S_t$ with mass $Z_t \le 1$, and $q(y) = 0$ elsewhere. Nucleus sampling with $p = 0.8$ keeps the smallest set with mass at least 0.8, so $Z_t \in [0.8, 1]$. It is near 1 for confident tokens and near 0.8 for uncertain ones. Both ways of reporting the log-prob then go wrong.

- *The sampler reports $\log q$.* At zero updates ($\theta = \theta_{old}$) the trainer's ratio is $\pi/q = Z_t$ on every kept token, not 1. On an uncertain token with $Z_t \approx 0.8$ the ratio is already at the edge of a PPO clip range of $[0.8, 1.2]$. The sequence ratio is $\prod_t Z_t$. Even an average $Z_t$ of 0.99 over a 215-token completion gives $0.99^{215} \approx 0.12$. The policy has not moved, and the loss already reports a large change.
- *The sampler reports $\log \pi$ but samples from $q$.* The ratio is 1 at zero updates, but the gradient estimate $\mathbb{E}_{y \sim q}[A\,\nabla \log \pi_\theta(y)]$ is an expectation under the wrong distribution. Tokens outside $S_t$ are never sampled, so the gradient never learns anything about them, and nothing corrects for it.

So **RL rollouts use top-p = 1 and top-k off**. Temperature is allowed, because $\mathrm{softmax}(z/\tau)$ is a proper distribution over the whole vocabulary. The trainer must divide by the same $\tau$. Sampling at 0.7 and training on $\log \mathrm{softmax}(z)$ is the same kind of bug.

**Eval-only top-k/top-p.** Evaluation needs the week-0 decoding config (temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20, as recorded in the noise-run `meta.json`) so that noise floor v2 is comparable with vLLM's. Take `lax.top_k` first, then apply nucleus filtering inside those k values. A candidate is kept if the mass strictly before it is below p, so the token that crosses p stays in. Never sort all 151,936 logits per step. On CPU, with probabilities (0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05), this sampler drew the first two tokens at about 0.63 and 0.37 and never drew the others.

```python
def sample_topk_topp(key, logits, temp, k=20, p=0.8):   # eval only: logits [B, V]
    vals, ids = jax.lax.top_k(logits.astype(jnp.float32) / temp, k)   # sorted, descending
    probs = jax.nn.softmax(vals, axis=-1)
    before = jnp.cumsum(probs, axis=-1) - probs          # mass strictly before each candidate
    vals = jnp.where(before < p, vals, -1e30)
    j = jax.random.categorical(key, vals)                # index into the k candidates
    return jnp.take_along_axis(ids, j[:, None], axis=-1)[:, 0]
```

Keep this path behind a flag that the RL code cannot set.

**The residual you should expect.** Even with a correct contract, the sampler computes logits incrementally from a bf16 cache, while the trainer runs a full forward pass. The kernels and the accumulation order differ, so the log-probs differ slightly. The acceptance test is a mean abs difference of at most about 1e-2 in bf16 between sampler log-probs and teacher-forced log-probs on the same token IDs, at temperature 1 and at 0.7. A mean $|\Delta \log \pi| = 0.01$ means per-token ratios around $e^{\pm 0.01} \approx 1 \pm 0.01$, far inside a 0.2 clip. Record the measured value. In week 4 it is your numerical floor, and ratio deviations smaller than it carry no information about policy change.

sections.heading: Your own LoRA, and the reference policy as a traced value
sections.md:
**The gradients at initialization, derived.** For one adapted linear map with scale $s = \alpha / r$,

$$
h = W x + s\,B A x, \qquad A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{in}},\; B \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{out} \times r}
$$

Let $g = \partial L / \partial h \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{out}}$ and $u = A x \in \mathbb{R}^r$. Then $h_i$ depends on $B_{ij}$ through $s\,B_{ij} u_j$, so $\partial L/\partial B_{ij} = s\,g_i u_j$. In matrix form:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial B} = s\,g\,(A x)^\top
$$

For $A$, the gradient reaches $u$ through $B$: $\partial L / \partial u = s\,B^\top g$. Since $u_j = \sum_k A_{jk} x_k$,

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial A} = s\,B^\top g\,x^\top
$$

At step 0, $B = 0$, so $\partial L / \partial A = 0$ exactly, while $\partial L / \partial B \ne 0$ (A is random, so $A x \ne 0$). **Only B moves on the first step.** On CPU, with a 64 to 32 layer, the gradient for A was exactly 0.0, and the gradient for B was nonzero and matched $s\,(xa)^\top g$ to 0.0 in the row-vector convention below. Adam's first update is about $\eta \cdot \mathrm{sign}(g)$ per element, because $\hat m / \sqrt{\hat v} = g/|g|$ at $t = 1$. So after step 0 every entry of B has magnitude about the learning rate, and from step 1 on A receives gradient too. The design consequence: at initialization $\Delta W = 0$, so a fresh RL adapter on the merged-SFT base starts exactly at the reference policy.

**The scale must be traced.** The RL step needs two forward passes in one program: policy ($s = \alpha/r$) and reference ($s = 0$). If $s$ is a Python attribute, jit treats it as a constant. Toggling it either recompiles or, worse, silently reuses the executable traced with the old value. Pass it as an array argument threaded down to every LoRA layer.

```python
class LoRALinear(nnx.Module):
    """Stores a = A^T [d_in, r] and b = B^T [r, d_out] (row-vector convention, like nnx.LoRA)."""
    def __init__(self, base: nnx.Linear, r: int, rngs: nnx.Rngs):
        d_in, d_out = base.kernel.shape
        self.base = base
        self.a = nnx.LoRAParam(nnx.initializers.he_uniform()(rngs.params(), (d_in, r), jnp.float32))
        self.b = nnx.LoRAParam(jnp.zeros((r, d_out), jnp.float32))

    def __call__(self, x, s):                     # s: traced fp32 scalar, alpha/r or 0
        z = (x @ self.a[...].astype(x.dtype)) @ self.b[...].astype(x.dtype)   # bf16 matmuls
        return self.base(x) + s.astype(x.dtype) * z

    def merged_kernel(self, s):                   # merge in fp32, cast once
        w = self.base.kernel[...].astype(jnp.float32) + s * (self.a[...] @ self.b[...])
        return w.astype(self.base.kernel.dtype)
```

The params are fp32 (so tiny Adam updates are not rounded away), and the matmuls run in bf16. Unmerge is the same expression with $-s$, applied to the fp32 kernel you kept, never to the bf16 one. Subtracting from a bf16 merged weight does not give back the original base.

**The five tests.**

1. *Identical to `nnx.LoRA`.* `nnx.LoRA` has no scale, so compare at $s = 1$. Copy `lora_a` and `lora_b` into your module and compare outputs. With equal params on CPU in fp32, the max difference was 0.0.
2. *Merged == unmerged.* `x @ merged_kernel(s)` against `module(x, s)` with a nonzero B. On CPU in fp32 the difference was 5.7e-6. In bf16, expect differences at the bf16 rounding level.
3. *Toggling scale does not recompile.* Use the compile counter from section 5. Call with `jnp.float32(2.0)`, then `0.0`, then `1.0`: one compile in total. At $s = 0$ the output must equal the base layer exactly, for any A and B.
4. *The merged export loads in HF with matching logits.* Transpose back to `[d_out, d_in]`, keep HF key names, write safetensors, load in `envs/torch`, and compare logits at the fp32 parity tolerance.
5. *Scale 0 on the merged-SFT base equals the SFT model.* Load the week-1 base and SFT adapter, compute log-probs on fixed sequences, merge (fp32, then bf16), add a fresh adapter, run with $s = 0$, and compare. The residual comes from casting the merged weight to bf16. Each merged element is rounded with relative error up to $2^{-8} \approx 0.4\%$, so expect a small, nonzero log-prob difference, and state its tolerance.

sections.heading: Chunked log-probs: why scan needs remat
sections.md:
The trainer needs only $\log \pi(y_t \mid \cdot)$ for the realized tokens, a $[B, L]$ array. With final hidden states $h_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{model}}$, tied embedding $E$ and temperature $\tau$:

$$
\log \pi(y_t) = \frac{z_{t, y_t}}{\tau} - \log \sum_{v=1}^{V} e^{z_{t,v}/\tau}, \qquad z_t = E\,h_t
$$

The obvious code computes $z$ for all tokens at once, and section 4 showed that this is 119.5 GB in fp32 at 256 x 768. The fix is to flatten the $B \cdot L$ tokens and process them in chunks of $C$ tokens. Each chunk computes $[C, V]$ logits, upcasts to fp32, takes the logsumexp and the target logit, and keeps only $[C]$ numbers.

**Why `lax.scan` alone does not save memory.** The forward pass of a scan is fine: each iteration's logits die at the end of the iteration. The backward pass is the problem. Reverse-mode autodiff needs, for each iteration, the residuals of that iteration's forward pass. For logsumexp the residual is the softmax $p = \mathrm{softmax}(z/\tau)$, because

$$
\frac{\partial \log \pi(y_t)}{\partial z_{t,v}} = \frac{1}{\tau}\big(\mathbb{1}[v = y_t] - p_{t,v}\big)
$$

JAX implements the scan backward pass by having the forward scan **stack every iteration's residuals** into an output of shape `[n_chunks, C, V]`. The total is the full tensor again, just built in pieces. You avoided materializing the logits as values and materialized them as residuals instead.

`jax.checkpoint` (or `nnx.remat`) on the chunk body changes what is saved. The only residuals are the body's inputs: the chunk of hidden states and targets. The embedding is loop-invariant, so it is not stacked. In the backward pass each chunk's logits are recomputed, used and freed. Peak memory becomes roughly one chunk's fp32 logits plus their gradient, plus the saved hidden states.

The numbers at 256 x 768 with chunks of 1,024 tokens:

- tokens: 196,608, so 192 chunks
- one chunk of fp32 logits: $1024 \cdot 151936 \cdot 4 = 622$ MB
- saved hidden states: $196{,}608 \cdot 2048 \cdot 2 = 0.8$ GB in bf16
- without remat, the stacked softmax: $192 \times 622$ MB = 119.5 GB

In practice you also microbatch the trainer, so the whole $B \cdot L$ is never in one call. The chunking still matters inside each microbatch: 8 x 768 x V in fp32 is 3.7 GB per copy.

```python
def chunked_logprobs(h, emb, targets, temp, chunk=1024, remat=True):
    """h [N, D] final-normed hidden (N = B*L flattened), emb [V, D], targets [N] -> [N] fp32."""
    N, D = h.shape
    hc, tc = h.reshape(N // chunk, chunk, D), targets.reshape(N // chunk, chunk)

    def body(carry, xs):
        h_i, t_i = xs
        logits = (h_i @ emb.T).astype(jnp.float32) / temp      # [chunk, V], lives one iteration
        lse = jax.nn.logsumexp(logits, axis=-1)
        tgt = jnp.take_along_axis(logits, t_i[:, None], axis=-1)[:, 0]
        return carry, tgt - lse

    if remat:
        body = jax.checkpoint(body)          # save only (h_i, t_i); recompute logits in backward
    _, lp = jax.lax.scan(body, None, (hc, tc))
    return lp.reshape(N)
```

Pad $N$ up to a multiple of `chunk`, and mask the padded positions in the loss, exactly like the week-1 masked log-prob. The value test compares against the naive `log_softmax` at a small shape. On CPU at the shape below the max difference was 1.9e-6. Use the same $\tau$ as the sampler.

**The memory test.** Compile the gradient and read XLA's own accounting:

```python
loss = lambda h: chunked_logprobs(h, emb, t, jnp.float32(1.0), remat=r).sum()
ma = jax.jit(jax.grad(loss)).lower(h).compile().memory_analysis()
assert ma.temp_size_in_bytes < bound
```

On CPU with $N = 8192$, $V = 32768$, $d_{model} = 256$ and chunks of 1,024, temp memory was **1,153 MiB without remat and 256 MiB with remat**. The full-vocab version was 1,024 MiB, which is exactly $N \cdot V \cdot 4$ bytes. The scan without remat was *worse* than not chunking at all, because it stacks the residuals and also needs working buffers. One fp32 chunk is 128 MiB, so the remat version sits at two chunks (logits and their gradient), as predicted. Write the test with a bound derived from the chunk size, for example 3 chunks plus the saved inputs. Then it fails if someone removes the checkpoint.

sections.heading: Resume, the two-level bootstrap, and noise floor v2
sections.md:
**What a checkpoint must contain.** A resumed run must be the same run. List everything that determines the next step:

- LoRA params in fp32: `nnx.state(model, nnx.LoRAParam)`. The frozen base is not saved. It is reloaded from safetensors.
- Optimizer state: `nnx.state(opt)`. In Flax 0.12 it holds `step` and `opt_state`, with Adam's `count`, `mu` and `nu` per LoRA leaf.
- The PRNG key, saved as `jax.random.key_data(key)` and restored with `jax.random.wrap_key_data` (typed keys are not plain arrays), or the base seed if every key is derived by `fold_in(step)`.
- The data-order state: epoch, shuffle seed, and position in the epoch.
- The config hash, so a resume with a changed config fails loudly.

This round trip ran on CPU with a toy model and `nnx.Optimizer(model, optax.adam(1e-2), wrt=nnx.LoRAParam)`. Three steps, save, restore into a fresh model, and three more steps gave losses and LoRA params bitwise equal to six uninterrupted steps.

```python
import orbax.checkpoint as ocp
mngr = ocp.CheckpointManager(ckpt_dir, options=ocp.CheckpointManagerOptions(max_to_keep=2))
state = {"lora": nnx.state(model, nnx.LoRAParam), "opt": nnx.state(opt),
         "key": jax.random.key_data(key), "data_pos": jnp.int32(pos)}
mngr.save(step, args=ocp.args.StandardSave(state)); mngr.wait_until_finished()
# resume in a new process: build the same structure from a fresh model and optimizer, then
abstract = jax.tree.map(ocp.utils.to_shape_dtype_struct, state)
restored = mngr.restore(mngr.latest_step(), args=ocp.args.StandardRestore(abstract))
nnx.update(model, restored["lora"]); nnx.update(opt, restored["opt"])
key, pos = jax.random.wrap_key_data(restored["key"]), int(restored["data_pos"])
```

**The test.** Run A takes $2N$ steps uninterrupted. Run B takes $N$ steps, saves, and is killed (a subprocess with `SIGKILL`, not a polite exit). A new process restores and runs $N$ more steps. Compare the final LoRA params, the optimizer state, and the per-step losses after the restore point. Require bitwise equality if you enable deterministic GPU ops (`--xla_gpu_deterministic_ops=true` in `XLA_FLAGS`, set before importing jax; verify the flag for your version). Otherwise use `allclose` with a stated tolerance, because atomic-add reductions on GPU can change summation order between runs. Also test a kill in the middle of a save. Orbax writes to a temporary directory and finalizes it, so `latest_step()` should return the previous complete checkpoint. Verify that, do not assume it.

**What the failures look like in the loss curve.** Adam's update is $\eta\,\hat m / \sqrt{\hat v}$ with $\hat m = m/(1-\beta_1^t)$ and $\hat v = v/(1-\beta_2^t)$. If `count` restarts at 1 while $m$ and $v$ are warm, the factor in front of $m/\sqrt{v}$ becomes $\frac{1/(1-0.9)}{\sqrt{1/(1-0.999)}} = 10/31.6 = 0.32$ instead of about 1. Updates shrink about 3x and recover over hundreds of steps, and any warmup schedule keyed on the count restarts at LR 0. The curve flattens after resume. The opposite mistake keeps the count but zeroes $m$ and $v$. The first update is then $\eta \cdot 0.1 g / \sqrt{0.001 g^2} = 3.2\,\eta\,\mathrm{sign}(g)$, a step 3x larger than normal in every coordinate, and the loss spikes. A restarted PRNG or data iterator repeats the first batches, so the post-resume losses replay the early part of the run.

**Why item-only resampling understates uncertainty.** From week 4 on, comparisons have training seeds. Arm A has $S_A$ training runs, arm B has $S_B$, and all are evaluated on the same $N$ items. The estimated gain $\hat\Delta$ has variance from two independent sources, approximately

$$
\mathrm{Var}(\hat\Delta) \approx \frac{\sigma_d^2}{N} + \frac{\sigma_A^2}{S_A} + \frac{\sigma_B^2}{S_B}
$$

Here $\sigma_d$ is the SD of the per-item paired difference, and $\sigma_A$, $\sigma_B$ are the SDs of an arm's mean score across training seeds. The single-level paired bootstrap from week 1 treats each run as fixed, so it sees only the first term. Week 0 gives a calibration for that term. Pairing sampling seeds s0 and s1 of the same checkpoint, the per-item difference in pass@1 has SD 0.104, so the item term is $0.104/\sqrt{500} = 0.46$ pts. Compare that with a standard error of 2.1 pts for one arm's mean over the same 500 items (the CI half-width of about 4 pts in the week-0 report). That gap is why pairing matters. Now suppose, for illustration, that training seeds vary by $\sigma_A = \sigma_B = 1.5$ pts, which is not unusual for DPO or RL. With 3 seeds per arm, the seed terms add $\sqrt{2 \cdot 1.5^2/3} = 1.22$ pts. The total SE is $\sqrt{0.46^2 + 1.22^2} = 1.31$ pts, 2.8x the item-only value. An item-only CI would call a 1.5-pt gain clearly significant when it is not.

The two-level bootstrap resamples both sources: seeds within each arm independently, and one shared draw of items applied to both arms so the pairing is kept.

```python
def two_level_paired_bootstrap(A, B, n_boot=2000, seed=0):
    """A [S_a, N], B [S_b, N]: per-item scores per training seed, same item order."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    (Sa, N), Sb = A.shape, B.shape[0]
    diffs = np.empty(n_boot)
    for j in range(n_boot):
        sa, sb = rng.integers(0, Sa, Sa), rng.integers(0, Sb, Sb)   # seeds, per arm
        it = rng.integers(0, N, N)                                 # items, shared
        diffs[j] = (B[sb][:, it].mean(0) - A[sa][:, it].mean(0)).mean()
    lo, hi = np.quantile(diffs, [0.025, 0.975])
    per_seed = (B[:min(Sa, Sb)] - A[:min(Sa, Sb)]).mean(1)          # paired by seed index
    return {"diff": float((B.mean(0) - A.mean(0)).mean()), "ci95": [float(lo), float(hi)],
            "per_seed": per_seed.tolist(), "same_sign": bool(np.all(per_seed > 0) or np.all(per_seed < 0))}
```

With 3 seeds, a resample of seeds is one of only $\binom{3+3-1}{3} = 10$ multisets per arm, so the seed part of the CI is coarse. That is why the protocol also requires the same sign on every seed and a gain above 2x the noise floor. Pytests pin the function down. With zero seed variance (identical rows), it must match `paired_bootstrap` up to Monte Carlo error. With injected per-seed offsets, the CI must get wider. On synthetic data with 500 items, identical rows gave a CI of [0.33, 2.05] pts against [0.27, 2.04] for `paired_bootstrap`, and offsets of plus or minus 2 pts widened it to [-1.5, 3.9] and made `same_sign` false.

**Noise floor v2.** The noise floor is a property of the sampler, so it is re-measured now. Use the week-0 protocol exactly: test split, 4 samples per item, seeds 0 to 2, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20 (your eval-only path), 768 max tokens, the same chat template (`enable_thinking=False`) and extractor. Write `completions.jsonl` and `meta.json` in the same format and score with `harness/score.py`. Week 0 predicted about 0.42 pts and measured 0.17 pts with vLLM. Expect the same order of magnitude, and a mean close to 45.8% basic pass@1. Your RNG differs from vLLM's, so check agreement with a paired bootstrap, not equality. An SD near 0 is not good news. It almost always means key reuse. Check that the samples for one item differ across seeds and across duplicated rows, that per-item pass rates are not all 0 or 1, and that temperature is actually applied (no argmax path at $\tau > 0$). Record the new sampler name and version in the results row.

chapters.lab:
Work in this order. Each step's test is the oracle for the next. Keep `harness/` jax-free. The new JAX code goes in top-level packages (`model/`, `sampler/`, `lora/`, plus a `logprob` module and a `ckpt` module), with tests under `tests/`.

**Mon AM (about 3 h): statistics and the OOD freeze**
1. Confirm the OOD split. Running `python3 -c "import json; d=json.load(open('data/splits.json')); print(len(d['ood']))"` should print 163. Check that `git diff data/splits.json` is empty after your work.
2. Add `two_level_paired_bootstrap` (section 9) to `harness/stats.py`. Add tests to `tests/test_harness.py`. With identical seed rows the result must match `paired_bootstrap` within about 0.3 pts. With per-seed offsets of plus or minus 2 pts the CI must be wider. Also test that `same_sign` is false when one seed flips. Run `uv run --project envs/jax pytest tests/test_harness.py -q`.
3. If weeks 1-2 ran in TRL, port the masked log-prob function and its tests now.

**Mon PM to Tue: model and parity (timebox 1.5 days)**
4. In `envs/torch`, write a script that loads Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B from the local cache in fp32 with TF32 off and saves, for 20 fixed chat-templated prompts (use MBPP dev prompts from `harness/prompts.py`), the token IDs, the full logits, and the hidden state after every layer to `.npz`. Also save 50 greedy 64-token continuations with the top-2 logit gap at every step. Save bf16 logits on the same prompts too.
5. Write `model/qwen3.py` (RMSNorm, rope, attend, Attention, MLP, Block, Qwen3) and `model/load.py` with the regex name map. Make the loader raise on unmapped, missing and extra keys. Expect 311 HF keys, with `lm_head.weight` asserted equal to the embedding, 310 loaded arrays and 1,720,574,976 parameters.
6. Write `tests/test_parity.py`. Set `jax_default_matmul_precision` to `highest` at the top, before any tracing. Check the fp32 max abs logit diff (target 1e-4 to 1e-3), per-layer hidden diffs, greedy identity on at least 95% of 50 prompts with the top-2-gap rule at the first divergence, and bf16 teacher-forced top-1 agreement of at least 99% plus the mean abs log-prob diff. Run it once at default precision too and record both numbers in the parity report.

**Tue PM to Wed: sampler MVP (timebox 2 days, due Wed evening)**
7. Add a `decode_step(tok, pos, slot, cache, kv_valid)` method to the model, and a prefill that returns `[B, V]` logits at the last position only.
8. Write `sampler/` with one left-padded bucket, cumsum positions (the same convention in prefill and decode), the `kv_valid` mask, `-1e30` masking via `jnp.where`, zeroed pad K/V, and the `while_loop` from section 5. Before allocating the cache, print its expected size (`2 * 28 * B * max_len * 8 * 128 * 2` bytes) and check it against the summed `nbytes` of the K and V arrays.
9. Tests: (a) teacher-forced vs sampler log-probs, mean abs at most 1e-2 in bf16 at temperature 1 and 0.7; (b) each batched row equals its batch-1 run, with one prompt that is mostly padding; (c) per-row EOS with log-prob 0 after done; (d) two seeds and two duplicated rows give different tokens at temperature 1; (e) zero recompiles after warmup, using the monitoring listener; (f) no NaN anywhere in the output with a batch that contains a mostly-pad row.

**Wed to Thu: LoRA, chunked log-prob, checkpoints**
10. Write `lora/` with `LoRALinear` and the scale threaded through the model call as a traced array. Add the five tests from section 7 (test 1 at scale 1, since `nnx.LoRA` has no scale). For test 4, export the merged weights with HF names and `[d_out, d_in]` layout, then compare logits in `envs/torch`. For test 5, use the week-1 Orbax adapter.
11. Write the chunked log-prob and two tests. The values must match the naive log-softmax at a small shape. `memory_analysis().temp_size_in_bytes` with remat must be below a bound of about 3 chunks plus the inputs, while the no-remat variant is above it. Record both numbers (on CPU at N=8192, V=32768, chunk 1024 they were 256 MiB and 1,153 MiB).
12. Write the Orbax save/restore and a kill-and-resume pytest that runs training in a subprocess, sends SIGKILL after the step-N save, resumes in a new process, and compares against an uninterrupted 2N-step run. Add a variant that drops the Adam `count` and confirm that the test fails.

**Thu to Fri: polish, budget, overnight**
13. Add length buckets (128/256/512 prompt lengths), early exit, and the eval-only `lax.top_k` plus nucleus sampler behind a flag the RL code cannot set. Rerun the zero-recompile test across all buckets.
14. Write the memory budget note: weights 3.44 GB, LoRA + Adam 280 MB, KV 112 KiB per token (64 x 768 = 5.6 GB, 256 x 768 = 22.5 GB), prefill logits only at the last position, chunked training logits, and remat activations. Compare it with `peak_bytes_in_use` from `jax.devices()[0].memory_stats()` after prefill, measured in a fresh process.
15. Overnight: noise floor v2. Run the test split, n=4, seeds 0-2, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20, max 768 tokens, writing `runs/week3_noise_test_qwen3-1_7b_s{0,1,2}/completions.jsonl` and `meta.json` in the week-0 format (generator = your sampler name and version). Score with `python -m harness.score runs/week3_noise_test_qwen3-1_7b_s0/completions.jsonl`, and the same for each seed. Commit from a clean tree first, so the results rows carry a real SHA. Compare SD and mean against 0.17 pts and 45.8%.

Anything unfinished in steps 13-15 goes into the week-4 Mon to Tue AM overflow list.
takeaways: Read every architecture choice off config.json and the HF code, and learn each mistake's symptom: uniform small error means precision, error growing with position means RoPE, error only in padded rows means masks or positions.
Run fp32 parity at 'highest' precision on both sides, judge fp32 greedy divergences by the top-2 gap, and test bf16 with teacher-forced top-1 agreement, never greedy identity.
Qwen3-1.7B needs 112 KiB of KV cache per token, 4x Qwen2.5-1.5B, so 256 x 768 (22.5 GB) does not fit next to 3.44 GB of weights on a 24 GB card, while 64-96 x 768 does.

A sampler that never recompiles fixes every shape up front (preallocated cache, left-padded buckets, while_loop) and passes params, step, temperature and LoRA scale as traced arguments of fixed dtype.

RL rollouts sample with top-p = 1 and top-k off, and the sampler returns untruncated log_softmax(logits/temperature) log-probs whose small bf16 gap from teacher forcing is logged as the numerical floor for importance ratios.
With B = 0 at init only B gets gradient on step 0, so a fresh adapter starts exactly at the reference policy, and a traced scale of 0 gives that reference without a second model or a recompile.
lax.scan stacks per-iteration residuals for the backward pass, so chunked log-probs save memory only when the chunk body is under jax.checkpoint.
A resume test compares against an uninterrupted run and must restore Adam's count, the PRNG key and the data position, and a multi-seed comparison needs a bootstrap over seeds as well as items.

chapters.title: Policy gradients you can trust
chapters.subtitle: Before you spend GPU nights on Qwen3-1.7B RL, check the estimator math on a toy problem, test every loss term against numbers you worked out by hand, and build one sample-verify-train process that fits in 24 GB and runs fast enough.
chapters.why:
Weeks 5, 6 and 8 each spend several nights, and some cloud money, on RL runs. Suppose the advantage has a NaN path, the KL term pushes down the wrong divergence, or gradient accumulation quietly reweights tokens. Those runs still produce curves. The curves just mean nothing, and you will not find out until a write-up fails review. This week moves each of those failure modes somewhere it is cheap to catch: a toy run with about 1M parameters, a categorical policy whose gradient you can compute exactly, and pytests that check numbers you worked out by hand.

This is also the week that tests research-engineer judgment most directly. A frontier-lab RE is expected to derive why an estimator is unbiased, say which divergence a loss actually minimizes, do the memory and FLOP arithmetic before launching, and pre-register choices so the result can be defended. You finish the week with a tested loss module, a pipeline that survives repeated sample-train cycles at the full week-5 config, a measured throughput number, and your weeks 1-2 headline re-run under the seed protocol.

sections.heading: The score-function gradient and why a baseline is free
sections.md:
Start with one prompt $x$. The policy $\pi_\theta$ samples a completion $y$, the verifier returns $r(x,y) \in \{0, 1\}$, and we want to raise the expected reward

$$
J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)}[r(x,y)] = \sum_y \pi_\theta(y \mid x)\, r(x,y).
$$

The reward is a test-harness result, so you cannot differentiate it. Move the gradient onto the probability instead, using $\nabla \pi = \pi \nabla \log \pi$:

$$
\nabla J = \sum_y \nabla \pi_\theta(y \mid x)\, r(x,y) = \sum_y \pi_\theta(y \mid x)\, \nabla \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x)\, r(x,y) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta}[r(x,y)\, \nabla \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x)].
$$

For a completion, $\log \pi(y \mid x) = \sum_t \log \pi(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})$. So the score is a sum of the per-token gradients you already compute in SFT. REINFORCE is SFT on your own samples, weighted by reward.

**The score has mean zero.** The rest of the chapter depends on this line:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi}[\nabla \log \pi(y)] = \sum_y \pi(y) \frac{\nabla \pi(y)}{\pi(y)} = \nabla \sum_y \pi(y) = \nabla 1 = 0.
$$

**Baselines.** Replace $r_i$ by $r_i - b$. If $b$ is independent of the sample $y_i$, then

$$
\mathbb{E}[b\, \nabla \log \pi(y_i)] = \mathbb{E}[b]\; \mathbb{E}[\nabla \log \pi(y_i)] = 0,
$$

so the expected gradient does not change. Independence is the condition that matters. A constant is independent of $y_i$. So is a value computed only from the other samples, because the $G$ samples for one prompt are drawn i.i.d.

**Leave-one-out (RLOO).** Draw $G$ samples. For sample $i$, use the mean of the other $G-1$ rewards: $b_i = \frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{j \ne i} r_j$. Those rewards do not depend on $y_i$, so the estimator stays unbiased.

**The include-self mean.** Now use $\bar r = \frac{1}{G}\sum_j r_j$, which contains $r_i$. The independence argument no longer applies, so do the algebra. Write $S_{-i} = \sum_{j \ne i} r_j = (G-1) b_i$:

$$
r_i - \bar r = r_i - \frac{r_i + S_{-i}}{G} = \frac{G-1}{G} r_i - \frac{G-1}{G} b_i = \frac{G-1}{G}(r_i - b_i).
$$

So the include-self estimator is exactly LOO times a constant. Its direction is unbiased, and its length is scaled by $(G-1)/G$, which is 0.875 at $G=8$. In effect it lowers the learning rate. It is not a different algorithm.

**Check the algebra numerically.** Take a 10-armed bandit with 3 rewarded arms, a uniform initial policy, $G = 8$, and 100,000 independent gradient estimates (the script is in the lab):

| advantage | mean of $\partial_{\theta_0}$ | true | total variance |
|---|---|---|---|
| none ($r_i$) | 0.0697 | 0.0700 | 0.0310 |
| LOO | 0.0699 | 0.0700 | 0.0247 |
| include-self mean | 0.0611 | 0.0700 | 0.0189 |

The include-self mean gives $0.0611 / 0.0700 = 0.873 \approx 7/8$ of the true gradient, and its variance is $0.875^2 \times 0.0247 = 0.0189$. Its variance is lower only because the gradient is shorter. Now add 1 to every reward, as a format bonus would. The no-baseline variance jumps from 0.031 to 0.211, while LOO stays at 0.0247, because $r_i - b_i$ cancels any offset shared by all samples. That is where the variance reduction comes from: the baseline removes the part of the reward that every sample shares.

**Dividing by the group std.** GRPO uses $(r_i - \bar r)/\sigma$, where $\sigma$ is the std of the group's rewards. $\sigma$ depends on every sample, $y_i$ included, and it changes from prompt to prompt. For binary rewards with pass fraction $p$, $\sigma = \sqrt{p(1-p)}$. A prompt at $p = 1/2$ gets weight $1/0.5 = 2$. A prompt at $p = 1/8$ gets $1/0.331 = 3.0$. So the update is a reweighted sum over prompts that favors nearly-solved and nearly-unsolved prompts. You can defend that choice, but it is not an unbiased estimate of $\nabla J$, so you pre-register it.

sections.heading: Group advantages by hand, and the 0/0 trap
sections.md:
With binary rewards every advantage has a closed form. Let $c$ of the $G$ samples pass and write $p = c/G$.

**GRPO, population std** (divide by $G$). Here $\bar r = p$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{p(1-p)}$, so a passing sample gets $A_+$ and a failing sample gets $A_-$:

$$
A_+ = \frac{1 - p}{\sqrt{p(1-p)}} = \sqrt{\frac{1-p}{p}}, \qquad A_- = \frac{-p}{\sqrt{p(1-p)}} = -\sqrt{\frac{p}{1-p}}.
$$

**GRPO, ddof=1** (divide by $G-1$, which is `torch.std`'s default). The std grows by $\sqrt{G/(G-1)}$, so every advantage shrinks by $\sqrt{(G-1)/G}$. At $G=8$ that factor is 0.935. Pick one convention, write it down, and test it.

**RLOO.** A passing sample sees $c-1$ passes among the other samples, and a failing one sees $c$:

$$
A_+ = 1 - \frac{c-1}{G-1} = \frac{G-c}{G-1}, \qquad A_- = -\frac{c}{G-1}.
$$

By the identity in section 1, this also equals $\frac{G}{G-1}(r_i - \bar r)$.

**No-std** (the Dr. GRPO flag): $A_i = r_i - \bar r$, so $1-p$ for a pass and $-p$ for a fail.

**Worked example**, $G = 8$ and $c = 2$, so $p = 0.25$:

| convention | pass | fail |
|---|---|---|
| GRPO, population std ($\sigma = 0.433$) | $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$ | $-0.577$ |
| GRPO, ddof=1 ($\sigma = 0.463$) | 1.620 | $-0.540$ |
| RLOO | $6/7 = 0.857$ | $-2/7 = -0.286$ |
| no-std | 0.750 | $-0.250$ |

Check that each row sums to zero over the group ($2 \times 1.732 - 6 \times 0.577 \approx 0$). Build the same table for $c=3$ yourself before you write the test.

**All-pass and all-fail groups.** If $c = 0$ or $c = G$, every $r_i - \bar r$ is 0, and so is $\sigma$. The correct advantage is exactly 0, because the group says nothing about which completion is better. Naive code computes $0/0 = $ NaN. One NaN in a 256-row batch turns every LoRA weight into NaN after a single Adam step.

There is a second, quieter trap. Even with `jnp.where(std > 0, ..., 0)`, the derivative of `jnp.sqrt` at 0 is infinite, and `where` does not stop a NaN from flowing backward through the branch it did not pick. The naive version below returns correct zeros in the forward pass, but `jax.grad` through it is NaN on the zero-variance group. The fix is the double-where pattern: also make the input to `sqrt` safe.

```python
import jax.numpy as jnp

def group_advantages(r, G, kind="grpo", ddof=0):
    """r: [P*G] rewards, grouped contiguously by prompt. Returns [P*G]."""
    r = r.reshape(-1, G).astype(jnp.float32)
    mean = r.mean(-1, keepdims=True)
    if kind == "none":
        a = r
    elif kind == "rloo":
        a = r - (r.sum(-1, keepdims=True) - r) / (G - 1)
    elif kind == "no_std":
        a = r - mean
    else:  # "grpo"
        var = ((r - mean) ** 2).sum(-1, keepdims=True) / (G - ddof)
        ok = var > 0
        std = jnp.sqrt(jnp.where(ok, var, 1.0))     # safe input: no inf grad
        a = jnp.where(ok, (r - mean) / std, 0.0)    # exact zeros, no NaN
    return a.reshape(-1)
```

On two groups of three with rewards `[1,0,0, 0,0,0]`, this returns `[1.414, -0.707, -0.707, 0, 0, 0]` for GRPO and `[1, -0.5, -0.5, 0, 0, 0]` for RLOO. `jax.grad` of its sum with respect to `r` is finite. A single-where version gives NaN in the last three entries. Your pytest asserts these numbers.

The gradient trap only fires when a cotangent reaches the advantage. In the loss the advantage is wrapped in `stop_gradient`, and binary rewards carry no gradient anyway. It does fire if something differentiable feeds the reward, such as a $\beta k_1$ penalty without `stop_gradient`, and it fires in your test. Use the double where and the `stop_gradient` together.

**How common are zero-variance groups on your spine?** Count them from the week-0 train-split samples (`runs/week0_sftpool_train_qwen3-1_7b`, 16 samples per prompt). For a prompt with $c$ passes out of 16, the chance that a random group of 8 is all-fail is $\binom{16-c}{8}/\binom{16}{8}$, and all-pass is $\binom{c}{8}/\binom{16}{8}$. Averaged over the 274 train prompts, 36.1% of groups are all-fail and 43.6% are all-pass, so **about 80% of groups at $G=8$ would carry zero signal**. Those samples used T=0.7, top-p 0.8 and top-k 20. RL rollouts at T=1 with no truncation are more diverse, so the real fraction will be lower. Still, log the zero-variance fraction from step 1. At the week-0 rate, only about 6 of the 32 prompts in a step teach anything.

sections.heading: KL to the reference: three placements, three different gradients
sections.md:
The reference $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is the merged-SFT model with the RL adapter at scale 0. You want to penalize $\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta \| \pi_{\text{ref}}) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\log \pi - \log \pi_{\text{ref}}]$. You only see samples from $\pi_\theta$, so you use a per-sample estimator. Write $\rho = \pi_{\text{ref}}(y)/\pi_\theta(y)$ for one sampled token or sequence.

- $k_1 = \log \pi - \log \pi_{\text{ref}} = -\log \rho$. Unbiased for the KL value. It can be negative and has high variance.
- $k_3 = \rho - 1 - \log \rho$. Always $\ge 0$, since $\log u \le u - 1$. Also unbiased: $\mathbb{E}_\pi[\rho] = \sum_y \pi_{\text{ref}}(y) = 1$, so $\mathbb{E}[k_3] = \mathbb{E}[k_1]$. Low variance.

Both are fine numbers to **log**. The question is what happens when you **differentiate** them. Autodiff does not know the samples came from $\pi_\theta$. It only differentiates the expression you wrote. Keep the true target in view:

$$
\nabla\, \mathrm{KL}(\pi \| \pi_{\text{ref}}) = \sum_y \nabla\pi\,(\log \pi - \log \pi_{\text{ref}}) + \sum_y \pi\, \nabla \log \pi = \mathbb{E}_\pi[k_1 \nabla \log \pi] + 0.
$$

**Placement 1: $k_1$ as a loss term.** $\nabla k_1 = \nabla \log \pi$, because $\log \pi_{\text{ref}}$ does not depend on $\theta$. Its expectation is the mean of the score, which is 0. On average it does nothing and only adds noise.

**Placement (a): $\beta k_1$ inside the reward, with no gradient.** Use $r - \beta\, \mathrm{sg}(k_1)$ as the reward, where sg is `stop_gradient`. Its policy-gradient term is $-\beta\, \mathbb{E}[k_1 \nabla \log \pi]$, which is exactly $-\beta \nabla \mathrm{KL}(\pi \| \pi_{\text{ref}})$ by the line above. For sequences, use the completion's summed per-token $k_1$, so that the penalty is the sequence-level KL. The baseline from section 1 then also centers the KL term.

**Placement (b): $k_3$ as a loss term** (DeepSeekMath GRPO). Differentiate it. $\log \pi_{\text{ref}}$ is constant, and $\nabla \rho = -\rho \nabla \log \pi$:

$$
\nabla k_3 = \nabla \rho - \nabla \log \rho = -\rho\, \nabla \log \pi + \nabla \log \pi = (1 - \rho)\, \nabla \log \pi.
$$

Take the expectation under $\pi$. The $\nabla \log \pi$ term is the score mean, which is 0. The other term is

$$
-\mathbb{E}_\pi[\rho\, \nabla \log \pi] = -\sum_y \pi_{\text{ref}}(y)\, \nabla \log \pi(y) = \nabla \Big[ \sum_y \pi_{\text{ref}} (\log \pi_{\text{ref}} - \log \pi) \Big] = \nabla\, \mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\text{ref}} \| \pi).
$$

So $k_3$ estimates one KL, but its gradient pushes down the other. When $\pi \approx \pi_{\text{ref}}$ the two KLs agree to second order, which is why it works in practice. They diverge when the policy moves far from the reference, which is exactly when you need the penalty. A related fact: $k_2 = \frac12 (\log \pi - \log \pi_{\text{ref}})^2$ has gradient $k_1 \nabla \log \pi$, so as an on-policy loss it gives the same gradient as placement (a).

**Test it on a categorical policy.** Use five logits $\theta$, a fixed $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ and 200,000 samples. The exact gradients come from `jax.grad` of the closed-form KLs. To set a tolerance you need per-sample gradients, and `vmap(grad)` gives them without building a $200{,}000 \times 200{,}000$ Jacobian:

```python
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp

theta = jnp.array([0.3, -0.2, 0.5, 0.0, -1.0])
ref = jax.nn.log_softmax(jnp.array([0.0, 0.1, -0.3, 0.2, 0.4]))
M = 200_000
a = jax.random.categorical(jax.random.key(0), theta, shape=(M,))

def kl(t):        # exact KL(pi || ref)
    lp = jax.nn.log_softmax(t); return (jnp.exp(lp) * (lp - ref)).sum()
def kl_rev(t):    # exact KL(ref || pi)
```
