chapters.title: Agents as token-ID environments
chapters.subtitle: Build a frozen task set, a blind sandbox, a token-exact multi-turn rollout and an eval with a matched-budget control, so week 8 has something trustworthy to train on.
chapters.why:
Week 8 runs RL on multi-turn episodes. RL optimizes whatever the environment actually rewards. It also trusts whatever sequence the rollout hands the trainer. This week you build both halves: the tasks and checker that define reward, and the rollout that defines the sequence. If the checker can be gamed, week 8 learns the game. If the rollout re-tokenizes text, week 8 computes ratios and masks on tokens nobody sampled. Neither failure crashes anything. Both show up only as curves that look a little worse than they should.

Agent environments and agent evals are now a large part of frontier-lab RE work. The skills tested in interviews and on the job are the ones in this chapter: keeping data as token IDs end to end, sandboxing untrusted code from a GPU process, keeping a jitted rollout at a fixed set of shapes, and designing a comparison whose control actually isolates the claim. A claim like "tools help by 15 points" without a matched-budget control is the kind of result a careful reviewer throws out.
prereqs: Ch 0: unbiased pass@k, bootstrap CIs over items, frozen ID splits and the plus_compatible list
Ch 0: why threads that launch fresh subprocesses are safe after importing jax, and what the rlimit sandbox does not protect against
Ch 0: Qwen3-1.7B memory arithmetic (3.44 GB bf16 weights, 112 KiB of KV cache per token)
Ch 1: masked per-token log-probs and why prompt positions contribute exactly 0
Ch 3: the KV-cache sampler (left-padded buckets, per-sequence done mask, untruncated log-probs) and the zero-recompile assertion
Ch 4-5: the importance ratio and KL term in the GRPO loss
Ch 6: the stricter held-out verifier gap as a hacking signal

sections.heading: An episode is a list of token IDs
sections.md:
An agent episode on this spine is a short loop. The policy $\pi_\theta$ reads a prompt $x$ and writes text that ends in a tool call. The environment runs the call and inserts the result. The policy continues. After at most 3 turns the episode ends and a checker assigns the reward $r(x, y)$.

Write the whole episode as one sequence of token IDs $c = (c_1, \dots, c_{|c|})$. Some IDs were sampled by the policy. The rest were inserted by the environment: the system block, the user prompt, chat-template headers and tool outputs. Call the set of policy positions $\mathcal{P}$. Week 8 trains on

$$\log \pi_\theta(y \mid x) = \sum_{t \in \mathcal{P}} \log \pi_\theta(c_t \mid c_{<t}).$$

Every term conditions on the exact prefix $c_{<t}$ the sampler saw. So the list the sampler produced and the list the trainer scores must be the same integers, and $\mathcal{P}$ must be known exactly. Text is a view of that list for humans. It is never the source of truth.

**What Qwen3 sees.** With `enable_thinking=False`, the prompt "Write f." renders to 15 IDs:

```
151644 872 198 | 7985 282 13 | 151645 198 | 151644 77091 198 | 151667 271 151668 271
<|im_start|>user NL | Write f . | <|im_end|> NL | <|im_start|>assistant NL | <think> NL NL </think> NL NL
```

Tool calls in Qwen3's trained format are JSON between `<tool_call>` (151657) and `</tool_call>` (151658), each followed or preceded by a newline. Results go back inside a user turn, wrapped in `<tool_response>` (151665) and `</tool_response>` (151666). Declaring one `run_tests(code)` tool in the system block costs about 140-160 tokens depending on the description (139 with a one-line description; measure yours, section 5 budgets 158). JSON escaping also inflates code: an 11-token function becomes a 27-token call object.

**Break 1: BPE is not concatenation-invariant.** Measured with the Qwen3 tokenizer in envs/jax:

| piece a | piece b | enc(a) + enc(b) | enc(a + b) |
|---|---|---|---|
| code fence (3 backticks) | two newlines | [73594, 271] | [13874, 19324] |
| `return x` + newline | newline + `<tool_response>` | [689, 856, 198, 198, 151665] | [689, 856, 271, 151665] |
| `print(1)` + newline | newline | [1350, 7, 16, 340, 198] | [1350, 7, 16, 692] |
| 4 spaces | 4 spaces + `return` | [257, 262, 470] | [286, 470] |
| `x =` | ` 1` | [87, 284, 220, 16] | [87, 284, 220, 16] |

The sampler can emit the first row's left side: the fence token then a double newline. Decoding gives the text of a fence plus two newlines, and re-encoding gives [13874, 19324], two IDs neither of which was sampled. The second row is the tool boundary. Append the tool text to the decoded history and the policy's last newline merges with the newline that opens the response. One sampled token disappears.

**Break 2: re-applying the template rewrites history.** Render user, assistant (with a tool call) and tool through `apply_chat_template`. The earlier assistant turn comes back without its empty think block. The template emits `<think>\n\n</think>\n\n` only for the turn being generated. For an earlier turn with no reasoning it drops it. The sampler saw those 4 IDs [151667, 271, 151668, 271] at the start of every turn. Re-templating deletes them, so every later position shifts by 4 per earlier assistant turn.

**What week 8 would compute.** On a re-tokenized $c'$ the ratio becomes

$$\rho_t = \exp\big(\log \pi_\theta(c'_t \mid c'_{<t}) - \log \pi_{\text{old}}(c_t \mid c_{<t})\big).$$

Numerator and denominator refer to different tokens and different prefixes, so $\rho_t$ is not an importance ratio for any action. The KL estimate is wrong the same way. The logged spans are now off by 4, so the mask trains on the tail of the tool output, which the policy never chose, and skips the first policy tokens of the next turn. Nothing crashes. The loss is just noisier and slightly biased.

**The rule.** The tokenizer splits special tokens out before BPE runs, so no merge crosses a special token. Build the context by concatenating ID lists. Encode each environment string once, on its own, between special tokens or fixed newline IDs. Never encode concatenated history. Log every span.

```python
IM_START, IM_END, NL = 151644, 151645, 198
TOOL_CALL_END, TOOL_RESP, TOOL_RESP_END = 151658, 151665, 151666
THINK_EMPTY = [151667, 271, 151668, 271]        # <think> NL NL </think> NL NL

def enc(s):            # one call per env string, never on concatenated history
    return tok.encode(s, add_special_tokens=False)

def header(role):      # <|im_start|>role NL
    return [IM_START] + enc(role) + [NL]

def user_turn(text):
    return header("user") + enc(text) + [IM_END, NL]

def gen_prompt():      # what the sampler sees before every assistant turn
    return header("assistant") + THINK_EMPTY

def tool_turn(content_ids):   # inserted after the policy stops on </tool_call>
    return ([IM_END, NL] + header("user") + [TOOL_RESP, NL] + content_ids
            + [NL, TOOL_RESP_END, IM_END, NL] + gen_prompt())

def test_single_turn_matches_hf_template():
    msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT}]
    ref = enc(tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, add_generation_prompt=True,
                                      enable_thinking=False, tokenize=False))
    assert user_turn(PROMPT) + gen_prompt() == ref
```

Both checks pass on the real tokenizer: the single-turn test, and a tool-turn test that renders user, assistant tool call and tool message with `apply_chat_template(..., tools=..., enable_thinking=False)` and compares everything after the last `</tool_call>` with `tool_turn(enc(output))`. `tool_turn` adds exactly 18 wrapper IDs around the content. Strip leading and trailing whitespace from the tool output before encoding it. In your ID list the wrapper newlines are separate IDs either way, but the HF template renders newline + content + newline as one string, so a content that starts or ends with a newline would merge there (198, 198 becomes 271) and the parity test would fail.

sections.heading: Tasks and checkers before any agent code
sections.md:
On Monday, before you write the environment, freeze the tasks. Each task record holds:

- `id` and `split` provenance (the source MBPP ID and its splits.json split)
- `prompt`: the MBPP text plus the one visible example assert, as in week 0
- `visible_test`: that same assert, the only test the tool may run
- `hidden`: the other two MBPP asserts plus the MBPP+ test
- `reference` and `known_wrong` solutions

**Where tasks come from.** Eval tasks come from test, restricted to the 165 plus_compatible test IDs, so the hidden checker is strictly stronger than anything the tool can run. Sample 75 with a fixed seed. Apply the prompt cap from section 5 (226 tokens including the 12 chat-template IDs). The longest test prompt is 1765 tokens, but the longest plus_compatible test prompt is 204, so the cap excludes none of the 165; keep the filter anyway so the invariant is checked. Warm-start and week-8 training tasks come from train only (274 items, 55 of them plus_compatible). Freeze both lists as new splits.json keys.

**Why the checker must be stronger than the tool.** Week 0 gives a single-turn baseline for this gap. On the 165 plus_compatible test items with seed s0 (4 samples each), 427 of 660 samples pass the visible assert (64.7%). Only 361 pass the full checker, all three asserts plus MBPP+ (54.7%). So 66 of 427 visible passes (15.5%) fail what they cannot see. That gap exists before any agent loop. A tool that lets the model iterate on the visible test will push visible-pass up, and some of that will not transfer.

Now suppose the tool ran the full checker. The agent could then retry until it passes. With $K$ attempts, success approaches the probability that any attempt passes. On the same week-0 data, any-of-3 is 61.2% against 54.5% for the first sample. Part of the tools arm's gain would be retry-with-oracle, which no deployment has. RL would also reward hardcoding the tested cases, since each tested input is visible in the output. Keep the tool's tests a strict subset: the shown assert, or tests the agent writes itself. Report, per arm, how often the final code passes the visible test but fails the checker. Week 8 tracks the same number as its hacking signal.

**The checker can be gamed today.** `harness/verifier.py` returns pass whenever the process exits with code 0. Run these through `run_program`, each followed by a failing assert, and all three return `{'status': 'pass'}`:

```python
# 1. exit before the asserts run
import sys; sys.exit(0)
# 2. same, bypassing SystemExit handlers
import os; os._exit(0)
# 3. an object equal to everything
class E:
    def __eq__(self, other): return True
def add(a, b): return E()
```

Week-0 numbers are fine, since a sampled model is not searching for these. RL will search. Two fixes cover the cheap cases. First, a completion nonce: the parent passes a random nonce on stdin (today it passes `DEVNULL`), the runner reads it before executing the program and prints it only after `exec` returns, and it treats `SystemExit` raised by candidate code as an error. The parent requires return code 0 and the nonce at the end of stdout. Second, reject results whose type the candidate defined. The asserts are plain program text, so there is no result object to inspect until you rewrite `assert a == b` into a call:

```python
# end of _sandbox_runner.py (tested with all three hacks and an int subclass)
nonce = sys.stdin.readline().strip()       # read before candidate code runs
sys.stdin.close()
_exit = os._exit                           # keep a reference before the guard

class _Eq(ast.NodeTransformer):            # assert a == b  ->  assert __eq_check(a, b)
    def visit_Assert(self, n):
        t = n.test
        if isinstance(t, ast.Compare) and len(t.ops) == 1 and isinstance(t.ops[0], ast.Eq):
            n.test = ast.Call(ast.Name("__eq_check", ast.Load()), [t.left, t.comparators[0]], [])
        return n

def __eq_check(out, exp):
    if type(out).__module__ == "__main__":  # class defined by the candidate
        raise TypeError(f"candidate-defined result type {type(out).__name__}")
    return out == exp

tree = ast.fix_missing_locations(_Eq().visit(ast.parse(src)))
try:
    exec(compile(tree, "program.py", "exec"), {"__name__": "__main__", "__eq_check": __eq_check})
except SystemExit as e:
    print(f"SystemExit({e.code}) in candidate", file=sys.stderr)
    _exit(3)
sys.stdout.write(nonce + "\n")
sys.stdout.flush()
```

MBPP+ tests compare through their own `assertion(out, exp, atol)` helper, and its `out != exp` is also fooled by `E` (the default `__ne__` inverts `__eq__`), so put the same type check at the top of that helper when you build the plus program.

This is not airtight. In-process code can inspect the runner's frames and find the nonce, or return a builtin type with a wrong value that happens to compare equal. The goal is to close the hacks a policy finds by accident. Week 8's tampering probe measures the rest.

After changing the runner, re-score every baseline (week-0 rule). Each task then gets two pytests: the reference passes the checker, and `known_wrong` fails it. A good known-wrong is the reference with one edit that still passes the visible test, such as an off-by-one on a boundary case. Add a leakage test: no hidden test string appears in the prompt, and (once the env exists) in no tool output of any saved trajectory.

sections.heading: A sandbox that is bounded and blind
sections.md:
The threat model changes this week. A sampled model writes code that is wrong by accident. A model under RL writes whatever earns reward. So the sandbox needs two properties. It is **bounded**: no execution can exhaust the machine. It is **blind**: the code cannot see or edit the checker.

**Bounded.** Keep the week-0 rlimits: `RLIMIT_AS` 4 GB, `RLIMIT_CPU` timeout+1, `RLIMIT_FSIZE` 16 MB, no core files. Add three things.

- **Kill the process group, not the child.** On timeout, `subprocess.run(..., timeout=...)` kills the direct child only. The guard sets `os.fork` to None, but `import posix; posix.fork()` still works, and grandchildren outlive the timeout. Use `Popen(start_new_session=True)` and `os.killpg(p.pid, SIGKILL)` on timeout. bwrap's `--die-with-parent` and its pid namespace also kill everything when the leader dies.
- **Cap process count correctly.** `RLIMIT_NPROC` counts every process and thread of your user ID, not just the sandbox's. Set it to 64 on a desktop that already runs 500 processes and every fork or thread creation inside the sandbox fails, legitimate ones included. Use a cgroup instead: `systemd-run --user --scope -p TasksMax=64 ...` caps the subtree.
- **Block the network.** rlimits cannot. A network namespace can.

**Blind.** Run a program through the current runner and see what it allows. `open('/home/pika/learn/ai-overview/data/items.jsonl').read()` works from inside it, and that file contains every hidden test and MBPP+ test. Under a tool that returns stdout, the agent can print the checker into its own context. It can also overwrite the file. The fix is a mount namespace that exposes only the interpreter, the venv and a fresh work dir. This command works on this machine:

```bash
PY=$(readlink -f envs/jax/.venv/bin/python)      # uv-managed interpreter
UVPY=$(dirname $(dirname $PY)); VENV=$(realpath envs/jax/.venv)
bwrap --unshare-all --die-with-parent --new-session \
  --ro-bind /usr /usr --symlink usr/lib /lib --symlink usr/lib64 /lib64 \
  --symlink usr/bin /bin --ro-bind $UVPY $UVPY --ro-bind $VENV $VENV \
  --proc /proc --dev /dev --tmpfs /tmp --bind $WORK /work --chdir /work \
  $VENV/bin/python -I -B /work/runner.py /work/program.py 5 4096
```

Inside it, numpy imports and a socket connect raises OSError (network unreachable). The repo directory exists only as the empty parents of the venv mount (listing it shows just `envs`), so `data/items.jsonl` raises FileNotFoundError, and writing into the venv fails with a read-only file system. The checker never runs inside the episode. After the episode, the final code goes to a separate checker process built from task files the agent's work dir never contained.

**Safe from a JAX process.** The rollout process holds a CUDA context. Forking it can deadlock on locks XLA threads held at fork time (chapter 0). The week-0 pattern still works: a `ThreadPoolExecutor` whose threads call `Popen` on a fresh `bwrap ... python -I`. The child is a new exec'd interpreter with no JAX state. A `multiprocessing` pool with `spawn` or `forkserver` is also fine, as long as workers never import jax.

**Truncate in ID space.** A tool output of 50 000 characters would break both the context budget and the shape plan. Encode the output once, then keep a head and a tail, because a traceback's last lines carry the error:

```python
MARKER = enc("[... truncated ...]")    # 5 IDs

def tool_content_ids(text, budget=222, head=48):
    ids = enc(text.strip())
    if len(ids) <= budget:
        return ids
    tail = budget - head - len(MARKER)
    return ids[:head] + MARKER + ids[-tail:]
```

The result has at most `budget` IDs. The truncated IDs are inserted as they are. They are never decoded and re-encoded. Log `len(ids)` before truncation so the taxonomy can count truncated outputs.

**The acceptance test.** One pytest submits four programs through the tool: one reads the checker file by absolute path, one loops forever, one fork-bombs with `posix.fork`, one allocates 10 GB. Assert, respectively: file not found, timeout within timeout+1 s with no surviving processes in the group, contained by TasksMax, MemoryError reported as error. Run it from a process that has already imported jax.

sections.heading: What re-prefilling costs
sections.md:
Multi-turn v1 re-prefills the full context every turn through the prefill path you tested in week 3. The alternative, in-cache continuation, keeps the KV cache and appends only the new tokens. Decide between them with arithmetic.

**FLOPs per prefill.** A dense forward pass costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token. Attention adds the score and value products. Per layer, $QK^\top$ and $AV$ each cost $2T^2 H d_h$ without a causal mask, and the mask halves the useful work:

$$F_{\text{prefill}}(T) \approx 2NT + 2 N_L T^2 H d_h .$$

With $N = 1.72 \times 10^9$, the linear coefficient is $3.44 \times 10^9$ FLOP per token. The quadratic coefficient is $2 \cdot 28 \cdot 16 \cdot 128 = 114\,688$ FLOP per token pair. Using all 1.72B parameters overcounts: sampling needs logits only at the last position, so the 311M-parameter tied head ($V \cdot d_{\text{model}}$) runs once, not $T$ times, and the per-token coefficient is closer to $2.82 \times 10^9$. The estimates below keep $2N$ as a round upper bound.

**A 3-turn trajectory.** Take contexts of 600, 1200 and 1800 tokens.

- Linear term, re-prefill: $3.44 \times 10^9 \times (600 + 1200 + 1800) = 3.44 \times 10^9 \times 3600 = 1.24 \times 10^{13}$ FLOP.
- Quadratic term: $\sum T^2 = (0.36 + 1.44 + 3.24) \times 10^6 = 5.04 \times 10^6$, times $114\,688$, is $5.8 \times 10^{11}$ FLOP, about 5% of the linear term.
- Total: about 13.0 TFLOP.
- Prefilling each token once (the in-cache ideal): $3.44 \times 10^9 \times 1800 + 114\,688 \times 1800^2 = 6.19 + 0.37 = 6.6$ TFLOP.

Re-prefill does about twice the work. In general, with $K$ turns of equal increment $\Delta$, re-prefill processes $\Delta K(K+1)/2$ tokens against $\Delta K$ once. The linear overhead factor is $(K+1)/2$: 2x at $K = 3$, 5.5x at $K = 10$. The quadratic term of re-prefill grows like $K^3$, against $K^2$ for prefilling once.

**Wall time.** The 4090's dense bf16 peak is about 165 TFLOP/s. Assume 40% of that in practice, 65 TFLOP/s. Then 13.0 TFLOP takes 0.20 s per trajectory. For 75 tasks x 3 trials = 225 trajectories, that is 45 s per arm. In-cache continuation would save about half: roughly 22 s per arm.

**Compare with decode.** Decode is bandwidth-bound. Each step reads all weights (3.44 GB, shared by the batch) plus every sequence's KV cache. KV is $2 \cdot N_L \cdot H_{kv} \cdot d_h \cdot 2\,\text{bytes} = 2 \cdot 28 \cdot 8 \cdot 128 \cdot 2 = 114\,688$ bytes per token.

- At $B = 1$: about 3.5 ms per step at 1008 GB/s. Three turns of about 300 tokens is 900 steps, or 3.2 s. That is 16 times the trajectory's re-prefill.
- At $B = 32$ with a mean context of 1200: $3.44 + 32 \cdot 1200 \cdot 114\,688 / 10^9 = 3.44 + 4.40 = 7.8$ GB per step, about 7.8 ms. The step's compute, $2N \cdot 32 \approx 0.11$ TFLOP, takes about 1.7 ms at 65 TFLOP/s, so bandwidth still binds. 900 steps is 7 s per batch. Re-prefilling the same 32 trajectories is $32 \times 0.20 = 6.4$ s.

So at small batch, decode dominates. At $B = 32$ the two are comparable. Either way a full arm is a minute or two of GPU time.

**Memory.** Re-prefill needs no extra persistent state. A cache of 2432 slots at $B = 32$ is $32 \cdot 2432 \cdot 114\,688 = 8.9$ GB. With 3.44 GB of weights, about 12.4 GB, which fits in 24 GB. Never materialize full prefill logits: $[32, 2048, 151936]$ in bf16 is 19.9 GB.

**Decision.** In-cache continuation saves about 20 s per arm and costs one to two days of careful cache-indexing work. At 2-3 turns and under 2k tokens, it is a stretch goal. It pays off with many turns, long tool outputs, or large RL batches where prefill is a real share of step time. Check this with a profiler trace of one 3-turn rollout. Read the prefill share; do not assume it.

sections.heading: Shapes: a fixed, small set of programs
sections.md:
**The symptom.** The first multi-turn eval prints dozens of `Compiling jit(prefill)` lines per task. Every turn's context has a different length. A jitted function is cached by the shapes and dtypes of its inputs, so each new length is a new trace and a new XLA compile. The last batch of the task list has a different batch size, so it compiles again.

**Bound every length first.** You can only bucket what is bounded. With prompt cap $P$, per-turn generation cap $g$, tool budget $u$, $w = 18$ wrapper IDs per tool turn and $K$ turns, the longest final context is

$$T_{\max} = P + K g + (K - 1)(w + u).$$

Pick $P = 384$ (158 system tokens plus a templated prompt of up to 226, which covers the 99th percentile of 169 and every plus_compatible test prompt), $g = 384$, $u = 222$, $K = 3$. Then:

- context before turn 1: at most 384, bucket 512
- before turn 2: at most $384 + 384 + 18 + 222 = 1008$, bucket 1024
- before turn 3: at most $1008 + 384 + 240 = 1632$, bucket 2048
- final: at most $1632 + 384 = 2016$

The tool budget of 222 keeps turn 2 inside the 1024 bucket with 16 IDs of slack (the hard limit is 238). On week-0 dev samples ($n = 16$), a cap of 384 truncates 4.9% of single-turn completions (512 would truncate 1.2%). Log the truncation rate as a taxonomy category, not a silent cap.

**Left-pad to the bucket.** Left padding puts every sequence's last real token at index $b - 1$. Logits for the next token are then at a single static index for the whole batch. Decode then writes at a shared slot $b, b+1, \dots$, and only RoPE positions differ per sequence. Size the cache for the largest bucket plus one turn: $2048 + 384 = 2432$.

```python
BUCKETS, B, PAD = (512, 1024, 2048), 32, 151643

def pack(ctxs):
    L = next(b for b in BUCKETS if max(map(len, ctxs)) <= b)
    ctxs = ctxs + [[PAD]] * (B - len(ctxs))          # fixed batch: dummy rows
    tok = np.full((B, L), PAD, np.int32)
    mask = np.zeros((B, L), bool)
    for i, c in enumerate(ctxs):
        tok[i, L - len(c):], mask[i, L - len(c):] = c, True
    pos = np.maximum(np.cumsum(mask, 1) - 1, 0).astype(np.int32)   # RoPE counts real tokens
    return tok, mask, pos

@nnx.jit
def prefill(model, cache, tok, mask, pos):
    h, cache = model.forward_cached(tok, pos, mask, cache)  # your week-3 model
    return model.logits(h[:, -1]), cache                     # [B, V], last slot only
```

Expected compiles for the whole eval: three prefill programs (one per bucket, each writing into the same 2432-slot cache) and one decode loop for $(B = 32, \text{max\_len} = 2432)$ whose start slot is a traced argument. All of them happen in warmup. The model is a jit argument, never a closure (chapter 0: closed-over arrays become HLO constants). If `nnx.jit`'s Python overhead shows in the decode loop, use `nnx.split` once and a plain `jax.jit` over the state, as in week 3.

**What else silently retraces.** Measured on the installed JAX 0.12 and Flax 0.12:

- A plain Python int or float passed as a positional jit argument is traced as a weak-typed scalar. Calling with `turn = 0, 1, 2` compiles once, not three times. But a later call with `jnp.int32(turn)` is a different key (strong type) and compiles again. Pick one convention and use explicit `jnp.int32` / `jnp.float32` everywhere.
- A value marked static (`static_argnums`), closed over, or used as a Python shape compiles once per distinct value. Keep `gen_cap` and the turn index out of shapes; the `lax.while_loop` bound can be a traced array.
- A Python scalar stored as an attribute of an `nnx.Module` is part of the static graph. Setting `model.lora_scale = s` to three different floats produced three compiles of the same function. Store the LoRA scale and temperature as arrays (or `nnx.Variable`s).
- Stop IDs: pass one `jnp.array([151658, 151645, 151643], jnp.int32)` and test membership with `jnp.isin`, not a Python tuple whose length or contents may change.

**The assertion.** Count compiles with a logging handler. JAX logs `Compiling jit(<name>) with global shapes ...`. Filter on your own function names, because eager ops such as `convert_element_type` and PRNG setup also log compiles:

```python
class CompileLog(logging.Handler):
    def __init__(self): super().__init__(); self.msgs = []
    def emit(self, rec):
        m = rec.getMessage()
        if m.startswith("Compiling ") and ("jit(prefill" in m or "jit(decode" in m):
            self.msgs.append(m[:160])

jax.config.update("jax_log_compiles", True)
log = CompileLog(); logging.getLogger("jax").addHandler(log)
run_eval(tasks[:B])                    # warmup: touches every bucket
n_warm = len(log.msgs)
run_eval(tasks)                        # the real pass
assert len(log.msgs) == n_warm, log.msgs[n_warm:]
```

Warmup must touch every bucket, or the first long trajectory compiles mid-eval. A scripted warmup batch with contexts of 500, 1000 and 2000 dummy IDs guarantees it. When the assertion fails, turn on `jax_explain_cache_misses`. It names the argument whose shape, dtype, weak type or static value changed.

sections.heading: The rollout loop and its stop IDs
sections.md:
The orchestration is plain Python around the jitted sampler. Each turn: pack contexts, prefill, decode until a stop ID or the cap, append the sampled IDs, run tools for sequences that stopped on a tool call, append the tool IDs, repeat.

```python
def run_episode(task, sample, tool, max_turns=3, gen_cap=384):
    ctx = system_ids() + user_turn(task.prompt) + gen_prompt()
    spans, logps = [], []
    for turn in range(max_turns):
        out = sample(ctx, gen_cap)        # out.ids include the stop token itself
        spans.append(("policy", len(ctx), len(ctx) + len(out.ids)))
        ctx, logps = ctx + out.ids, logps + out.logps
        if out.ids[-1] != TOOL_CALL_END:  # answered, hit EOS, or hit the cap
            break
        call = parse_tool_call(out.ids)   # JSON; parse errors become an error string
        content = tool_content_ids(tool(call, task) if call else "error: invalid tool call")
        ins = tool_turn(content)
        spans.append(("env", len(ctx), len(ctx) + len(ins)))
        ctx = ctx + ins
    return dict(task_id=task.id, ids=ctx, spans=spans, logps=logps,
                turns=turn + 1, final_code=final_code(ctx, spans))
```

In the batched version, sequences that finish early stay in the batch as done rows. That keeps $B$ fixed and wastes a little compute. The stop token belongs to the policy span: the model sampled it, and week 8 trains on it. The `<|im_end|>` and newline after `</tool_call>` are inserted by the environment and sit in the env span. `parse_tool_call` may decode the policy span to read the JSON; that text is used only to run the tool and is never re-encoded into the context.

**The bug: invented tool results.** Trajectories run past the tool call, then the model writes `<tool_response>` itself, invents an output and answers. The stop check only looks for `<|im_end|>`. In Qwen3's trained format `</tool_call>` is usually followed by `<|im_end|>`, so the model often stops anyway. At temperature 0.7 it sometimes does not. With a home-made protocol the model was never trained on, such as a fenced "output" block, it almost never stops. The fix is per-sequence stop IDs inside the decode loop:

```python
# inside the lax.while_loop body, after sampling nxt: [B]
nxt = jnp.where(done, PAD, nxt)
is_stop = jnp.isin(nxt, stop_ids)           # stop_ids: traced int32 array
done = done | is_stop | (n_gen + 1 >= gen_cap)
```

Then run the real tool and insert its output where the template puts tool responses. Check that your token-level template matches Qwen3's for a tool turn, using the same `enable_thinking` setting you log. A mismatch moves the model off its trained format, and the tool-error rate is where it shows.

**The tests week 8 depends on.**

1. **Concatenation.** For every saved trajectory, `ids` equals the in-order concatenation of the prompt IDs, each policy span's sampled IDs and each env span's inserted IDs. The spans tile `[len(prompt), len(ids))` with no gap or overlap.
2. **Stop.** Drive the loop with a scripted fake policy that emits a tool call and then keeps emitting a fake `<tool_response>`. Assert the policy span ends exactly at 151658 and the next span is the logged env span with the real tool output.
3. **Template.** The single-turn test from section 1, plus the tool-turn test against `apply_chat_template` on a few tool outputs, including a multi-line traceback.
4. **Boundary.** A test that finds a case where decode-then-encode of a sampled policy span differs from the span. The first row of the table in section 1 is enough. This test documents why the others exist.
5. **Log-prob alignment.** `len(logps)` equals the number of policy positions. Teacher-forcing the saved `ids` through the trainer reproduces the sampler log-probs on policy positions within the week-3 tolerance (about 1e-2 mean abs in bf16).

Test 5 is the one that would catch re-templating: the 4-ID shift makes it fail on every multi-turn trajectory.

sections.heading: An eval that isolates execution feedback
sections.md:
**The confound.** Suppose LLM+tools beats LLM-only by 15 points. The tools arm got up to 3 turns, so it had more attempts and generated more tokens. The gain could come from extra samples or from self-revision, not from what the test output said. Week-0 data shows the extra-attempts effect alone is real. On the 165 plus_compatible test items, a single sample passes the checker 54.5% of the time. Take 3 independent samples and submit the first that passes the visible assert (else the first sample): 58.2%. That is +3.7 points with no feedback loop at all, using the same information the tool gives.

**The arms.** Run all of them on the same 75 task IDs, 3 trials each:

- **A, LLM-only:** one turn.
- **B, LLM+tools:** up to 3 turns; the tool runs the visible assert.
- **C, matched budget:** best-of-3 independent samples selected by the visible assert. Optionally also self-revision for 3 turns with no execution output inserted.
- **D, placebo (optional):** arm B with each tool output replaced by an uninformative string of the same token length. Turns, tokens and shapes stay fixed; only the information is removed.

Each hypothesis predicts a different ordering. If execution feedback matters, B beats C and D. If extra attempts explain the gain, B is about C. If extra tokens and reflection explain it, B is about D. Report tokens per task and turns used, so the claim is gain at a matched budget.

**The statistics.** For task $i$, compute the success rate over its 3 trials in each arm, $a_i$ and $b_i$, and the paired difference $d_i = b_i - a_i$. The estimate is $\bar d$. Its variance is

$$\operatorname{Var}(d_i) = \operatorname{Var}(a_i) + \operatorname{Var}(b_i) - 2\operatorname{Cov}(a_i, b_i).$$

MBPP tasks are bimodal: on dev at $n = 16$, 30.5% of items never pass and 32.5% always pass. Hard tasks are hard in both arms, so the covariance is large and pairing removes most of the variance.

Worked comparison at $n = 75$, $p = 0.5$:

- One proportion: $1.96\sqrt{0.25/75} = 1.96 \times 0.0577 = \pm 11.3$ points.
- Unpaired difference: $1.96\sqrt{2 \times 0.25/75} = \pm 16.0$ points.
- Paired: say tools gains $+2/3$ on 15 tasks, loses $1/3$ on 3, and ties on 57. Then $\bar d = (15 \cdot 0.667 - 3 \cdot 0.333)/75 = 0.12$. $E[d^2] = (15 \cdot 0.444 + 3 \cdot 0.111)/75 = 0.0933$, so $\operatorname{Var}(d) = 0.0933 - 0.0144 = 0.0789$ and $\operatorname{SD} = 0.281$. $SE = 0.281/\sqrt{75} = 0.0324$, so the CI is $12 \pm 6.4$, or $[5.6, 18.4]$.

The unpaired interval, $12 \pm 16$, includes 0. The paired one does not, and it is about 2.5 times narrower.

**Why not McNemar.** McNemar tests discordant pairs of single binary outcomes per item per arm. Three trials give a rate in $\{0, 1/3, 2/3, 1\}$, not a binary. McNemar applies only if you throw away trials 2 and 3. Use the paired bootstrap over tasks, or Wilcoxon signed-rank on $d_i$.

There is no training seed this week, so the protocol is a one-level paired bootstrap over task IDs. `harness/stats.py` already has `paired_bootstrap`, which resamples per-task rates. Resampling trials within each resampled task also captures completion-sampling noise:

```python
def paired_task_bootstrap(a, b, n_boot=10_000, seed=0):
    """a, b: [n_tasks, n_trials] 0/1 arrays, rows aligned by task ID."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    T, K = a.shape
    diffs = np.empty(n_boot)
    for j in range(n_boot):
        t = rng.integers(0, T, T)                        # resample tasks
        ka, kb = rng.integers(0, K, (2, T, K))           # resample trials within task
        ra = np.take_along_axis(a[t], ka, 1).mean(1)
        rb = np.take_along_axis(b[t], kb, 1).mean(1)
        diffs[j] = (rb - ra).mean()
    return float(b.mean() - a.mean()), np.quantile(diffs, [0.025, 0.975])
```

On a synthetic version of the worked example (the 15/3/57 split, ties at random 0 or 1) it returns $0.12$ with $[0.053, 0.196]$, slightly wider than the analytic $[0.056, 0.184]$ because of the within-task resampling. Resampling the two arms' tasks independently gives about $[-0.03, 0.28]$, the unpaired picture. With arms A-D you have up to 6 pairwise comparisons. Pre-register B vs C as the primary one, and apply Holm or label the rest exploratory.

**The table.** Per arm: success with bootstrap CI, paired difference vs A and vs C with CI, mean turns, tool-error rate (invalid JSON, crashed tool), tokens per task, visible-pass-but-checker-fail rate, decoding config and cost.

sections.heading: Failure taxonomy, LLM judges and the warm-start pool
sections.md:
**A taxonomy that points at levers.** Hand-code 50 failures, sampled across arms, blind to arm where you can. Write a one-line definition per category before coding. Each category should suggest a week-8 change:

| category | how you recognize it | week-8 lever |
|---|---|---|
| renamed function or missing helper | NameError on a name the tests reference (163 of the 174 week-0 dev NameErrors) | valid-call or format bonus |
| misread signature | TypeError (230 on week-0 dev) | none; capability |
| logic error | AssertionError on hidden tests | none; capability |
| overfit to visible test | passes visible, fails checker | hidden-test reward is already right; watch it |
| hardcoded visible case | literal of the visible output in code | tampering probe |
| invalid tool call | JSON parse error, wrong tool name | valid-call bonus, warm start |
| ignored feedback | resubmits identical code after a failing tool output | warm-start trajectories that use feedback |
| regression after feedback | turn 1 passes visible, final fails it | final-answer selection rule |
| ran out of turns or tokens | no final code, or generation cap hit | turn cap, gen cap |
| timeout | infinite loop in candidate | none; sandbox works |
| env or harness bug | wrong span, missing tool output | fix before week 8 |

The last row matters most. Every trajectory you code is also a test of the environment.

**Validating an LLM judge.** Use one only for a dimension the checker cannot see, such as "did the agent use the test output to fix its code". Hand-label 30-50 trajectories first, blind to arm, against a written rubric. Tune the judge prompt on about 10. Measure agreement on the rest. Raw agreement is inflated when one label dominates, so report Cohen's kappa:

$$\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}.$$

Worked example: 40 held-out labels, the judge agrees on 34, so $p_o = 0.85$. Hand labels say yes on 20; the judge says yes on 22. Then $p_e = (20/40)(22/40) + (20/40)(18/40) = 0.275 + 0.225 = 0.50$ and $\kappa = (0.85 - 0.50)/0.50 = 0.70$. Break agreement down by arm too. A judge that agrees on arm A but not arm B can manufacture a difference between them. For pairwise judgments, run both orderings and average them, because judges prefer one position. If kappa is low, drop the judge and use the hand labels or drop the dimension. Success is always decided by the code checker, never by the judge.

**The warm-start pool.** Overnight, sample $m$ attempts per train task with the tools arm and keep the successes, about 200 trajectories for week 8's SFT warm start. Success filtering is biased. A task with per-attempt success $p$ contributes $mp$ trajectories on average, so at $m = 8$ a task with $p = 0.9$ contributes 7.2 and one with $p = 0.1$ contributes 0.8. Easy tasks get 9 times the weight. They are also mostly one-turn successes, so the pool teaches little about using feedback.

Cap successes per task. With cap 2, the easy task contributes about 2. The hard task contributes $E[\min(X, 2)] = P(X \ge 1) + P(X \ge 2)$ with $X \sim \text{Bin}(8, 0.1)$:

$$P(X \ge 1) = 1 - 0.9^8 = 0.570, \quad P(X \ge 2) = 0.570 - 8(0.1)(0.9^7) = 0.570 - 0.383 = 0.187.$$

That is 0.76, so the ratio drops from 9x to 2.6x. Prefer trajectories that failed a tool run and then succeeded. Week 0 says what to expect: single-turn sampling at $n = 16$ solved 177 of 274 train prompts at least once under the full checker and left 97 unsolved. Record counts per task and per turn count, and report them.

Provenance check: every task ID in the pool is in the train split, and no eval task ID or hidden test string appears in any trajectory. If an API or teacher model writes trajectories, check its terms. Tokenize each segment once into the Qwen3 token-level template with logged spans. Label them off-policy: fine for SFT, but they have no sampler log-probs, so RL cannot use them directly. Report the source mix.

sections.heading: Stretch: in-cache continuation
sections.md:
Build this only after the eval table exists. The goal: after a tool call, append the inserted IDs and the next turn to the existing KV cache instead of re-prefilling.

**What must be per-sequence.** In a ragged batch, each sequence's real length differs after the first turn. You need:

- a write position `start: [B] int32`, the next free cache slot of each sequence
- a RoPE position `rope: [B] int32` that counts only real tokens
- a validity mask `valid: [B, T_max] bool` over cache slots

One scalar position breaks as soon as two sequences have different lengths. Their new keys land at the wrong slots and get the wrong rotation.

**Writing under jit.** Pad each appended chunk to a fixed bucket $C$, right-padded with a chunk mask. Write it with a vmapped `dynamic_update_slice`:

```python
def write_chunk(ck, cv, valid, k_new, v_new, cmask, start):
    # ck, cv: [B, T_max, H_kv, d_h]  k_new, v_new: [B, C, H_kv, d_h]
    # cmask: [B, C] bool (real tokens first)  start: [B] int32
    upd = lambda c, x, s: jax.lax.dynamic_update_slice(c, x, (s, 0, 0))
    ck = jax.vmap(upd)(ck, k_new, start)
    cv = jax.vmap(upd)(cv, v_new, start)
    valid = jax.vmap(lambda m, x, s: jax.lax.dynamic_update_slice(m, x, (s,)))(
        valid, cmask, start)
    return ck, cv, valid, start + cmask.sum(1)   # next chunk overwrites the pad slots
```

RoPE positions for the chunk are `rope[:, None] + jnp.cumsum(cmask, 1) - 1`. The attention mask for chunk queries is `valid` (over keys) combined with causality inside the chunk.

> `dynamic_update_slice` clamps an out-of-range start so the slice fits. Writing a 4-slot chunk at position 8 into a 10-slot cache writes slots 6 to 9, not 8 to 11. It silently overwrites two real entries and raises no error. Size `T_max` to at least the largest final context plus one chunk bucket, and assert `start + C <= T_max` on the host, where the lengths are known. Alternatively use a scatter with `mode="drop"`.

**Holes.** If you advance `start` by $C$ instead of the real count, pad slots stay inside the cache between real entries. Then the mask has to exclude holes in the middle, not just at the end. Masking only a suffix gives wrong attention for every later token. Advancing by the real count avoids most holes, but the left padding from the first prefill and the per-sequence offsets still make the mask per-slot.

**The parity test.** Build a ragged batch of 3 sequences with different prompt lengths and different tool-output lengths, over 3 turns. For each sequence, compare against a fresh full prefill of the same concatenated token IDs:

- logits at every real position of the appended chunks, not just the last one
- log-probs of the next tokens
- every sequence in the batch, not just sequence 0 (sequence 0 is often the longest, where a scalar-position bug is invisible)

Use `jax_default_matmul_precision="highest"` and fp32, with a tight tolerance (around 1e-4 max abs; set it from a measured run). In bf16, check log-prob agreement within the week-3 sampler tolerance. Then rerun the zero-recompile assertion across turns: chunk buckets add a fixed number of programs, never one per turn.

chapters.lab:
Do these in order. Keep agent code outside `harness/` (which stays jax-free) except the stats helper, for example in `agent/`. Each step ends with a pytest under `tests/`.

   ```bash
   uv run --project envs/jax python -c "from harness.verifier import run_program as r; print(r('import sys\nsys.exit(0)\nassert False\n'), r('import os\nos._exit(0)\nassert False\n'))"
   ```
   Both print pass today. In `harness/verifier.py`, pass a `secrets.token_hex(16)` nonce as `input=` instead of `stdin=DEVNULL` and require it at the end of stdout. In `harness/_sandbox_runner.py`, add the nonce read, the SystemExit handling and the AST `assert a == b` rewrite with the candidate-type check; add the same check to the MBPP+ `assertion` helper. Add tests for all three hacks, the AlwaysEqual class and an `int` subclass with a lying `__eq__` to `tests/test_harness.py`. Re-score the week-0 runs with `uv run --project envs/jax python -m harness.score runs/<run>/completions.jsonl` and confirm the numbers barely move (they should; a sampled model does not exploit these).
3. **Task file (Mon).** Write `agent/tasks.py` to build `data/agent_tasks.jsonl` and two new splits.json keys: `agent_eval` (75 IDs sampled with a fixed seed from test ∩ plus_compatible, templated prompt ≤ 226 tokens) and `agent_train` (train only). Each record has id, split provenance, prompt, visible_test, hidden tests, reference and known_wrong. Write `tests/test_agent_tasks.py`: the reference passes the checker, known_wrong fails it while passing the visible test, the visible test appears in the prompt, and no hidden test string does.
4. **Sandbox.** Write `agent/sandbox.py` around the bwrap command from section 3 (it already works on this machine), plus `Popen(start_new_session=True)`, `os.killpg` on timeout and `systemd-run --user --scope -p TasksMax=64`. Write `tests/test_agent_sandbox.py` with the four attacks: read `data/items.jsonl` by absolute path, `while True: pass`, a `posix.fork` loop, `bytearray(10 << 30)`. Run it after `import jax`. Add a test that ID-space truncation keeps outputs within the 222-token budget.
5. **Token-level template (Tue AM).** Write `agent/template.py` with `user_turn`, `gen_prompt` and `tool_turn`. Test single-turn equality against `apply_chat_template(..., enable_thinking=False)`, tool-turn equality (everything after the last `</tool_call>` of a templated user / tool-call / tool conversation equals `tool_turn(enc(output.strip()))`), the 18-ID wrapper, and a boundary test showing encode(fence) + encode(two newlines) differs from encode of the joined string.
6. **Rollout (Tue).** Write `agent/env.py` on top of your week-3 sampler: buckets (512, 1024, 2048), B = 32 with dummy rows, cache max_len 2432, traced stop IDs [151658, 151645, 151643], gen cap 384, span and log-prob logging, LoRA scale and temperature as arrays rather than Python attributes. Tests: context equals the concatenation of spans; the scripted fake-policy stop test; teacher-forced log-probs match sampler log-probs on policy positions; the compile counter shows 3 prefill programs and 1 decode program, and zero new compiles on a second full pass.

8. **Eval (Wed-Thu).** Run arms A, B, C (D if time allows) on `agent_eval`, 3 trials each, using the week-0 decoding config (temperature 0.7, top_p 0.8, top_k 20). Save trajectories as JSONL (task_id, trial, ids, spans, logps, tool outputs, final_code, checker status, visible status). Add `paired_task_bootstrap` next to `paired_bootstrap` in `harness/stats.py` with a test, then write the table from section 7 into `runs/week7_agent_eval.md`, with a results row per arm carrying the 3.2.8 meta.
9. **Taxonomy (Thu).** Sample 50 failures across arms, hand-code them into the section-8 categories, and record counts per arm with example trajectory IDs. Fix any env-bug rows before going further. Run the leakage check over every saved tool output.
10. **Overnight: warm-start pool.** Run arm B on `agent_train` with m = 8 attempts, cap 2 successes per task, and prefer feedback-using trajectories. Plot histograms per task and per turn count. Run the provenance check (train IDs only, no hidden test strings).

12. **Stretch (Fri).** In-cache continuation, with the ragged 3-turn parity test and the clamp assertion.

Exit check: the eval table compares A, B and C on frozen tasks with paired CIs, the checker runs only after the episode and outside the tool's view, the taxonomy explains the main failures, and every saved trajectory passes the span and concatenation tests.
takeaways: A multi-turn episode is a list of token IDs with logged policy and environment spans; text is only a view, and re-tokenizing or re-templating it silently changes IDs (Qwen3 drops 4 think-block IDs per earlier turn).

Special tokens are split before BPE, so build contexts by concatenating ID lists and encoding each environment string once, and test the result against apply_chat_template for single-turn and tool turns.

The tool must run a strict subset of what the checker runs; on week-0 data, 15.5% of visible-test passes already fail the hidden checker, and the current exit-code checker can be passed by sys.exit(0), os._exit(0) or an always-equal object.
A sandbox for agents must be bounded (process-group kill, cgroup task cap, rlimits) and blind (a mount and network namespace that hides the checker and the repo).
At 3 turns and under 2k tokens, re-prefill costs about 2x the ideal prefill but only about 20 s per eval arm, so in-cache continuation is a stretch goal; the overhead factor (K+1)/2 grows with turns.

Bound every length (prompt cap, generation cap, tool budget), left-pad to a few buckets, keep the batch size fixed, keep static args and Python module attributes out of turn-varying values, then assert zero compiles after warmup.
A tools-vs-no-tools gain means nothing without a matched-budget control: best-of-3 by the visible test alone adds 3.7 points on week-0 data.
Pair by task: per-task rates from 3 trials, bootstrap over task IDs, no McNemar; in the worked example at n = 75 the paired CI is about 2.5 times narrower than the unpaired one.

chapters.title: Training an agent on tokens it did not write
chapters.subtitle: Multi-turn GRPO on Qwen3-1.7B: the loss mask and its three tests, KV and compile budgets, length bias across turns, and a shaped-reward experiment that a hacked bonus cannot win.
chapters.why:
Weeks 4-6 trained a policy whose rollouts were made only of its own samples. Week 7 built an agent whose episodes interleave model turns with tool output. This week puts the two together. The RL math barely changes. What changes is bookkeeping: which tokens the policy is responsible for, which length you normalize by, how many compiled programs a variable-length loop produces, and how the sampler's token IDs reach the trainer unchanged. Almost every multi-turn RL bug lives in that bookkeeping, and most of them do not crash anything. They show up as a reward curve that looks plausible and means nothing.

Frontier labs train agents this way at much larger scale, and the failure modes are the ones you will meet on a 4090: a mask off by one token, re-tokenized context, a shaping bonus that the policy harvests, seeds confounded with hardware. A research engineer is trusted when they can show with a test that the pipeline computes what the paper says, and when they design the comparison so that a hacked metric cannot pass for progress. This chapter teaches both, and it ends with scorecard row 3: does agent RL interest you enough to make it the capstone?
