Ch 3: KV-cache sampler with buckets, traced LoRA scale, chunked log-softmax, zero-recompile assertion, two-level paired bootstrap
Ch 4: GRPO and RLOO advantages, clipped surrogate, pre-registered KL placement (k1 in reward or k3 in loss), selective donation
Ch 5: the per-step logging set (zero-variance fraction, KL, entropy, sampler-trainer mismatch) and early-kill rules
Ch 6: Dr. GRPO length normalization, reward hacking, stricter held-out verifier
Ch 7: the token-ID multi-turn env with re-prefill, tool-output truncation, logged spans, and the ~200 warm-start trajectories

sections.heading: An episode is one sequence with two authors
sections.md:
In week 5 a rollout was a prompt followed by tokens the policy sampled. In week 8 a rollout is an **episode**: the prompt, then model turn 1, then tool output, then model turn 2, and so on, up to 2-3 model turns. Lay it out as one flat array of token IDs:

```
[system+user+assistant header] [model turn 1 ... <|im_end|>] [\n<|im_start|>user\n<tool_response>\n ... tool text ... \n</tool_response><|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\n] [model turn 2 ... <|im_end|>] ...
   env (prompt)                 model                          env (inserted)                                                                              model
```

Every token has exactly one author. The model wrote the turn bodies, including the `<|im_end|>` that ended each turn, because the sampler drew that token and stopped. The environment wrote everything else: the prompt, the template wrapper around each tool response, the tool text itself, the newline after `<|im_end|>` and the next assistant header (plus the empty `<think>\n\n</think>\n\n` block if you run Qwen3 in non-thinking mode).

Why does authorship decide the loss? Write the probability of a whole episode $\tau$. Let $M$ be the set of model positions and $E$ the set of env positions, and let $h_t$ be all tokens before position $t$:

$$
p_\theta(\tau) = \prod_{t \in M} \pi_\theta(\tau_t \mid h_t) \; \prod_{t \in E} P_{\text{env}}(\tau_t \mid h_t)
$$

Take the log and differentiate. The env factor does not depend on $\theta$: the sandbox returns the same stdout whatever the LoRA weights are. So

$$
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\tau) = \sum_{t \in M} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(\tau_t \mid h_t)
$$

The score-function (policy-gradient) identity then gives

$$
\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}_\tau\Big[A(\tau) \sum_{t \in M} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(\tau_t \mid h_t)\Big]
$$

The sum runs over model positions only. Including env positions would add $\nabla \log \pi_\theta(\text{tool text})$, which trains the model to *predict tool output*. That is a different objective. It teaches the model to hallucinate test results, and it is not the gradient of expected reward.

Now look closely at $h_t$. For a model token in turn 2, $h_t$ contains the tool output. The model computes keys and values at those tool positions with its own weights. So $\pi_\theta(\tau_t \mid h_t)$ depends on $\theta$ through the computation done *at* tool positions, even though no loss term sits there. Gradient flows into the LoRA weights of every layer through the K/V of tool tokens. That is correct and required: it is how the model learns to *read* a traceback.

> Do not "protect" tool tokens with `stop_gradient` on their hidden states or K/V. That computes the gradient of a different function, one where the model cannot learn how its reading of tool output affects its next action. The mask zeroes loss terms. It does not cut the graph.

Two consequences follow, and the rest of the chapter rests on them. First, the trainer must see exactly the IDs the sampler saw, because $h_t$ is part of what is being differentiated. Second, any test of the mask has to separate "tool tokens carry no loss" from "tool tokens influence nothing". The second statement is false, and a test that asserts it will fail on a correct implementation.

sections.heading: Keeping token IDs end to end
sections.md:
The episode is built in Python on the host, one turn at a time. The rule from week 7 is absolute: **append IDs, never re-render text.** The chat template is applied at the token level. You tokenize the fixed template pieces once, at startup, and you tokenize only the new tool text each turn.

The env also logs each inserted span at the moment it inserts it. The trainer will later build its loss mask by a different route, and test (c) compares the two.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Episode:
    segments: list[tuple[str, list[int]]] = field(default_factory=list)  # ("env"|"model", ids)
    env_spans: list[tuple[int, int]] = field(default_factory=list)       # [start, end), logged by env
    sampler_logp: list[float] = field(default_factory=list)              # one per model token
    n_ids: int = 0

    def add_env(self, ids: list[int]):
        self.env_spans.append((self.n_ids, self.n_ids + len(ids)))
        self.segments.append(("env", ids)); self.n_ids += len(ids)

    def add_model(self, ids: list[int], logp: list[float]):
        assert len(ids) == len(logp)
        self.segments.append(("model", ids)); self.n_ids += len(ids)
        self.sampler_logp += logp

# Built once from the tokenizer (special tokens are single IDs in Qwen3).
# TOOL_OPEN  = ids of "\n<|im_start|>user\n<tool_response>\n"
# TOOL_CLOSE = ids of "\n</tool_response><|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\n"
def tool_turn(tok, text: str, cap: int) -> list[int]:
    body = tok.encode(text, add_special_tokens=False)[:cap]  # truncate in IDs, not chars
    return TOOL_OPEN + body + TOOL_CLOSE
```

The loop is: `ep.add_env(prompt_ids)`, sample a turn, `ep.add_model(ids, logp)`, run the extracted code in the sandbox (`harness/verifier.py` `run_program`), `ep.add_env(tool_turn(...))`, repeat. The last model turn ends the episode, or the episode ends early when the model submits and the checker passes.

Why not decode everything to text and call `apply_chat_template` again on the conversation? Because BPE tokenization is not concatenative. `encode(a + b)` need not equal `encode(a) + encode(b)`: characters at the seam can merge into one token (two `\n` become the single `\n\n` token) or split differently. Templates also render historical turns differently from the turn in progress; Qwen3's template strips `<think>` content from earlier assistant turns, and the details depend on the template version. You do not need to reason about the Jinja. You need a test that makes it irrelevant:

```python
def test_trainer_ids_roundtrip(episode_fixture, build_batch):
    ep = episode_fixture                       # >= 2 turns, one truncated tool output
    batch = build_batch([ep], L=2048)          # the trainer's own batch builder
    row = batch["ids"][0]
    pad = int((batch["attn"][0] == 0).sum())   # left padding
    expected = [t for _, seg in ep.segments for t in seg]
    assert row[pad:].tolist() == expected      # nothing dropped, nothing added
```

This is the round-trip test from the deliverables: trainer input IDs equal sampled IDs plus env-inserted IDs. It is cheap and it catches the most common multi-turn bug, so it runs first whenever anything at a turn boundary looks wrong.

**Positions.** With left padding the trainer computes `positions = cumsum(attn) - 1` (clipped at 0), so the first real token is at position 0 in every row. Even a uniform offset would not matter: RoPE makes the query-key score depend only on the difference of positions. What does matter is a *restart*. With in-cache continuation, if turn 2's chunk is prefilled with positions starting again at 0, the relative distances between turn-2 queries and turn-1 keys are wrong, and turn 2 is scored in a scrambled context. Re-prefilling the full concatenated IDs each turn (the week-7 v1 path) cannot have this bug, which is one reason to keep v1 as the reference.

sections.heading: The mask and its three tests
sections.md:
The trainer predicts token $t+1$ from logits at position $t$. So the loss lives on **targets**, and the mask must be shifted with them: `logits[:, :-1]` against `labels = ids[:, 1:]`, with `loss_mask[:, 1:]`, where `loss_mask[j]` is True when input token $j$ was written by the model. Many off-by-one bugs this week come from applying the input mask to the targets without the shift.

The trainer's mask builder walks `segments` (not `env_spans`), lays out left padding and truncation, and marks model segments True. Here is the masked GRPO loss with the k3 term, written for clarity with full logits (in your stack it uses the week-3 chunked log-softmax):

```python
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp
from flax import nnx

def token_logp(model, ids, labels, pos, attn, m):
    logits = model(ids, pos, attn)[:, :-1].astype(jnp.float32)  # [B, L-1, V]
    labels = jnp.where(m, labels, 0)                             # sanitize masked labels
    tgt = jnp.take_along_axis(logits, labels[..., None], axis=-1)[..., 0]
    return tgt - jax.nn.logsumexp(logits, axis=-1)               # [B, L-1]

def grpo_loss(model, b, beta):
    m = b["loss_mask"][:, 1:]                                    # targets, not inputs
    logp = token_logp(model, b["ids"], b["labels"], b["pos"], b["attn"], m)
    adv = jnp.where(m, b["adv"], 0.0)                            # [B, L-1], per token
    ref = jnp.where(m, b["ref_logp"], logp)                      # double where: log_rho = 0 when masked
    log_rho = ref - logp                                         # log(pi_ref / pi_theta)
    k3 = jnp.exp(log_rho) - log_rho - 1.0
    ratio = jnp.exp(logp - jax.lax.stop_gradient(logp))          # mu=1, pi_old = pi_theta
    per_tok = jnp.where(m, -adv * ratio + beta * k3, 0.0)
    return per_tok.sum() / b["norm"], per_tok
```

(The clipped surrogate from week 4 replaces `-adv * ratio` when $\mu > 1$. With $\mu = 1$ and the trainer's own log-probs as $\pi_{old}$, the ratio is exactly 1 and only its gradient, $\nabla \log \pi_\theta$, matters.)

**Why `where` and not multiply.** Masked positions can hold garbage: a pad label, a label equal to $V$ that indexes past the vocabulary, a reference log-prob of `inf`. JAX's `take_along_axis` fills out-of-range gathers with NaN for float outputs (try it on CPU: an index of 5 into a length-5 axis returns `nan`). Multiply by a float mask and $0 \times \text{NaN} = \text{NaN}$: the whole loss is NaN. (With a *boolean* mask XLA may rewrite the multiply into a select and hide the problem. Do not rely on that.) `jnp.where(m, x, 0.0)` selects, so the forward value is exactly 0.

The backward pass needs one more step. The gradient of `where` sends cotangent 0 into the unselected branch, but that 0 is then multiplied by the branch's local derivative. If that derivative is `inf` (for example the derivative of `exp(log_rho)` when the masked `ref_logp` is huge), you get $0 \times \infty = \text{NaN}$ in the gradient even though the loss is finite. The fix is the **double where**: sanitize the inputs of the dangerous op at masked positions (`labels` and `ref` above) as well as its output. This is the pattern in the JAX FAQ entry on NaN gradients with `where`.

Now the three tests. Each checks one property, and none of them asserts the false statement from section 1.

**(a) Zero at tool positions.** `per_tok` and `adv` are exactly 0 wherever `m` is False: `assert (per_tok[~m] == 0).all()`. Exact equality, because `where` produces an exact 0.

**(b) Tool targets cannot matter.** Keep `ids`, `pos` and `attn` fixed. Replace the *labels*, *advantages* and *reference log-probs* at tool positions with junk, and require bit-identical loss and gradients.

```python
def test_tool_targets_do_not_change_grad(model, batch):
    tool = ~batch["loss_mask"][:, 1:]
    vg = nnx.value_and_grad(lambda m, b: grpo_loss(m, b, 0.04)[0],
                            argnums=nnx.DiffState(0, nnx.LoRAParam))
    l0, g0 = vg(model, batch)
    junk = dict(batch,
        labels=jnp.where(tool, 151936, batch["labels"]),   # = V: out of range on purpose
        adv=jnp.where(tool, 1e6, batch["adv"]),
        ref_logp=jnp.where(tool, 1e30, batch["ref_logp"])) # exp overflows if not sanitized
    l1, g1 = vg(model, junk)
    assert jnp.array_equal(l0, l1)
    for a, c in zip(jax.tree.leaves(g0), jax.tree.leaves(g1)):
        assert jnp.array_equal(a, c)
```

The junk is chosen to break specific mistakes. A label of $V$ breaks a missing label sanitizer. A `ref_logp` of $+10^{30}$ breaks a single `where`: on a toy model, dropping the `ref = jnp.where(...)` line leaves the loss bit-identical but turns every LoRA gradient leaf into NaN, so a test that only compared losses would pass. (A junk value of $-10^{30}$ would not catch it: $\exp$ of a very negative number is 0, and its derivative is finite.)

Three more details make it a real test. Use `array_equal`, not `allclose`: a leak of size $10^{-6} \times 10^6$ would hide inside a tolerance. Before the test, set every LoRA `B` to small random values. With $B = 0$ (the init), the gradient with respect to every `A` is identically zero whatever the loss, so half the leaves would pass trivially. Run on CPU or with `XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_deterministic_ops=true`, because some GPU reductions are not bit-reproducible between calls even with identical inputs.

Why is it wrong to perturb `ids` instead? Because changing tool input IDs legitimately changes $h_t$ for every later model token, so loss and gradient *should* change. A test that changes inputs and expects no change fails on a correct implementation. A test that changes inputs and expects *some* change proves nothing about the mask.

**(c) The mask equals the env's log.** The env logged `env_spans` at insertion time. The trainer built `loss_mask` from `segments` after padding and truncation. These are independent routes to the same answer, which is what keeps the test from being a tautology. If the test built its expected mask with the trainer's own function, it would pass whatever that function did.

```python
def test_mask_matches_env_spans(episodes, build_batch):
    b = build_batch(episodes, L=2048)
    for i, ep in enumerate(episodes):
        pad = int((b["attn"][i] == 0).sum())
        mask = b["loss_mask"][i]
        assert not mask[:pad].any()                         # padding
        for s, e in ep.env_spans:                           # prompt + every tool span
            assert not mask[pad + s: pad + e].any()
        assert int(mask.sum()) == len(ep.sampler_logp)      # every sampled token, incl. <|im_end|>
```

Padding, env spans and model tokens partition the row, so "no True outside model segments" plus "count equals the number of sampled tokens" pins the mask exactly.

The fixture is where the test earns its keep. Include at least: two or more turns; a tool output cut exactly at the truncation cap (an off-by-one in the cap shows up as one tool token marked True or one sampled token marked False at the span end); left padding; an episode that ended early after turn 1; and a turn that hit the per-turn token cap without emitting `<|im_end|>`. Then break the builder on purpose, shifting the mask by one token, and confirm the test fails. A mask test you have never seen fail is not yet a test.

sections.heading: Advantages and KL on model tokens
sections.md:
The RL algebra is week 4's, applied per episode. Each task is a group of $G$ episodes with scalar outcome rewards $r_1, \dots, r_G$ (tests pass or not at the end of the episode).

**Worked example.** $G = 4$, $r = [1, 0, 0, 1]$.

GRPO normalizes by the group mean and standard deviation:

$$
\bar r = 0.5, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{4}\sum_i (r_i - \bar r)^2} = \sqrt{\tfrac{4 \cdot 0.25}{4}} = 0.5, \qquad A_i = \frac{r_i - \bar r}{\sigma + \epsilon} = [+1, -1, -1, +1]
$$

That is the population SD, which is `jnp.std`'s default (`ddof=0`). PyTorch's `torch.std` defaults to the sample SD, $\sqrt{1/3} = 0.577$, which gives $\pm 0.866$. A 13% difference in effective learning rate is invisible in a curve, so know which one your code uses and pin it in a test. (With $\epsilon = 10^{-6}$ the computed value is $0.999998$, so compare with a tolerance of about $10^{-5}$, not exact equality.)

RLOO uses the mean of the *other* $G-1$ rewards as the baseline:

$$
A_i = r_i - \frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{j \ne i} r_j = r_i - \frac{G\bar r - r_i}{G-1} = \frac{G}{G-1}(r_i - \bar r)
$$

For the example: $\tfrac{4}{3}(\pm 0.5) = \pm 2/3$. Check one directly: for a success the other three rewards are $[0, 0, 1]$ with mean $1/3$, so $A = 1 - 1/3 = 2/3$. RLOO is GRPO without the SD division, scaled by $G/(G-1)$.

```python
def grpo_adv(r, eps=1e-6, std_norm=True):        # r: [P, G]
    a = r - r.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return a / (r.std(axis=1, keepdims=True) + eps) if std_norm else a

def rloo_adv(r):
    G = r.shape[1]
    return G / (G - 1) * (r - r.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True))

def broadcast_adv(adv_ep, loss_mask):            # [B], [B, L] -> [B, L-1]
    return jnp.where(loss_mask[:, 1:], adv_ep[:, None], 0.0)
```

**When rewards stop being binary.** With a valid-call bonus (section 9) or $k_1$ subtracted from the reward, rewards take values like $0.1$ or $1.1$. Two things change. The GRPO advantage depends only on the *ranking and spread inside the group*, so a group that differs only by a small bonus gets unit-sized advantages after SD division; RLOO keeps them proportionate. And a group can no longer be "dead" just because all outcomes agree: a bonus difference revives it. Section 9 works the numbers.

**Which tokens.** The scalar $A_i$ multiplies every model token of episode $i$, in every turn. Turn-1 tokens that wrote a buggy first draft get the same advantage as turn-2 tokens that fixed it. That is the outcome-only credit assignment you chose, and it is unbiased: the policy gradient in section 1 has one $A(\tau)$ for the whole sum. Tool and template tokens get 0 through `broadcast_adv`.

**The k3 KL estimator, derived.** Let $\rho = \pi_{ref}(y_t \mid h_t) / \pi_\theta(y_t \mid h_t)$ at the sampled token. Define

$$
k_3 = \rho - \log \rho - 1
$$

Two facts. First, $x - \log x - 1 \ge 0$ for all $x > 0$, with equality at $x = 1$ (it is convex with derivative $1 - 1/x$, zero at 1). So every sample is non-negative, unlike $k_1 = -\log\rho$, which is negative whenever the sampled token is more likely under the reference. Second, if $y_t \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid h_t)$:

$$
\mathbb{E}[\rho] = \sum_y \pi_\theta(y)\frac{\pi_{ref}(y)}{\pi_\theta(y)} = \sum_y \pi_{ref}(y) = 1, \qquad \mathbb{E}[-\log\rho] = \sum_y \pi_\theta(y) \log\frac{\pi_\theta(y)}{\pi_{ref}(y)} = \mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta \,\|\, \pi_{ref})
$$

so $\mathbb{E}[k_3] = 1 + \mathrm{KL} - 1 = \mathrm{KL}$.

Look at what the derivation assumed: **$y_t$ was drawn from $\pi_\theta$.** Tool tokens were drawn from the sandbox. At those positions $\rho$ is a ratio of two models' predictions of compiler output, and its average estimates nothing. So the KL is computed and averaged over model tokens only, for a statistical reason as well as an engineering one. Its gradient, $\nabla_\theta k_3 = (1 - \rho)\nabla_\theta \log\pi_\theta$, would otherwise push the model's prediction of tool text toward the reference's.

Placement follows the week-4 pre-registration. Either (a) subtract $\beta \cdot k_1$ summed over model tokens from the episode reward, with no gradient through it, before computing advantages, or (b) add $\beta \cdot k_3$ to the per-token loss on model tokens, as in `grpo_loss` above. Log both $k_1$ and $k_3$ either way.

**The reference.** After the warm start (section 6) you merge the SFT adapter into the base and add a fresh RL adapter. The reference is the merged model with the RL adapter's `scale` set to 0, passed as a traced argument so the same compiled program computes both. At step 0 the RL adapter's $B$ is zero, so the adapter adds exactly $0$ in both paths and $\pi_\theta$ and $\pi_{ref}$ run identical arithmetic: $k_1$ should be exactly 0 on every token. If it is not, your reference path differs from your policy path in something other than the adapter, and every later KL number carries that offset.

sections.heading: Zero-variance groups and how strong a warm start should be
sections.md:
A group whose $G$ rewards are all equal has $r_i - \bar r = 0$ for every member. Under GRPO the numerator is 0, so the $\epsilon$ in the denominator does not matter; under RLOO the advantage is 0 directly. The group contributes nothing to the policy-gradient term. (If KL is a $k_3$ loss term, it still acts on the group's tokens and pulls them toward the reference. If KL is $k_1$ in the reward, the rewards are no longer exactly equal, and the group's advantages are driven by KL noise alone; log that case too.)

For a task with true per-episode success rate $p$, the $G$ outcomes are independent Bernoulli draws, and the group is dead when all succeed or all fail:

$$
P(\text{zero variance}) = p^G + (1-p)^G
$$

At $G = 8$:

| $p$ | $p^8$ | $(1-p)^8$ | dead fraction |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 0.0039 | 0.0039 | 0.8% |
| 0.8 | 0.168 | $2.6 \times 10^{-6}$ | 16.8% |
| 0.9 | 0.430 | $10^{-8}$ | 43.0% |

The curve is flat near 0.5 and climbs steeply toward the ends. Moving a task from 0.8 to 0.9 more than doubles its chance of being wasted.

The batch-level fraction is the mean of this formula over the tasks' own pass rates, not the formula at the mean pass rate. Week 0 gives a sobering real number. The sftpool run sampled each of the 274 MBPP train prompts 16 times (single-turn, basic tests). Mean pass@1 is 52.6%, which sounds like the ideal middle. But the per-prompt rates are bimodal: 116 prompts passed 16 of 16, 90 passed 0 of 16, and only 68 are in between. Plugging each prompt's $\hat p = c/16$ into $p^8 + (1-p)^8$ and averaging gives **81%** dead groups at $G = 8$. The formula at the mean pass rate would have said 1%.

That plug-in is biased upward, for the same Jensen reason the pass@k plug-in was biased in week 0: $p^G$ is convex, so $\mathbb{E}[\hat p^G] \ge p^G$. The unbiased estimate uses the same combinatorics as pass@k. With $c$ passes in $n$ samples, the chance that a random size-$G$ subset is all-pass is $\binom{c}{G}/\binom{n}{G}$, whose expectation over $c \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p)$ is exactly $p^G$:

```python
from math import comb
def p_dead(n: int, c: int, G: int) -> float:
    return (comb(c, G) + comb(n - c, G)) / comb(n, G)
# week-0 sftpool, 274 prompts x 16: mean p_dead(16, c, 8) = 0.797
# only the 68 prompts with 0 < c < 16: 0.184;  the 51 with 2 <= c <= 14: 0.079
```

So 80% of a naive batch would be dead. Restricting to prompts the base model sometimes solves cuts it to 18%. The week-7 agent tasks will have their own distribution, so compute this from your warm-started checkpoint before launching. That is one overnight sampling run, and it is cheaper than discovering the problem from a flat reward curve.

**What this says about the warm start.** SFT on successful trajectories raises pass rates on the training tasks, which is its purpose: it teaches the format of a tool call and the habit of reading the result. But if it lifts most tasks to around 0.9, you are at the 43% row, and the tasks it lifted to 1.0 are dead for good. Signs the warm start is too strong: the zero-variance fraction over the first 20 steps is above about 50%, and it is dominated by all-pass groups. Responses, in order of cost: drop or down-weight tasks whose measured rate is above about 0.85, train the warm start for fewer steps or on fewer trajectories, or raise $G$ (at $G = 16$ and $p = 0.9$ the dead fraction falls to $0.9^{16} = 18.5\%$, at twice the sampling cost per task). Log the fraction every step, split into all-pass and all-fail. They have opposite fixes.

sections.heading: The warm start, the merge and the fresh adapter
sections.md:
The ~200 successful week-7 trajectories (report the actual count, whatever it is) become the SFT set. Each is already an `Episode` with segments, so the SFT loss reuses the same mask builder:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{SFT} = -\frac{1}{C}\sum_{\text{episodes}} \sum_{t \in M} \log \pi_\theta(\tau_t \mid h_t)
$$

with $C$ the number of model tokens in the batch or a constant, chosen once. The model-token mask matters here for the same reason as in RL. Without it, the model is trained to produce `<tool_response>` blocks and plausible tracebacks itself. A model that has learned to write fake tool output will sometimes skip the tool and "report" a passing test. Your checker catches the false claim, but the behavior wastes turns and pollutes RL from step 0.

The step is the week-1 step with the episode batch:

```python
opt = nnx.Optimizer(model, optax.adamw(2e-4), wrt=nnx.LoRAParam)

@nnx.jit
def sft_step(model, opt, b):
    def loss_fn(model):
        m = b["loss_mask"][:, 1:]
        logp = token_logp(model, b["ids"], b["labels"], b["pos"], b["attn"], m)
        return -jnp.where(m, logp, 0.0).sum() / b["norm"]
    loss, grads = nnx.value_and_grad(loss_fn, argnums=nnx.DiffState(0, nnx.LoRAParam))(model)
    opt.update(model, grads)
    return loss
```

Then follow section 3.1 of the plan. Merge the SFT adapter in fp32: $W' = W + (\alpha/r) B A$, computed in fp32 from the bf16 base and the fp32 adapter, then cast to bf16. (Flax stores kernels as $[d_{in}, d_{out}]$ and computes $xW$, so the kernel update is the transpose, $(\alpha/r) A^\top B^\top$; `lora_a` is $[d_{in}, r]$ and `lora_b` is $[r, d_{out}]$, and the product `lora_a @ lora_b` already has the kernel's shape.) Re-run log-prob parity between the adapter model and the merged model on a fixed batch. Then attach a fresh RL adapter with $B = 0$. Two reasons to merge rather than keep training the SFT adapter: the reference becomes simply "the merged weights at RL scale 0", one set of base arrays shared by sampler, reference and trainer; and the RL adapter's norm then measures the RL change alone, which week 10 will want.

The merge test has one sharp edge. Merging changes the arithmetic: $W'x$ with $W'$ rounded to bf16 is not bit-equal to $Wx + (\alpha/r)B(Ax)$. Expect per-token log-prob differences around $10^{-2}$ nats in bf16, the same scale as the sampler-trainer mismatch. Run the parity check at `highest` matmul precision on a few sequences, with a tolerance you write down in advance.

sections.heading: Length normalization when episodes span turns
sections.md:
The loss is a sum of per-token terms divided by a normalizer. In multi-turn RL the choice of normalizer quietly changes the objective.

The true policy gradient (section 1) weights every model token of episode $i$ by $A_i$, with no division by length. Let $L_i = |M_i|$ be episode $i$'s number of model tokens. Three common normalizers:

1. **Per-episode mean** (original GRPO): $\frac{1}{B}\sum_i \frac{A_i}{L_i}\sum_{t \in M_i} \nabla \log\pi_\theta$. Each token gets weight $A_i / (B L_i)$.
2. **Constant** (Dr. GRPO style): $\frac{1}{C}\sum_i A_i \sum_{t \in M_i} \nabla\log\pi_\theta$ with a fixed $C$, for example $B \times 1536$ (3 turns × a 512-token cap). Each token gets $A_i / C$.
3. **Token-level over the batch** (DAPO style): divide by $\sum_j L_j$ for the batch. Each token gets $A_i / \sum_j L_j$, the same scale for every token within a batch.

Option 2 is the true gradient times $1/C$: the direction is exact. Option 3 has the exact direction within each batch; only the scale varies from batch to batch. Option 1 multiplies episode $i$'s contribution by $1/L_i$, a weight correlated with the behavior you are training.

**Worked example.** Two episodes, $L = 100$ and $L = 400$ model tokens (drop the common $1/B$).

- Both correct, $A = +1$. Per-episode mean gives $1/100 = 0.01$ per token to the short one and $1/400 = 0.0025$ to the long one: the short success gets 4× the per-token push. Both episodes get the same total push of 1, spread thinner over the long one.
- Both wrong, $A = -1$. The short failure's tokens get $-0.01$ each; the long failure's get $-0.0025$. Being wrong at length is cheap.

The net pressure is toward short episodes when right and long ones when wrong. In week 6 this showed up as length drift in single-turn RL. Multi-turn sharpens it, because $L_i$ now varies with the number of turns: an episode that solves the task in one turn might have 150 model tokens, and one that uses all three turns and fails might have 1200. Under option 1 the 3-turn failure is penalized 8× less per token.

With constant normalization, $C = 1536 B$, every token in both examples gets $\pm 1/C$, and the bias is gone.

**Which length.** If you use option 1 or 3, $L_i$ must be the number of **masked model tokens**, `loss_mask[i, 1:].sum()`, not the sequence length. Suppose an episode has 600 model tokens and 1100 tool and template tokens. Dividing by 1700 instead of 600 shrinks its gradient by almost 3×, and the shrinkage is largest for exactly the episodes that read long tracebacks. The `norm` field in the batch is computed in one place, and a pytest pins it:

```python
def test_norm_counts_model_tokens(episodes, build_batch):
    b = build_batch(episodes, L=2048, norm="constant", C=1536 * len(episodes))
    assert b["norm"] == 1536 * len(episodes)
    b = build_batch(episodes, L=2048, norm="tokens")
    assert b["norm"] == sum(len(ep.sampler_logp) for ep in episodes)  # model tokens, not L
```

Log model-token length and turns per episode per arm every step. If one arm's length drifts and the other's does not, that is a finding, and you want to see it before reading the outcome metric.

sections.heading: Memory, step time and a fixed number of compiled programs
sections.md:
**KV cache.** From Qwen3-1.7B's `config.json`: $N_L = 28$, $H_{kv} = 8$, $d_h = 128$. Per token in bf16:

$$
2\,(K,V) \times 28 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2\ \text{bytes} = 114{,}688\ \text{B} = 112\ \text{KiB}
$$

This is 4× the 28.7 KB/token of Qwen2.5-1.5B in the plan's original week-3 estimate, because Qwen2.5-1.5B has 2 KV heads and Qwen3-1.7B has 8. Size from this model's config, not a remembered number.

A fixed-`max_len` cache reserves every slot whether or not the episode uses it. At 2048 slots: $2048 \times 114{,}688 = 234.9$ MB per episode.

**What is left for KV on a 24 GB card.** By default JAX preallocates 75% of GPU memory, about 18 GB, unless `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION` says otherwise. From that pool subtract:

- bf16 weights: counting the tied embedding once, $151936 \times 2048 = 0.31$B embedding plus $28 \times 48.2$M per layer (attention $2048 \times (2048 + 1024 + 1024 + 2048)$ = 12.6M... in fact q and o are $2048 \times 2048$ each and k, v are $2048 \times 1024$ each, 12.6M; MLP $3 \times 2048 \times 6144$ = 37.7M) is about 1.66B parameters, so 3.3 GB
- RL LoRA at $r = 16$ on all linear layers: per layer $r(d_{in} + d_{out})$ summed over q, k, v, o, gate, up, down is $16 \times (4096 + 3072 + 3072 + 4096 + 3 \times 8192) = 622{,}592$; × 28 = 17.4M params. In fp32 with gradient and two Adam moments: 17.4M × 16 B = 0.28 GB
- prefill workspace for a wave: one $[64, 2048, 6144]$ bf16 MLP intermediate is 1.6 GB, plus attention and residual buffers
- decode logits, last position only: $64 \times V \times 4$ B = 39 MB

That leaves roughly 12-14 GB for KV, so $13 \times 10^9 / 2.349 \times 10^8 \approx 55$ episodes, about 50-60 depending on headroom. Confirm it against `jax.devices()[0].memory_stats()["peak_bytes_in_use"]` from a real wave. 256 rollouts at 2048 would need $256 \times 234.9$ MB = 60 GB of KV alone, so no single call. Sample in waves of 32-64, return only IDs, log-probs and lengths, and free the cache before the train step.

> One line in the prefill can wreck this budget. If prefill computes logits at every position, a wave of 64 × 2048 produces a $[64, 2048, 151936]$ bf16 tensor: 40 GB. The sampler needs logits only at the last real position of each sequence. Slice the hidden state first, then apply the LM head.

**Step time, before you size runs.** Decode is memory-bound: each step reads the weights once (3.3 GB) and the KV cache. With a fixed $[64, 2048]$ cache and plain masked attention, every step reads all 2048 slots whether they are live or not: $64 \times 2048 \times 114{,}688 = 15.0$ GB, about 4.5× the weights. At the 4090's ~1 TB/s that is a floor of about 18 ms per decode step. (An attention that reads only live slots would read about $64 \times 1000 \times 114{,}688 = 7.3$ GB at an average context of 1000 tokens, a floor near 11 ms. Smaller cache buckets for early turns are a cheap way to get part of that.) Three turns at a 512-token cap is up to 1536 decode steps, so about 28 s per wave at the roofline, about 2 minutes for four waves of 256 rollouts, and realistically 2-3× that. Then add three re-prefills per episode, the sandbox (0.13 s per program per worker, run in parallel on CPU), and a train step over 256 sequences of up to 2048 tokens. Week 5's step time does not transfer. Measure the multi-turn step on the real config, then compute how many steps fit in a night.

**Compiled programs.** A multi-turn loop is variable in many ways: turns per episode, tokens per turn, tool-output length, episodes that finish early. None of that may reach a shape. Fix every shape and count the programs in advance:

- prefill: total context padded to buckets {512, 1024, 1536, 2048}, wave size fixed at 64: 4 programs
- decode step: cache $[64, 2048]$, one program, reused every turn
- reference and policy log-probs: one program, `scale` traced
- train microstep at $[8, 2048]$ and the optimizer apply: 2 programs

Prediction: 8 programs. Finished episodes stay in the wave with a done mask instead of being removed, because removing them changes $B$. Tool output is truncated in IDs on the host and the context is padded to the bucket. To assert the count, use the fact that Python code inside a jitted function runs only while JAX traces it:

```python
import collections
TRACES = collections.Counter()

def counted(name, f):
    def g(*args, **kw):
        TRACES[name] += 1          # executes at trace time only
        return f(*args, **kw)
    return g

decode_step = nnx.jit(counted("decode", decode_step_impl))
# ... after 3 warm-up RL steps:
before = sum(TRACES.values())
for _ in range(20): rl_step()
assert sum(TRACES.values()) == before <= 8, dict(TRACES)
```

If the count grows, turn on `jax_log_compiles` and `jax_explain_cache_misses` to see which argument changed, as in week 0.

sections.heading: A shaped reward that cannot pass for progress
sections.md:
The experiment compares outcome-only reward against outcome plus a bonus for each valid tool call. The bonus is meant to help early exploration: calls that parse and run are rewarded before the policy can solve tasks. The danger is that the policy learns to collect the bonus.

**Why a per-call bonus changes the optimum.** Ng, Harada and Russell (1999) showed that adding $F(s, s') = \gamma\Phi(s') - \Phi(s)$ for some potential $\Phi$ over states leaves the optimal policy unchanged. The core of the proof is one line. Sum the shaping along any trajectory with $\gamma = 1$:

$$
\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\big(\Phi(s_{t+1}) - \Phi(s_t)\big) = \Phi(s_T) - \Phi(s_0)
$$

The sum telescopes. With $\Phi$ zero at terminal states, it is $-\Phi(s_0)$, which no action can change. So every policy's return shifts by the same amount, and the ranking of policies is preserved. A per-call bonus $b$ is not of this form: it adds $b \times (\text{number of valid calls})$, which the policy controls.

**Worked example.** Three turns, bonus 0.1 per valid call, outcome reward 1.

- Policy H (honest): one useful call, solves 55% of tasks. Expected reward $0.55 + 0.1 = 0.65$.
- Policy S (spam): a trivial valid call every turn (`print(1)`), solves 40%. Expected reward $0.40 + 0.3 = 0.70$.

S wins on training reward and loses on the thing you care about. Cap the bonus at 0.1 per episode and the comparison flips: S gets 0.50, H gets 0.65. The cap removes the incentive to spam but not the incentive to make at least one call when a call does not help; only the outcome-based headline protects against that.

There is a second, less obvious amplifier: **GRPO's SD normalization.** Take an all-fail group whose members made different numbers of valid calls, so $r = [0.1, 0.1, 0, 0.1]$. Without the bonus this group would be dead. With it, $\bar r = 0.075$ and $\sigma = 0.0433$, so the advantages are $[+0.58, +0.58, -1.73, +0.58]$. A bonus 10× smaller than the outcome produces unit-sized advantages in exactly the groups where no one solved the task. RLOO, without the division, gives $[+0.033, +0.033, -0.1, +0.033]$, which is proportionate. If you keep std normalization, expect the bonus arm to be driven by call-making on hard tasks, and log the reward split per group type.

**The design.**

- Headline metric: held-out outcome pass@1 (tests pass) on the frozen split, $n$ samples per item, never the training reward, which contains the bonus. Both arms are compared at matched steps.
- Bonus capped per episode and well below the outcome reward (≤ 0.1 vs 1).
- Logged per arm, every step: reward split into outcome and bonus, calls per episode, turns per episode, tool-error rate, model-token length, zero-variance fraction, sampler-trainer mismatch.
- Inspect about 30 bonus-arm trajectories and categorize each call: useful, repeated, no-op, unrelated to the task.
- Decision rule from section 3.2 of the plan: gain above 2× the noise floor, two-level paired CI excluding 0, and the same sign on every seed. Pre-register all of this, plus KL placement, the on-policy choice and the compute plan, in a note committed before launch.

With this design a reviewer who says "the bonus arm wins on reward" has not made a claim about the headline. The answer is the paired held-out outcome difference with its CI, and the reward decomposition showing how much of the reward gap is bonus.

**Recognizing the failure.** Suppose the bonus arm shows training reward rising steadily, tool-error rate falling to 0, turns per episode pinned at the maximum, and held-out outcome pass@1 flat. Plot the reward decomposition: outcome component and bonus component per step, stacked, for both arms. If the bonus component accounts for the whole rise and the outcome component tracks the control arm, the policy is harvesting. The tool-error rate of 0 is a symptom, not an achievement: trivial calls never fail. The results row reports a shaping failure (for example, "bonus arm: training reward +0.2, entirely bonus; held-out outcome pass@1 difference vs outcome-only with its paired CI including 0"), and the write-up proposes a capped or potential-based bonus as the follow-up. A trajectory pair (honest vs spam on the same task) is also a good week-10 interpretability target.

**Optional tampering probe.** Give the agent write access to the test file, keep a pristine hidden copy, and score with the hidden copy. Log the fraction of episodes that modify the visible test. It is a cheap, concrete measurement of a hacking behavior that labs care about.

sections.heading: Mismatch at turn boundaries, seeds across hardware, and what to do if nothing learns
sections.md:
**Reading a mismatch trace.** Every step you log $|\log\pi_{sampler} - \log\pi_{trainer}|$ per model token. In bf16, ~$10^{-2}$ nats is normal numerics. Suppose turn-1 tokens sit at $10^{-2}$ but the first few tokens of turns 2 and 3 exceed 1 nat. Turn 1 being clean rules out global causes: a sampler temperature that differs from the trainer's, or log-probs taken from a top-p-truncated distribution, would show up on turn 1 too. What is special about turns 2 and 3 is that they follow inserted tokens. In order of likelihood and cheapness:

1. **Re-tokenized context.** The trainer scores IDs that were never sampled. Test: the round-trip assertion from section 2.
2. **Positions or attention mask after concatenation.** Positions restart at a turn, or pad tokens are counted. Test: teacher-forced log-probs of one unpadded episode vs the same episode inside a left-padded batch. They should agree to numerics.
3. **Template tokens inserted differently** by the sampler path and the trainer path (a missing `\n` after `<|im_end|>`, a missing empty think block). Test: dump and diff the IDs in a window around every boundary.
4. **In-cache continuation only:** a stale or mis-offset KV write position. Test: continuation vs a full prefill of the same IDs.

Run test 1 first. It is a one-line equality, and when it fails it explains the whole symptom.

**Seeds across hardware.** The plan runs 3 seeds per arm: 2 locally, 1 on a rented H100. Hardware changes numerics (different kernels, reduction orders and matmul precision), and RL amplifies small numeric differences into different trajectories. If all of one arm ran on the H100, the arm difference would include a hardware difference you cannot separate out.

Pair by seed index. Seed $k$ of both arms uses the same hardware, data order and PRNG key. Seeds 1 and 2 of both arms run on the 4090; seed 3 of both arms runs on the H100. Evaluate every checkpoint with the same local harness, so the eval is not a second hardware factor. Record the accelerator in each results row.

The analysis resamples at two levels: seeds first, then items within the drawn seeds. With hardware-paired seeds, resample seed indices jointly so each bootstrap draw keeps pairs on matching hardware:

```python
import numpy as np

def two_level_paired_bootstrap(a, b, n_boot=4000, seed=0, joint_seeds=True):
    """a, b: [S, N] per-item pass@1, rows = seeds (row k of a and b paired), cols = shared item IDs."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    S, N = a.shape
    out = np.empty(n_boot)
    for i in range(n_boot):
        sa = rng.integers(0, S, S)
        sb = sa if joint_seeds else rng.integers(0, S, S)
        items = rng.integers(0, N, N)
        out[i] = b[sb][:, items].mean() - a[sa][:, items].mean()
    per_seed = (b - a).mean(axis=1)
    return {"diff": float((b - a).mean()), "ci95": np.percentile(out, [2.5, 97.5]).tolist(),
            "per_seed": per_seed.tolist(), "sign_agree": bool(np.all(per_seed > 0) or np.all(per_seed < 0))}
```

`joint_seeds=False` is the protocol's within-arm resampling. It is valid, but it mixes hardware within a draw and widens the CI: on a synthetic example with a 0.05 hardware offset on seed 3 and a true gain of 0.03, the joint CI was about [0.022, 0.033] and the independent one [-0.003, 0.060]. Report the per-seed paired differences next to the CI. With only 3 seeds the sign check is coarse: under no effect, all three differences share a sign with probability $2 \times (1/2)^3 = 25\%$ (all three positive, 12.5%), which is why it is one of three conditions and not the decision alone. Under cut #1 there are 2 local seeds per arm, the result is labeled exploratory, and no headline claim is made.

**If nothing learns.** The fallback deliverable is a verified pipeline plus a written diagnosis. Make it specific. Walk this list and record a number for each: the mask tests and the round-trip test pass; zero-variance fraction, split into all-pass and all-fail; the fraction of model tokens with non-zero advantage; LoRA gradient norm per step (zero means no signal, huge means a normalization bug); KL $k_1$ and $k_3$ (flat at 0 means the policy is not moving); sampler-trainer mismatch per turn; and reward on a small subset of tasks of intermediate difficulty. "80% of groups were all-fail after turn 1 because tool output was truncated before the traceback line" is a result. "It did not work" is not.

chapters.lab:
Work in this order. Monday is reading and pre-registration; runs launch by Wednesday evening; Friday afternoon is buffer.

1. **Read the env's output, then the config.** Load one saved week-7 trajectory and print its segments with their authors. Open the HF cache `config.json` for Qwen3-1.7B and confirm `num_hidden_layers=28`, `num_key_value_heads=8`, `head_dim=128`. Write the KV arithmetic (114,688 B/token, 234.9 MB per 2048-slot episode) at the top of your week-8 notes.
2. **Episode and batch builder.** Add `Episode` (segments, `env_spans`, `sampler_logp`) to your week-7 env module and a `build_batch(episodes, L, norm)` that left-pads, computes `pos = cumsum(attn) - 1`, builds `loss_mask` from segments, broadcasts advantages, and computes `norm`. The builder must not read `env_spans`.
3. **Tests first.** Create `tests/test_agent_mask.py` with: the round-trip ID test; property (a); property (b) with random nonzero LoRA `B`, the junk values from section 3 (label = V, adv = 1e6, ref_logp = +1e30), `jnp.array_equal`, run on CPU (`JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu uv run --project envs/jax pytest tests/test_agent_mask.py`); property (c) with fixtures for 2+ turns, a tool output cut exactly at the cap, left padding, an early finish and a turn that hit the token cap; and the `norm` test. Break the builder by one token and confirm (c) fails; delete the `ref = jnp.where(...)` line and confirm (b) fails on NaN gradients. Add a pytest that runs your week-4 advantage functions on `[1, 0, 0, 1]` and checks `[1, -1, -1, 1]` (GRPO, ddof=0, tolerance 1e-5) and `[2/3, -2/3, -2/3, 2/3]` (RLOO), plus `[0.1, 0.1, 0, 0.1]` to see the SD amplification.
4. **Predict the zero-variance fraction.** Reproduce the week-0 number from `runs/week0_sftpool_train_qwen3-1_7b/scored.jsonl` using `harness.stats.per_item_counts(rows, "basic")` and `p_dead(16, c, 8)` (expect 0.797 on all 274 prompts, 0.184 on the 68 with 0 < c < 16). Write it down; you will compare with the warm-started checkpoint.
5. **Warm start.** SFT on the successful week-7 trajectories with the same mask (record the count). Merge in fp32, cast to bf16, run parity at `highest` precision against a pre-written tolerance. Attach a fresh RL adapter with B = 0 and assert k1 is exactly 0 at step 0. Sample n=16 per training task from the merged checkpoint overnight and compute per-task `p_dead`; drop tasks above ~0.85 if the dead fraction exceeds ~50%.
6. **Compile budget and memory.** Wrap prefill, decode, log-prob, train microstep and apply with the trace counter; assert at most 8 programs and no growth over 20 steps after 3 warm-up steps. Confirm the prefill applies the LM head to the last position only. Record peak memory for one wave of 64 at 2048 from `jax.devices()[0].memory_stats()["peak_bytes_in_use"]` and compare with the section-8 estimate.
7. **Measure the step time** on the real multi-turn config (e.g. 32 tasks x G=8, 3 turns, 512-token cap) for 5 steps, split into decode, prefill, sandbox and train. Compare decode with the ~18 ms/step roofline. Compute steps per night and the H100 hours for 1 seed per arm. Only now size the runs.
8. **Pre-register.** Commit `notes/week8_prereg.md` before launch: hypothesis, arms (outcome-only vs outcome + valid-call bonus capped at 0.1 per episode), headline held-out outcome pass@1 with n per item, decision rule (2x noise floor, two-level paired CI excludes 0, sign agreement), KL placement, on-policy choice, normalization (constant C = 1536 x B), seed-to-hardware assignment (seeds 1-2 local for both arms, seed 3 of both arms on the H100), compute plan with cost.
9. **Launch** seed 1 of both arms locally Wednesday evening. Check step-20 logs: turns/episode, tool-error rate, zero-variance split, model-token length, reward split into outcome and bonus, mismatch per turn. Then seed 2 locally and the burst for seed 3 (burst checklist from plan 3.4).
10. **Analyze.** Evaluate every final checkpoint with the same local harness. `harness/stats.py` currently has only the single-level `paired_bootstrap`; if you did not add `two_level_paired_bootstrap` in week 3, add it now next to it, with a unit test on synthetic data. Plot per-seed curves plus the mean, the stacked reward decomposition per arm, and categorize ~30 bonus-arm trajectories. Write results rows with git SHA (clean tree), config hash, decoding config, seeds, accelerator, accelerator_hours, cost_usd and per-item JSONL paths. Fill scorecard row 3 and update cost_usd in the README.
takeaways: The gradient of an episode's log-probability sums over model tokens only, because the environment's tokens do not depend on the weights; tool tokens still shape gradients as context through the K/V the model computes at their positions.

Mask with jnp.where and also sanitize the inputs of exp and gather at masked positions; a float-mask multiply turns an out-of-range label into a NaN loss, and a single where can leave the loss finite while the gradient is NaN.

The decisive mask test changes labels, advantages and reference log-probs at tool positions with inputs fixed and demands bit-identical loss and gradients, using nonzero LoRA B and junk values chosen to break each known mistake.
Keep token IDs end to end and test that trainer IDs equal sampled plus env-inserted IDs; it is the first test to run when mismatch jumps at turn boundaries.

Zero-variance probability is p^G + (1-p)^G averaged over tasks, estimated without bias by (C(c,G)+C(n-c,G))/C(n,G); the week-0 train pool gives about 80% dead groups at G=8, so measure and filter before a strong warm start makes it worse.
Per-episode loss normalization biases toward short correct and long wrong episodes, more sharply in multi-turn; normalize by a constant, and count masked model tokens wherever a length is used.
A per-call bonus is not potential-based and can be harvested, and GRPO's SD normalization inflates it into full-size advantages in all-fail groups; the headline is always held-out outcome pass@1.
Size runs from Qwen3-1.7B's 112 KiB/token KV and a measured multi-turn step time, fix every shape to a predicted program count, and pair seeds by hardware so the arm comparison is not confounded.

chapters.title: Shipping claims and proving sharding before you pay for it
chapters.subtitle: Week 9 turns finished work into public claims that hold up, then makes week 11 cheaper by testing sharding on fake devices and one short TPU run.
chapters.why:
Weeks 5 to 8 produce results that are real but still private. A frontier-lab interviewer reads your public work before you get into a room. A post that overclaims costs you more than having no post. This week you turn the RLVR note and the sampler note into claims that meet the statistics protocol (REVIEW.md section 3.2), where every number has a command that reproduces it.

The second half lowers the risk of week 11, the only week where you pay for multi-chip hardware. Sharding bugs are cheap to find on 8 fake CPU devices and expensive to find on a TPU slice billed by the hour. Research engineers get hired to work out per-chip memory and communication on paper, predict the collectives in the HLO, and tell float noise from a real bug from the size of the error. This chapter teaches those skills on the Qwen3-1.7B spine.
prereqs: Ch 0: unbiased pass@k, bootstrap CIs, noise floor (0.17 pts basic, 0.66 pts plus on MBPP test)
Ch 1: masked log-probs, fp32 LoRA params and filtered optimizer state
Ch 3: NNX Qwen3 model, KV-cache sampler, parity tests at highest matmul precision
Ch 4: PRNG discipline with fold_in and split, vLLM throughput reference
Ch 5-6: RLVR headline runs with 3 training seeds and two-level paired bootstrap

sections.heading: The buffer comes first, the posts come second
sections.md:
Week 9 has a fixed priority order. Do not reorder it.

1. Absorb slippage from weeks 5 to 8. Write down what you cut, in the repo, with a date.
2. Publish post #1 (RLVR note) and post #2 (JAX KV-cache sampler + single-process RL on a 4090).
3. If time remains: the fake 8-device sharding test, then a TPU dry run under 1 h, then a refactor with a golden regression test. The second-model check (Qwen3-0.6B, 1 seed) gets cut first.

The usual way to fail this week is to start a new experiment because it feels more productive than writing. It is not. An unpublished result does nothing for your portfolio. Anything optional that does not get done moves to week 11 Mon, and you record that move in writing. A holiday never counts as buffer. Holiday weeks pause the week index.

> Write the posts from the results table, not from memory. Every number in the post should link to a results row with a git SHA, config hash and per-item JSONL.

sections.heading: Public claims that survive a skeptical reader
sections.md:
A reader asks one question of post #1: is the gain real or noise? You answer with the three-part rule from REVIEW.md section 3.2. Each part rules out a different kind of noise.

**Sampling noise on one checkpoint.** The noise floor is the SD of pass@1 across 3 sampling seeds on the same checkpoint. In week 0 on MBPP test it was 0.17 pts (basic tests) and 0.66 pts (plus tests), so a headline gain must exceed $2\sigma$: 0.35 or 1.32 pts. If the week-3 sampler replaced vLLM, re-measure it. The number belongs to the sampler, not to the model.

**Item noise and seed noise.** The two-level paired bootstrap resamples training seeds within each arm, then resamples the shared item IDs. Pairing matters. One proportion at $n=500$ items, $p=0.46$, with one sample per item has a 95% CI of about

$$
\pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{0.46 \cdot 0.54}{500}} \approx \pm 4.4 \text{ pts}.
$$

The week-0 CI of [41.8, 49.9] (about $\pm 4.0$) is a little narrower because each item averages 4 samples, which removes some within-item sampling noise but none of the between-item spread. The paired difference cancels per-item difficulty, which is most of that variance, so its CI is much narrower.

**Training-seed luck.** The sign of the paired difference must be the same on every training seed. Show per-seed curves plus the mean, never the mean alone.

For pass@k use the unbiased estimator with $n$ samples per item, $c$ of them passing:

$$
\widehat{\text{pass@}k} = 1 - \frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}},
$$

with $n \ge 2k$ and a CI at every $k$. If you compare more than about 5 things, apply Holm or label them exploratory. Label every single-seed result "exploratory" in the sentence that states it, not in a footnote. Report the gap between the basic verifier and the stricter held-out MBPP+ verifier. A gain that disappears on plus tests means the model learned the tests, not the task. Link the pre-registration note you committed before the run, so the reader can see the decision rule was fixed in advance.

**Post #2 needs a fair benchmark.** Run vLLM and your JAX sampler with the same model, dtype, batch size, prompt and output lengths, decoding settings (temperature, no top-p in the RL path), and EOS rule (or a fixed output length). Exclude warmup and compile time. Report median and p90 over at least 10 runs. Leave JAX preallocation on. Run vLLM in its own process at a different time so it never shares the GPU.

Put both numbers next to the bandwidth roofline. Decode is memory-bound: each step reads every weight once plus the KV cache of every sequence. For Qwen3-1.7B the weights are $1.72 \times 10^9 \times 2$ B $= 3.44$ GB in bf16. KV bytes per token are

$$
2 \cdot N_L \cdot H_{kv} \cdot d_h \cdot 2\,\text{B} = 2 \cdot 28 \cdot 8 \cdot 128 \cdot 2 = 114{,}688\ \text{B}.
$$

At $B=64$ and a 1024-token context, the KV cache is $64 \cdot 1024 \cdot 114688 \approx 7.5$ GB. One step reads about 10.9 GB, so at the 4090's ~1 TB/s it takes at least ~11 ms. That caps throughput at about $64/0.011 \approx 5.9$k tokens/s for that configuration.

The bound depends on $B$ and on the *average* context during decode (prompt plus half the output, not the maximum). At $B=256$ and an average context of 300 tokens, the step reads $3.44 + 256 \cdot 300 \cdot 114688 \approx 12.2$ GB, which allows about $256/0.0122 \approx 21$k tokens/s. So the week-0 vLLM figure of 12.7k to 14.7k tokens/s, logged at a larger batch, does not contradict the 5.9k bound. Always compare a measured number with the roofline for its own batch and lengths. Then say what the number does not show: other batch and prompt sizes, continuous batching, and paged attention. Those go in the week-11 update.

sections.heading: How JAX decides how many devices exist
sections.md:
You do not need 8 chips to test 8-way sharding. XLA's CPU backend can pretend to have 8 devices. Each fake device runs real partitioned programs with real collectives, so a sharding bug shows up the same way it would on a TPU.

The trap is timing. The CPU backend reads `XLA_FLAGS` the first time it initializes, which is the first call that needs a backend: `jax.devices()`, the first array, the first jit. From then on the count is fixed for the process. On the installed JAX 0.12, setting the flag after `import jax` but before any of those calls still gives 8 devices, and setting it after `jax.devices()` silently leaves 1. Any module you import may create an array at import time and initialize the backend. That is why the safe rule is to set the flag before `import jax`, in the shell or in `conftest.py`.

Here is what goes wrong. With 1 device, `jax.make_mesh((8,), ("data",))` raises `ValueError: Number of devices 1 must be >= the product of mesh_shape (8,)`. But a test that builds its mesh from `jax.devices()` quietly makes a 1-device mesh. Every `NamedSharding` is then replicated, no collectives run, and sharded == unsharded passes because both runs are the same computation. A green test that tests nothing is worse than a missing test. So the first line of the test asserts the count.

```python
# tests/conftest.py  (pytest imports this before any test module)
import os
os.environ["XLA_FLAGS"] = (
    os.environ.get("XLA_FLAGS", "") + " --xla_force_host_platform_device_count=8"
)
os.environ["JAX_PLATFORMS"] = "cpu"       # keep the 4090 out of it

# tests/test_sharding.py
import jax
jax.config.update("jax_default_matmul_precision", "highest")

def test_device_count():
    assert len(jax.devices()) == 8, jax.devices()
```

The alternative, `jax.config.update("jax_num_cpu_devices", 8)`, also works on JAX 0.12, and it fails loudly: called after backend init it raises `RuntimeError: jax_num_cpu_devices config should be updated before backends are initialized`. Run the sharding tests in their own process (`pytest tests/test_sharding.py`), because another test file that touches JAX first would fix the count at 1. The `tests/conftest.py` applies to every file in `tests/`. That is fine here, because the harness tests never import JAX. `scripts/check_jax.py` already does this the safe way: it runs the sharding check in a child process with the flag in its environment. Once, on purpose, remove the flag and watch the assertion fail. That is how you know the guard works.

sections.heading: Per-chip memory: DP versus FSDP
sections.md:
Start by counting bytes per parameter in mixed-precision Adam training. You keep fp32 master weights (4 B), fp32 gradients (4 B), and Adam's first and second moments $m$ and $v$ (4 B each):

$$
4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16\ \text{B/param}, \quad +2\ \text{B if you also keep a bf16 compute copy.}
$$

(The ZeRO paper also arrives at 16 B, as 2 B fp16 weights + 2 B fp16 grads + 12 B of fp32 master weights, $m$ and $v$. The total is the same, but the bytes sit in different places.)

**Pure data parallelism (DP)** replicates all of this on every chip and splits only the batch. **FSDP** (ZeRO-3) shards parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the $n$ chips. Each chip owns $1/n$ of every tensor and all-gathers a layer's weights just before it uses them.

Worked numbers, $n = 8$, against v5e's 16 GB of HBM per chip:

| model | DP per chip | FSDP-8 per chip |
|---|---|---|
| 300M | $300\text{M} \times 16 = 4.8$ GB | $4.8/8 = 0.6$ GB |
| Qwen3-1.7B (1.72B) | $27.5$ GB, does not fit | $3.44$ GB |

Where does 1.72B come from? Count from the config. The tied embedding is $V \cdot d_{model} = 151936 \cdot 2048 = 311$M. Each layer has $q$ and $o$ ($2 \cdot 2048^2$), $k$ and $v$ ($2 \cdot 2048 \cdot 1024$, since $H_{kv} d_h = 1024$) and the MLP ($3 \cdot 2048 \cdot 6144$), which is 50.3M. The norms add only a few thousand per layer. Then $311\text{M} + 28 \times 50.3\text{M} = 1.72$B.

FSDP adds a transient cost: the gathered bf16 weights of the layer in flight. One Qwen3 layer is $50.3\text{M} \times 2 = 101$ MB. The embedding is 622 MB if you gather all of it at once.

At 300M both fit, and activations usually dominate. Saving the residual stream once per layer (per-layer remat) costs $B \cdot L \cdot d_{model} \cdot N_L \cdot 2$ B. At $B=8$, $L=1024$ that is $8 \cdot 1024 \cdot 2048 \cdot 28 \cdot 2 \approx 0.94$ GB. Full fp32 logits $[B, L, V]$ would be $8 \cdot 1024 \cdot 151936 \cdot 4 \approx 5.0$ GB, which is why chapter 3 chunks the vocab.

Check the arithmetic against the compiler. `jax.jit(f).lower(...).compile().memory_analysis()` returns a `CompiledMemoryStats` with `argument_size_in_bytes`, counted per device. On the toy two-matrix MLP from section 6 ($2 \times 32 \times 128$ fp32 = 32,768 B of weights, global batch 64 sharded 8 ways), it reported 34,816 B per device under DP and 6,144 B under FSDP. Under FSDP that is $32768/8 = 4096$ B of weights. Both cases add the same 2,048 B of input shards ($x$ and $y$, each $8 \times 32 \times 4$ B). The prediction is exact. To call `jax.jit` on an NNX model, split it first: `graphdef, state = nnx.split(model)`, and merge inside the function.

sections.heading: Communication: ring all-reduce and the FSDP bill
sections.md:
Let $P$ be the bytes of parameters, or of gradients, and $n$ the number of devices. Ring all-reduce has two phases.

**Reduce-scatter.** Split the buffer into $n$ chunks of $P/n$. Over $n-1$ steps each device sends one chunk to its neighbor, and the neighbor adds it to its own copy. At the end each device holds the full sum of one chunk. Bytes sent per device: $(n-1) \cdot P/n$.

**All-gather.** Over another $n-1$ steps the reduced chunks circulate until every device has all of them. Again $(n-1)P/n$.

$$
\text{DP all-reduce} = \frac{2(n-1)}{n} P \approx 2P.
$$

The cost per device barely depends on $n$. That is why ring all-reduce scales.

FSDP needs three collectives per step: all-gather the params in the forward pass, all-gather them again in the backward pass (unless you keep them), and reduce-scatter the gradients:

$$
\text{FSDP} = \frac{3(n-1)}{n} P \approx 1.5\times \text{DP}.
$$

You pay 1.5x the traffic for about $n$x less state memory. Use the dtype each collective actually moves: params are usually all-gathered in bf16, while grads may be reduced in fp32 or bf16. For Qwen3-1.7B with all traffic in bf16 ($P = 3.44$ GB, $n=8$): DP sends $2 \cdot \tfrac78 \cdot 3.44 = 6.0$ GB per device per step, and FSDP sends $3 \cdot \tfrac78 \cdot 3.44 = 9.0$ GB. If you reduce gradients in fp32, the gradient term doubles.

Predict the collectives, then look. Dump the compiled HLO and count the ops. Count instructions, not substrings. A plain `txt.count("all-reduce")` also matches instruction names like `%all-reduce.3` and their uses, so it overcounts.

```python
import re
txt = jax.jit(train_step).lower(state, xs, ys).compile().as_text()
ops = ("all-reduce", "all-gather", "reduce-scatter")
print({op: len(re.findall(rf"\s{op}(?:-start)?\(", txt)) for op in ops})
```

On the fake CPU mesh, the toy DP step has 1 all-reduce. XLA fused the loss and both gradients into one tuple all-reduce. The FSDP step has 2 all-gathers, one per weight, and no second gather in the backward pass, because XLA kept the small gathered weights alive. You can't count on that at real scale, where the memory is the reason you chose FSDP. The FSDP step also shows no `reduce-scatter`. Its single all-reduce sums the full `f32[128,32]` and `f32[32,128]` gradients, and a dynamic-slice then keeps each device's shard. The output gradients are still sharded `P('data', None)`, so the math is right, but the CPU backend implemented it as all-reduce plus slice. On TPU or GPU you should see a reduce-scatter. If the TPU HLO for FSDP shows only full-size all-reduces and the gradient out-shardings are replicated, your gradients are being replicated, so check the out-shardings.

sections.heading: The sharding test, and telling noise from bugs
sections.md:
The test builds the same model twice, once unsharded and once sharded under a mesh, and compares the loss and every gradient leaf. In Flax 0.12, a `Param` created with a `with_partitioning` annotation inside `jax.set_mesh` is sharded at creation (eager sharding). On JAX 0.12, `jax.make_mesh` gives Explicit axes by default.

```python
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp, numpy as np
from flax import nnx
from jax.sharding import NamedSharding, PartitionSpec as P

class MLP(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, f, rngs, fsdp=False):
        init = nnx.initializers.lecun_normal()
        if fsdp:
            init = nnx.with_partitioning(init, ("data", None))
        self.w1 = nnx.Param(init(rngs.params(), (d, f)))
        self.w2 = nnx.Param(init(rngs.params(), (f, d)))
    def __call__(self, x):
        return jax.nn.gelu(x @ self.w1[...]) @ self.w2[...]

def loss_fn(m, x, y):
    return jnp.mean((m(x) - y) ** 2)          # global mean: XLA inserts the collective

x = jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(1), (64, 32))
y = jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(2), (64, 32))
step = nnx.jit(nnx.value_and_grad(loss_fn))
l0, g0 = step(MLP(32, 128, nnx.Rngs(0)), x, y)

mesh = jax.make_mesh((8,), ("data",))
with jax.set_mesh(mesh):
    m = MLP(32, 128, nnx.Rngs(0), fsdp=True)  # fsdp=False gives the DP case
    xs = jax.device_put(x, NamedSharding(mesh, P("data")))
    ys = jax.device_put(y, NamedSharding(mesh, P("data")))
    l1, g1 = step(m, xs, ys)

assert abs(float(l1 - l0)) / abs(float(l0)) < 1e-5
for (path, a), (_, b) in zip(nnx.to_flat_state(g0), nnx.to_flat_state(g1)):
    a, b = np.asarray(a[...]), np.asarray(b[...])
    rel = np.abs(a - b).max() / (np.abs(a).max() + 1e-12)
    assert rel < 1e-5, (path, rel)
```

Measured on the installed stack (fp32, highest precision): loss relative error $1.7 \times 10^{-7}$, gradient relative error $3.4 \times 10^{-7}$ and $3.1 \times 10^{-7}$ on the two leaves, for both DP and FSDP. Print the max absolute error too, not just the relative one.

**Why not bit-identical?** Sharding changes the order of the sums. A sum over the batch becomes 8 partial sums plus a collective. Floating-point addition is not associative. In fp32, $(10^8 + 1) - 10^8 = 0$, because the spacing of fp32 numbers near $10^8$ is 8, while $(10^8 - 10^8) + 1 = 1$. Each rounding step costs up to $\epsilon/2$ relative, where $\epsilon_{\text{fp32}} = 2^{-23} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-7}$ and $\epsilon_{\text{bf16}} = 2^{-7} \approx 7.8 \times 10^{-3}$. Rounding errors from a different order behave roughly like a random walk, so they grow like $\sqrt{n}\,\epsilon$. So in fp32 at highest precision you expect $10^{-7}$ to $10^{-5}$ relative error, and in bf16 about $10^{-2}$.

**What bugs look like.** A real bug gives errors of order 1, or an exact integer ratio. A wrong spec, a wrong axis, or a wrong mask gives order-1 error. A dropped or doubled mean gives a ratio of exactly $n$. So: $3 \times 10^{-7}$ is numerics. $0.4$ is a bug. A ratio of exactly $8.000$ is a reduction bug. The guard term in the denominator stops leaves near zero from producing a huge relative error out of nothing.

**The 8x bug, and a trap in current JAX.** Say each device computes the mean loss on its own shard inside `shard_map` and then reduces the gradients. The loss can match to $4 \times 10^{-7}$ while the gradients are exactly 8x too large. The loss matches because it is `pmean`ed separately for logging. So loss parity alone proves nothing about gradients.

The classic cause is `psum` on the grads where you meant `pmean`. On JAX 0.12, with the default `check_vma=True`, there is a second cause. The weights enter `jax.shard_map` replicated (`P()`), and the transpose of that implicit broadcast is a psum. So the gradient you get back is already summed over the data axis. Measured here with a local-mean loss: no reduction gives 8.0x, `pmean` also gives 8.0x, and `psum` gives 64x. Only `check_vma=False` brings back the old "pmean the grads" recipe (1.0x). The robust fix is to normalize the local loss by the global batch and let the implicit psum do the rest:

```python
B_global, d = x.shape
def local(w, x, y):                           # runs on one device's shard
    f = lambda w: jnp.sum((x @ w - y) ** 2) / (B_global * d)
    l, g = jax.value_and_grad(f)(w)
    return jax.lax.psum(l, "data"), g          # g is already summed over "data"

step = jax.jit(jax.shard_map(local, mesh=mesh, in_specs=(P(), P("data"), P("data")),
                             out_specs=(P(), P())))
```

That gives 1.0x. Under an Explicit mesh, `device_put` the inputs with matching shardings first, or `shard_map` raises a spec mismatch. The jit + `NamedSharding` route above is even simpler, because XLA inserts the collective for you. Inject the bug once, on purpose, and confirm the per-leaf check catches it.

sections.heading: Can Qwen3-1.7B be tensor-parallel 8 or 16 ways?
sections.md:
Tensor parallelism (TP) splits a layer's weight matrices across devices: attention by heads, the MLP by the $d_{ff}$ width, the embedding by vocab. Every dimension you shard must divide by the mesh axis size. Check the cached `config.json`: $H=16$, $H_{kv}=8$, $d_h=128$, $d_{ff}=6144$, $V=151936$, tied embeddings.

| dim | TP=8 | TP=16 |
|---|---|---|
| Q heads 16 | 2 per device | 1 per device |
| KV heads 8 | 1 per device | 0.5, does not divide |
| $d_{ff}$ 6144 | 768 | 384 |
| $V$ 151936 | 18992 | 9496 |

At TP=8 everything divides. At TP=16 the KV heads do not. You have two options. You can replicate each KV head across the pair of devices whose Q heads share it in the GQA group. That costs memory and a matching gradient sync for those weights. Or you can use a 2D mesh such as data=2, model=8. Qwen3's QK-norm normalizes each head separately over $d_h$, so sharding by head does not affect it. Check divisibility before you choose the mesh. On JAX 0.12, `device_put` of an `(8, 128)` array with `P("model")` on a 16-way axis raises `ValueError: ... does not evenly divide the dimension size 8`. Padding is something you would have to add yourself.

sections.heading: The TPU dry run, and the precision trap
sections.md:
The dry run has one job: make week 11 boring. It has to use the **same slice type and region** as week 11. A different slice can have different quota (default multi-chip quota is often zero), topology, HBM and compile behavior, so it would lower no risk at all. Debug the install on Kaggle TPU first, where that is possible, so the paid hour isn't spent on `pip`. The log must show each of these (checked against REVIEW.md section 3.4):

1. Quota confirmed and the slice provisioned (spot or TRC).
2. The pinned stack installs. `jax.devices()` shows the expected chip count.
3. The sharding test passes on real chips.
4. The week-11 train step runs for about 10 min on one chip.
5. Rerun hits the persistent compilation cache, so compile time drops.
6. Orbax checkpoint to a same-region bucket, kill, resume.
7. Auto-shutdown and a budget alert set. Results pulled. Slice deleted the same day, with the delete confirmation in the log. `accelerator_hours` and `cost_usd` logged.

**The precision trap.** Your fp32 parity check against the 4090 fails at about $10^{-2}$ relative. That is bf16-sized error, and it is no coincidence. On TPU the default matmul precision runs fp32 matmuls as a single bf16 pass. The GPU side does something similar: by default JAX allows TF32 for fp32 matmuls on the 4090, and TF32's 10-bit mantissa gives errors around $10^{-3}$. Set the precision explicitly on both sides for the parity test:

```python
jax.config.update("jax_default_matmul_precision", "highest")
```

The gap should drop to $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-5}$. Do not train with that setting. On TPU, `highest` emulates fp32 with about six bf16 passes per matmul, so it is several times slower. Parity proves correctness. Throughput runs keep the default or explicit bf16 compute. Record the precision setting in the results row, next to the JAX version and the allocator settings.

sections.heading: Refactoring without moving numbers
sections.md:
After a refactor, dev pass@1 for the same checkpoint and the same sampling seed moves by 0.7 pts. That is larger than either week-0 noise floor, but the noise floor is the wrong yardstick anyway. It measures what changes when you change the seed. Here nothing should change at all.

Work through it in order:

1. **Is the baseline deterministic?** Run the old code twice. If the two runs match bit for bit, any difference after the refactor is a bug. If they don't (GPU nondeterministic ops and autotuning can flip one sampled token, and after that the whole sequence diverges), compare greedy outputs and teacher-forced logits within tolerance instead.
2. **Which items changed?** Diff the per-item JSONL.
3. **Where do they first diverge?** Diff the token IDs of a changed item.
4. **Usual suspects:** config hash, chat template (`enable_thinking=False`), decoding config, sampler version, and PRNG key derivation.

PRNG derivation is the quiet one. If you change the order of `fold_in` and `split`, or swap the two `fold_in` arguments below, every sampled output changes while greedy decoding stays identical. So a greedy-only check misses it, and the golden test should include a few sampled items too.

```python
import json

def sample_key(base, item_idx, sample_idx):    # freeze this function
    k = jax.random.fold_in(base, item_idx)
    return jax.random.fold_in(k, sample_idx)

# tests/test_regression.py: golden per-item outputs for a fixed checkpoint
def test_golden():
    gold = {r["id"]: r for r in map(json.loads, open("tests/golden/dev_greedy.jsonl"))}
    new = run_eval(ckpt=GOLDEN_CKPT, split="dev", greedy=True, limit=50)  # your harness
    bad = [i for i, r in new.items() if r["tokens"] != gold[i]["tokens"]]
    assert not bad, f"{len(bad)} items diverged, first: {bad[:5]}"
```

Key items by ID, not by position, so reordering the dataset doesn't hide or fake a change. Commit the golden file before you start the refactor.

chapters.lab:
**Order matters. Stop wherever the week runs out, and write down what moved to week 11 Mon.**

1. **Slippage log.** Add a dated section to `README.md` listing what was cut in weeks 5 to 8 and why.
2. **Post #1 (RLVR note).** For each headline number, check the three criteria against the results row: gain > 2x noise floor (re-measured if the sampler changed), two-level paired CI excludes 0, same sign on every seed. Add the per-seed curves figure, the basic-vs-plus verifier gap, and pass@k CIs with $n \ge 2k$. Mark single-seed rows exploratory. Link the pre-registration note. Every number links to a README command.
3. **Post #2 (sampler).** Rerun the tokens/s benchmark: same model, dtype, batch, lengths, decoding and EOS rule, warmup excluded, median and p90 over ≥10 runs, preallocation on, vLLM in a separate process. Add the roofline for the same batch and average context (weights 3.44 GB + KV 114,688 B/token × B × context, ÷ ~1 TB/s), the parity results and the memory budget. Run each README command from a clean shell and check that it reproduces within the reported spread.
4. **Fake-device sharding test.** Create `tests/conftest.py` (sets `XLA_FLAGS` and `JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu`) and `tests/test_sharding.py`:
   - `assert len(jax.devices()) == 8`, then `jax_default_matmul_precision="highest"`.
   - DP (replicated params, `P("data")` batch) and FSDP (`nnx.with_partitioning(init, ("data", None))` under `jax.set_mesh`).
   - Compare loss and every grad leaf, max abs and relative error, assert rel < 1e-5.
   - Print `compile().memory_analysis().argument_size_in_bytes` (jit over `nnx.split` state) and the HLO collective counts using the regex from section 5. Predict both on paper first. For the toy MLP: 34,816 vs 6,144 B, and 1 all-reduce vs 2 all-gathers + 1 all-reduce on CPU.
   - Run: `uv run --project envs/jax pytest tests/test_sharding.py -q` (its own process).
   - Remove the flag once and watch the assertion fail. Inject the shard_map 8x gradient bug (local-mean loss, `P()` weights) once and watch the per-leaf check fail, then apply the global-batch normalization and watch it pass.
5. **Memory and comms worksheet.** In the post #2 draft or a notes file, write out DP vs FSDP-8 state for 300M and 1.72B (16 B/param) and the per-device bytes $2\tfrac{n-1}{n}P$ vs $3\tfrac{n-1}{n}P$, with the dtype each collective moves. Check TP=8/16 divisibility against `~/.cache/huggingface/.../Qwen3-1.7B/config.json`.
6. **TPU dry run (<1 h).** Same slice type and region as week 11. Debug on Kaggle TPU first. Log all seven checklist items, including the delete confirmation, `accelerator_hours` and `cost_usd`. Run parity at `highest` and at the default, record both, and look for reduce-scatter in the TPU FSDP HLO.
7. **Refactor.** First commit `tests/golden/dev_greedy.jsonl` from a fixed checkpoint (plus a few sampled items with frozen `sample_key`), and check whether the old code is deterministic by running it twice. Then refactor, run `tests/test_regression.py`, and run `pytest tests/test_harness.py` to confirm the harness is unchanged.
8. **Cut-first.** Week-5 headline on Qwen3-0.6B, 1 seed, labeled exploratory.
takeaways: Publish before you explore: an unpublished result does nothing for you, and a claim that fails the three statistics criteria hurts you.
XLA_FLAGS is read once, at backend init, and a late flag fails silently. If the device count is not asserted, a sharding test can pass on 1 device for the wrong reason.
Mixed-precision Adam costs 16 B per param. Qwen3-1.7B needs 27.5 GB per chip under DP and 3.44 GB under FSDP-8, and v5e has 16 GB.
Ring all-reduce sends about 2P per device and FSDP about 3P in exchange for n times less state. Predict the collectives, then count HLO instructions, not substrings.
Reduction-order noise in fp32 is 1e-7 to 1e-5 relative. Bugs are order 1 or an exact integer factor such as 8.0.
On JAX 0.12 shard_map, grads of replicated params come back already psummed, so normalize the local loss by the global batch or let jit with NamedSharding insert the collective.
Parity runs at highest matmul precision. Production runs do not, and the results row records which one was used.
A refactor must reproduce the same seed exactly. Golden per-item outputs and frozen PRNG derivation catch the changes the noise floor would excuse.
