chapters.title: Looking inside the model you trained
chapters.subtitle: Link a behavior change caused by SFT, DPO or RL to a direction in the residual stream, and add the controls that make the link more than a correlation.
chapters.why:
Weeks 1 to 8 gave you checkpoints that behave differently. SFT changed format and pass rate, RL changed how often the policy games the verifier, and the agent learned to call tools. All of that evidence is behavioral. This week asks where in the network the change lives, and how you would convince a skeptical reviewer that a vector you found is the change itself and not a side effect of length, padding or a few surface tokens. You also close the area evidence: scorecard row 4 and the two capstone finalists.

For a research-engineer role the payoff has two halves. The engineering half is owning a forward pass well enough to add capture and interventions as traced arguments, with no hook framework, no recompiles and a memory budget you worked out on paper. The research half is experimental hygiene under a huge search space: 28 layers, 2048 dimensions, many positions and many strengths. Probes memorize, directions overfit in-sample, and interventions can "work" just by breaking the model. The controls you build this week are the ones interpretability teams apply to every claim.
prereqs: Ch 0: memory arithmetic for Qwen3-1.7B (bf16 weights 3.44 GB, [B, L, V] logits) and the noise floor
Ch 0: the jit cache key and diagnosing recompiles with jax_log_compiles
Ch 1: masked per-token log-probs, LoRA layout and the paired bootstrap
Ch 1: the general-capability slice and forgetting measurement
Ch 3: your own NNX Qwen3 forward, LoRA with a traced scale, and merge/export
Ch 4-6: the merged-SFT reference for RL and the week-6 reward-hacking signal
Ch 8: tool-token masks and saved trajectories (if you use agent samples)
Section 3.2 statistics protocol: paired CIs, noise floor, Holm correction, pre-registration

sections.heading: Three rungs of evidence on a residual stream
sections.md:
Start from the model you built in week 3. Qwen3 is a pre-norm residual network. Write $h_0 = E[x]$ for the token embeddings, with $E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d_{model}}$, $V = 151936$ and $d_{model} = 2048$. Each of the $N_L = 28$ blocks reads a normalized copy of the stream and adds its output back:

$$a_l = h_{l-1} + \mathrm{Attn}_l(\mathrm{RMSNorm}(h_{l-1}))$$

$$h_l = a_l + \mathrm{MLP}_l(\mathrm{RMSNorm}(a_l))$$

The embeddings are tied, so the logits are $E \, \mathrm{RMSNorm}(h_{28})$. No block overwrites the stream. Each one only adds a vector to it. The stream at layer $l$ is therefore the sum of everything written so far. That makes a fixed direction $\hat d \in \mathbb{R}^{2048}$ a natural candidate for a feature: any block can write along it, and any later block can read it with a dot product.

A claim that "behavior X lives in direction $\hat d$ at layer $l$" can be supported at three levels:

1. **Readable.** A linear probe on $h_l$ predicts the label on held-out prompts. Typical failure: the label can be read from surface tokens, so the probe says nothing about internal computation.
2. **Correlated with training.** Across base, SFT, DPO and RL, the projection $h_l \cdot \hat d$ moves together with the behavior rate. Typical failure: each model saw different text, so the activations differ because the inputs differ.
3. **Causal.** Removing $\hat d$ lowers the behavior and adding it raises the behavior, while random directions and a capability check do not move. Typical failure: the intervention just damages the model, and any damage lowers a fragile behavior.

The week is organized around closing each failure with a control. Sections 2 and 3 build the instrument. Sections 4 to 7 build the evidence and its statistics. Section 8 looks at the weights directly, and section 9 assembles the headline figure.

A running example: MBPP prompts show one example test, such as `assert check_isosceles(6,8,12)==False`. A cheap hack under RL is to special-case that visible input, for example `if (a,b,c)==(6,8,12): return False`. This passes the visible assert and fails the hidden tests, and your week-6 hacking signal labels samples like it. Use whatever behavior your own runs actually changed. If your RL runs did not hack, a format or length behavior that RL changed is a fine target.

sections.heading: Capture and intervention as traced arguments
sections.md:
You own the forward pass, so you do not need hooks. The forward takes an intervention spec as an argument and returns captured activations as an output. The design problem is doing this without recompiling.

**Why a Python function per experiment retraces.** `nnx.jit` caches compiled programs by a key. The key contains the pytree structure of the arguments, the shape, dtype, weak_type and sharding of each array leaf, and the value or identity of every static argument. A Python callable is not an array, so it can only be static. A new function object, or a new closure over new values, is a new key, and each new key triggers a trace and an XLA compile. For a 1.7B model each compile takes tens of seconds (the step-0 time you measured in week 0). A sweep of 5 strengths times 3 layers times 2 modes would compile 30 times.

Scalars hide the same trap. A Python float captured by a closure is baked into the program as a constant. A Python float passed as an argument is traced as a weak-typed scalar, so a later call with `jnp.float32(2.0)` has a different weak_type and compiles again. In this repo's env, `f(x, 2.0)` followed by `f(x, jnp.float32(2.0))` grew the jit cache from 1 to 2 entries, and `jax_explain_cache_misses` reported `now f32[]{weak_type=False} and before f32[]{weak_type=True}`. Python control flow on the strength, such as `if alpha != 0:`, fails under tracing or forces the value to be static. The rule is that every knob is a `jnp` array with a fixed dtype and shape.

**One fixed intervention with all knobs traced.** Use a single function with these array parameters:

- `dir`: $[d_{model}]$ fp32, unit norm
- `alpha`: scalar fp32, the steering strength (not the LoRA alpha)
- `w_add`, `w_abl`: $[N_L]$ fp32 per-layer weights for steering and ablation, which also act as the mode flag

Inside the layer loop, apply

$$h \leftarrow h - w^{abl}_l (h \cdot \hat d)\hat d + w^{add}_l \, \alpha \, \hat d$$

Both modes are computed on every call and the weights select between them. The extra cost per layer is one $[B, L, d_{model}]$ dot with a vector plus an axpy, a few times $BLd_{model}$ FLOPs. The block itself costs about $2 \cdot 50.3\text{M} \cdot BL$ FLOPs for its matmuls ($12.6$M attention plus $37.7$M MLP parameters), so the intervention costs nothing measurable. Setting both weight vectors to zero gives the no-op. Sweeping the layer means moving a one-hot in `w_add`, which changes data, not code.

```python
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp
from flax import nnx

def intervene(h, iv, l):
    d = iv["dir"]                                   # [d_model], unit norm
    proj = (h.astype(jnp.float32) @ d)[..., None]   # [B, L, 1]
    dh = -iv["w_abl"][l] * proj * d + iv["w_add"][l] * iv["alpha"] * d
    return (h.astype(jnp.float32) + dh).astype(h.dtype)

class Qwen3(nnx.Module):          # your week-3 model, only the loop shown
    def __call__(self, ids, positions, mask, iv, cap_idx, resp_mask):
        h = self.embed(ids)
        caps_last, caps_mean = [], []
        n_resp = jnp.maximum(resp_mask.sum(1, keepdims=True), 1)
        for l, layer in enumerate(self.layers):
            h = layer(h, positions, mask)
            h = intervene(h, iv, l)
            hf = h.astype(jnp.float32)
            caps_last.append(jnp.take_along_axis(hf, cap_idx[:, None, None], 1)[:, 0])
            caps_mean.append((hf * resp_mask[..., None]).sum(1) / n_resp)
        logits = self.lm_head(self.final_norm(h))
        return logits, {"last": jnp.stack(caps_last), "mean": jnp.stack(caps_mean)}
```

In Flax 0.12, keep the layers in an `nnx.List`. If your stack scans over stacked layers instead of a Python loop, carry the layer index in the scan and index `w_abl[l]` with it. The capture then comes out of the scan as a stacked output, which already has the $[N_L, B, d_{model}]$ layout.

**The two tests.** First, the no-op equals the plain forward. Second, sweeps cause zero new compiles. A trace counter is the simplest proof, because the Python body of a jitted function runs only when it traces:

```python
TRACES = 0

@nnx.jit
def fwd(model, ids, positions, mask, iv, cap_idx, resp_mask):
    global TRACES; TRACES += 1
    return model(ids, positions, mask, iv, cap_idx, resp_mask)

def make_iv(d, alpha, w_add, w_abl):
    return dict(dir=(d / jnp.linalg.norm(d)).astype(jnp.float32),
                alpha=jnp.asarray(alpha, jnp.float32),
                w_add=jnp.asarray(w_add, jnp.float32),
                w_abl=jnp.asarray(w_abl, jnp.float32))

def test_zero_recompiles(model, ids, positions, mask, cap_idx, resp_mask, d_rand):
    z = jnp.zeros(28, jnp.float32)
    run = lambda iv: fwd(model, ids, positions, mask, iv, cap_idx, resp_mask)
    run(make_iv(d_rand, 0.0, z, z))                  # warmup trace
    n0 = TRACES
    for alpha in [0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0]:
        for l in [6, 14, 22]:
            run(make_iv(d_rand, alpha, z.at[l].set(1.0), z))   # steer
            run(make_iv(-d_rand, 0.0, z, z.at[l].set(1.0)))    # ablate
    assert TRACES == n0
```

For the no-op test, $h - 0 \cdot p \cdot \hat d + 0$ is exactly $h$ in IEEE arithmetic for finite $p$. Two no-op specs with different directions must therefore give bit-identical outputs from the same program. A separately compiled plain forward is a different program, and XLA may fuse it differently, so compare against it with a tolerance. On a 4-layer toy pre-norm model in this repo's env, the two no-op specs were bit-identical, the jitted no-op matched the eager plain forward to $9.5 \times 10^{-7}$ in fp32, and the 30-call sweep added zero traces. When the counter does move, turn on `jax_log_compiles` and `jax_explain_cache_misses`. The explanation names the argument that changed.

> Do not pass `alpha=2.0` in one call and `jnp.float32(2.0)` in the next. Build every spec through one constructor like `make_iv` so dtypes never drift.

sections.heading: A memory budget for capture
sections.md:
Activation capture is the easiest way to run out of memory this week, and the arithmetic takes one line.

Full fp32 residual streams for all 28 layers at $B = 32$, $L = 512$:

$$28 \times 32 \times 512 \times 2048 = 939.5\text{M elements}, \qquad 939.5\text{M} \times 4\ \text{B} = 3.76\ \text{GB}$$

That is per batch, on top of 3.44 GB of bf16 weights and the forward pass itself. Keeping the embedding output $h_0$ as well makes 29 points and 3.89 GB. Copied to the host for 1,000 items, the full streams would take about 117 GB. Per-token streams are clearly the wrong unit to store.

The forward has a second, larger term that capture does not need. Full-vocab logits at the same batch are

$$32 \times 512 \times 151936 = 2.49\text{B elements} = 4.98\ \text{GB in bf16},\ 9.96\ \text{GB in fp32}$$

For a capture pass, skip the LM head entirely (return before `lm_head`). If you need log-probs too, compute only the masked log-probs with the chunked log-softmax from week 3.

**What to store.** Store one vector per item per layer, not one per token. Two positions are useful:

- the last prompt token, at index `cap_idx`, which is the state just before the model writes the response
- the mean over the response span under the response mask, which summarizes what the model did

For 1,000 contrastive items, one position, all 28 layers, fp32:

$$28 \times 1000 \times 2048 \times 4\ \text{B} = 229\ \text{MB}$$

Two positions take 459 MB. bf16 halves both, and you can upcast for analysis. If you only need a few layers, capture only those.

**Reduce on device.** The gather and the masked mean in the section-2 code run inside the jitted forward, so only $[N_L, B, d_{model}]$ leaves the device. At $B = 32$ that is $28 \times 32 \times 2048 \times 4\ \text{B} = 7.3$ MB per batch. Never return the full $[B, L, d_{model}]$ stream and slice it in numpy. The device-to-host copy and host RAM become the bottleneck, not the GPU.

**Index from the mask, not from the end.** With right padding, `h[:, -1]` is a pad position. How many real tokens precede it, and how many pads, varies by item, so reading it leaks length into every probe. Compute the index per item: `cap_idx = prompt_len - 1` for the last prompt token, or `mask.sum(1) - 1` for the last real token. With left padding, compute positions from the mask with a cumsum. Otherwise RoPE sees shifted positions and every activation is slightly off-distribution.

Save activations as one array per position with shape $[N_L, N, d_{model}]$ and a parallel list of item IDs. Check the file size against the 229 MB prediction. If it is 100x larger, you saved per-token states.

sections.heading: Directions: difference of means, ablation and steering
sections.md:
**Difference of means.** Pick a layer $l$ and a capture position. Let $P$ be the positive set (samples that show the behavior) and $N$ the negative set. Then

$$\mu_+ = \frac{1}{|P|}\sum_{i \in P} h_l^{(i)}, \qquad \mu_- = \frac{1}{|N|}\sum_{i \in N} h_l^{(i)}, \qquad d = \mu_+ - \mu_-, \qquad \hat d = \frac{d}{\lVert d \rVert}$$

The projections of the two class means onto $\hat d$ differ by exactly $\hat d \cdot \mu_+ - \hat d \cdot \mu_- = \hat d \cdot d = \lVert d \rVert$. So $\lVert d \rVert$ is the natural unit of distance along the direction: moving the negative mean by $\lVert d \rVert$ along $\hat d$ lands it on the positive mean's projection.

Why not use the probe's weight vector? A logistic or LDA probe direction is close to $\Sigma^{-1} d$, where $\Sigma$ is the within-class covariance. $\Sigma^{-1}$ upweights low-variance dimensions that happen to separate the classes. That helps classification and often hurts intervention, because the model may barely use those dimensions. Difference of means is the standard choice for steering and ablation. The probe tells you about decodability.

**In-sample separation is inflated.** In 2048 dimensions, noise alone produces a large $\lVert d \rVert$. Suppose there is no signal and each coordinate has variance $\sigma^2$. Then $d$ is a difference of two independent sample means, with covariance $\sigma^2(1/|P| + 1/|N|) I$, so

$$\mathbb{E}\lVert d \rVert^2 = d_{model}\, \sigma^2 \left(\frac{1}{|P|} + \frac{1}{|N|}\right)$$

With $|P| = |N| = 300$ and $\sigma = 1$ this is $2048 \times 2/300 = 13.7$, so $\lVert d \rVert \approx 3.7$. On the fit items the class means are about $3.7\sigma$ apart along $\hat d$ from pure noise. On fresh items the gap is about zero, because a fixed direction cannot separate new noise. A Gaussian simulation in this repo's env gave an in-sample gap of 3.64 and a held-out gap of $-0.13$. Always fit $\hat d$ on one split and measure separation, probe accuracy and intervention effects on others.

**Directional ablation.** Remove the component along $\hat d$:

$$h' = h - (h \cdot \hat d)\,\hat d = (I - \hat d \hat d^\top) h$$

Check the projection, using $\hat d \cdot \hat d = 1$:

$$h' \cdot \hat d = h \cdot \hat d - (h \cdot \hat d)(\hat d \cdot \hat d) = 0$$

The operator $P = I - \hat d \hat d^\top$ is a projection: $P^2 = I - 2\hat d \hat d^\top + \hat d (\hat d^\top \hat d) \hat d^\top = P$, so ablating twice equals ablating once. Your test asserts that $|h' \cdot \hat d| / \lVert h' \rVert$ is near zero on captured outputs. On the toy model with all-layer ablation it was $4.4 \times 10^{-8}$ in fp32. bf16 has a unit roundoff of $2^{-8} \approx 0.4\%$, so projecting in bf16 leaves a residual of order $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-2}$ relative to $\lVert h \rVert$. That is why the code upcasts before projecting.

Ablating at one layer is a weak test. Every later block reads the stream and can write $\hat d$ back, so the behavior can survive. The stronger version ablates at every layer and every position, which you get by setting `w_abl` to all ones. An equivalent weight edit projects $\hat d$ out of every matrix that writes to the stream: `o_proj`, `down_proj` and the embedding. Qwen3 ties the embedding and the unembedding, so editing $E$ also changes the logit readout. Use the activation version, or untie a copy before editing.

Zero is not always a typical value of $h \cdot \hat d$. If both classes sit at a large positive offset, setting the projection to 0 pushes every item off-distribution. The variant $h' = h - (h \cdot \hat d - m)\hat d$, with $m$ the mean projection over negatives, moves items to the negative-class level instead. Pick one in the pre-registration.

**Steering.** Add the direction:

$$h' = h + \alpha \hat d$$

Because the stream is additive, a vector added at layer $l$ is still present at every later layer unless something removes it.

**Why the same $\alpha$ does different things at different layers.** Each block reads $\mathrm{RMSNorm}(h) = g \odot h / \mathrm{rms}(h)$ with $\mathrm{rms}(h) = \lVert h \rVert / \sqrt{d_{model}}$. So a block sees only the direction $u = h / \lVert h \rVert$, scaled by $\sqrt{d_{model}}\, g$. Write $c = u \cdot \hat d$. Expanding $\lVert h + \alpha \hat d \rVert \approx \lVert h \rVert (1 + c\,\alpha/\lVert h \rVert)$ and keeping first-order terms in $\alpha / \lVert h \rVert$,

$$\frac{h + \alpha \hat d}{\lVert h + \alpha \hat d \rVert} \approx u + \frac{\alpha}{\lVert h \rVert}\left(\hat d - c\, u\right)$$

Since $\lVert \hat d - c u \rVert^2 = 1 - 2c^2 + c^2 = 1 - c^2$, the change in what the block reads has size $(\alpha / \lVert h \rVert)\sqrt{1 - c^2} \le \alpha / \lVert h \rVert$. In pre-norm models $\lVert h_l \rVert$ usually grows with depth, because every block adds to the stream and nothing normalizes the stream itself. Many LLMs also have a few dimensions with very large values that dominate $\lVert h \rVert$ (Sun et al.). As an illustration, if $\lVert h \rVert$ is about 50 at layer 6 and 400 at layer 24, then $\alpha = 20$ perturbs the input direction by 40% at layer 6 and by 5% at layer 24. Measure your own per-layer norms before you choose a grid.

The fix is to express $\alpha$ in a per-layer unit: $\alpha = k\, \sigma_l$ with $\sigma_l$ the std of $h_l \cdot \hat d$ across items, or $\alpha = k \lVert d_l \rVert$. Then $k$ means the same thing at every layer (with the second unit, $k = 1$ is one class gap), and the sweep is comparable across layers.

```python
import numpy as np

def fit_direction(acts, labels, fit_idx):
    """acts: [N_L, N, d_model] fp32; labels: [N] in {0,1}; fit_idx: fit-split item indices."""
    A, y = acts[:, fit_idx], labels[fit_idx].astype(bool)
    d = A[:, y].mean(1) - A[:, ~y].mean(1)                       # [N_L, d_model]
    d_hat = d / np.linalg.norm(d, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return d_hat, np.linalg.norm(d, axis=1)

def layer_units(acts, d_hat, eval_idx):
    proj = np.einsum("lnd,ld->ln", acts[:, eval_idx], d_hat)    # [N_L, n_eval]
    resid_norm = np.linalg.norm(acts[:, eval_idx], axis=2).mean(1)
    return proj.std(1), resid_norm                              # sigma_l, mean ||h_l||
```

sections.heading: Probes, capacity and control tasks
sections.md:
A probe is a classifier on frozen activations. It answers one question: can the label be decoded linearly from $h_l$ on items the probe has not seen? Two things make that question easy to get wrong in 2048 dimensions.

**Capacity: Cover's counting result.** Take $N$ points in general position in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and a linear classifier with a bias. Cover (1965) counted the labelings it can realize. When $N \le d + 1$, all $2^N$ labelings are linearly separable. At $N = 2(d+1)$ exactly half are. So an unregularized logistic probe on $N = 400$ activations of dimension 2048 with random labels reaches 100% train accuracy, and its held-out accuracy is chance, because there is nothing to learn. A run in this repo's env on Gaussian data (400 train, 400 held out) gave train 1.000 and held-out 0.440. With an L2 penalty of $10^{-2}$ it gave train 1.000 and held-out 0.485. Both held-out numbers are within noise of 50% for 400 items (the 95% interval of a chance classifier is about $\pm 5$ points). L2 alone does not stop memorization at this size.

The consequences for the protocol:

- Train accuracy means nothing. Report held-out accuracy only, with splits by prompt, against a baseline.
- Choose the L2 strength on a validation split.
- Reduce capacity if you need to: project onto the top principal components (fit the PCA on the training split only), or collect more items so $N$ is well above $d$.
- Run the control task below, which measures the same capacity effect per layer.

**Splits by prompt.** Your contrastive set has several samples per prompt. Hacking depends heavily on the prompt: some MBPP items invite special-casing, others are never hacked. If samples of one prompt land in both train and test, the probe can learn "this prompt tends to be hacked" from prompt-identity features that every layer carries. Test accuracy then rises without any representation of hacking. Split by prompt ID, and keep the split fixed across layers and across models.

**Hewitt-Liang control task.** Hewitt and Liang asked how much of a probe's accuracy comes from the probe's own capacity to memorize. Their control task assigns each word type a random label, fixed for that type. The representation contains word identity, but a random property is not encoded anywhere, so the only way to solve the control task is to memorize the type-to-label map. Train the same architecture, with the same regularization and the same budget, on both tasks, and report

$$\text{selectivity}_l = \text{acc}^{real}_l - \text{acc}^{control}_l$$

with both accuracies measured on held-out data. High accuracy with low selectivity means the probe is expressive enough to memorize. It does not mean the layer encodes the behavior.

The subtle part is choosing what counts as a type. The control label must be a function of something that appears on both sides of the split, or the control is trivially at chance.

- **Per-prompt random label with a prompt split.** Held-out control accuracy should be 50% by construction. This is a leak detector: if it is clearly above 50%, the split or the features leak prompt identity. It does not measure capacity.
- **Per-type random label for a recurring type.** For example, a random label per token ID at the capture position, or per bucket of a surface feature that appears in both splits. This is the Hewitt-Liang measurement: how much a probe of this capacity can memorize surface identity.

Run both, keep the prompt split for the real task, and plot accuracy and selectivity per layer.

```python
import jax.numpy as jnp, optax
from flax import nnx

class Probe(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, rngs):
        self.lin = nnx.Linear(d, 1, kernel_init=nnx.initializers.zeros, rngs=rngs)
    def __call__(self, x):
        return self.lin(x)[:, 0]

@nnx.jit
def probe_step(probe, opt, x, y, l2):
    def loss_fn(p):
        ce = optax.sigmoid_binary_cross_entropy(p(x), y).mean()
        return ce + l2 * jnp.sum(p.lin.kernel[...] ** 2)
    loss, grads = nnx.value_and_grad(loss_fn)(probe)
    opt.update(probe, grads)
    return loss

def heldout_acc(X, y, tr, te, l2, steps=300):
    mu, sd = X[tr].mean(0), X[tr].std(0) + 1e-6       # train-split stats only
    Z = (X - mu) / sd
    probe = Probe(X.shape[1], nnx.Rngs(0))
    opt = nnx.Optimizer(probe, optax.adam(1e-2), wrt=nnx.Param)
    for _ in range(steps):
        probe_step(probe, opt, Z[tr], y[tr], jnp.asarray(l2, jnp.float32))
    return float(((probe(Z[te]) > 0) == (y[te] > 0.5)).mean())

# per layer l: sel[l] = heldout_acc(acts[l], y_real, tr, te, l2) - heldout_acc(acts[l], y_ctrl, tr, te, l2)
```

Choose `l2` on a validation split carved from the training prompts, and use the same value for the real and control tasks. Because the shapes are identical across layers, `probe_step` compiles once.

**Debug: 98% at layer 0.** Layer 0 is essentially the token embeddings. If a hacked-vs-honest probe reads 98% there, the label is visible in the tokens: literal `if` branches on the example input, `assert` lines, test-file edits in agent samples, response length or code-fence format. Run these checks in order:

1. Check the capture position. With right padding, index $-1$ reads a pad and leaks length. With left padding and a wrong position index, you read the wrong token.
2. Fit two baselines on the same split: a length-only logistic regression and a bag-of-tokens classifier (token counts over the response, restricted to the few thousand most frequent IDs). If bag-of-tokens also reaches about 98%, the probe is not evidence of an internal representation.
3. Match pairs on prompt and length, then rerun.
4. Capture on the prompt only, before the response. For samples from one model, prompt-only states are identical for every sample of a prompt, so the probe can now only predict which prompts get hacked. If accuracy stays high, you were measuring a prompt property.

The curve you hope to see is near baseline at layer 0, rising through the middle layers, with selectivity that stays clearly positive. A curve that is flat and high from layer 0 onward is a surface feature.

sections.heading: Contrastive sets and identical inputs across checkpoints
sections.md:
A direction is only as clean as the contrast that defines it. Treat the contrastive set as a dataset with its own confound audit.

**Building it from your runs.** Use dev or train prompts, never test. For each prompt, collect samples from the checkpoint where the behavior appears (RL for an SFT-to-RL change, or the week-6 and week-8 rollouts for hacked vs honest). Label each sample with an automatic checker: the hacking signal, a format statistic or the tool-call pattern. Then pair within prompt: a positive and a negative for the same prompt, with response lengths within about 10%. Drop prompts that have only one class. Save the item IDs, the prompt IDs and the split assignment, as you did for `data/splits.json` in week 0.

Write down the confound check for each of these before computing a single direction:

- **Length.** Report the mean response length per class after matching.
- **Format.** Code fences, `<think>` blocks, trailing usage blocks (the week-0 extraction issue) and `finish_reason=length` truncations. Drop truncated samples.
- **Padding position.** Every capture index is computed from the mask.
- **Surface tokens.** Report the bag-of-tokens baseline accuracy from section 5.
- **Prompt identity.** Split by prompt.

**Three splits.** Partition prompts into a fit split (compute $\hat d$ and train probes), a selection split (choose the layer, position and strength) and a report split (every number in the write-up). With about 200 dev prompts, 80 / 60 / 60 is a reasonable start. Section 7 explains why the selection split cannot be skipped.

**Comparing checkpoints on identical token IDs.** To ask how base, SFT, DPO and RL differ inside, teacher-force the same sequences $(x, y)$ through all four models. Each model runs one forward over the same token IDs, and you capture the same positions. Because the inputs are identical, any difference in $h_l$ comes from the weights.

If instead each model generates its own response, the activations mix two effects: different weights, and different text with different content, length and format. RL responses on MBPP are often shorter and more uniform than base responses, so a direction found that way may simply encode "short code". Generation is still the right tool for behavior rates. Activation comparisons use teacher forcing.

Teacher forcing also gives a behavioral readout for free. Compute $\log \pi(y \mid x) = \sum_t \log \pi(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})$ for the positive and the negative response of each pair under each model, with the week-1 masked log-prob function. A model that has learned the behavior assigns relatively more probability to positives, and you can put that next to the projection change.

**Memory plan.** The model family shares one base:

- Base: bf16 weights, 3.44 GB.
- SFT and DPO adapters sit on the base (DPO continued the SFT adapter, so it has its own A and B). Each is rank 16 on all 7 projections. Per layer that is $16 \times (2 \cdot 4096 + 2 \cdot 3072 + 3 \cdot 8192) = 622{,}592$ parameters, so 17.43M over 28 layers, or 70 MB in fp32.
- The RL adapter was trained on the merged-SFT base. That is a different weight matrix, so either load a second bf16 copy (another 3.44 GB) or apply the SFT and RL adapters unmerged on the original base.

With a traced scale per adapter slot, one compiled forward serves all four models: base is $(s_{sft}, s_{dpo}, s_{rl}) = (0, 0, 0)$, SFT is $(1, 0, 0)$, DPO is $(0, 1, 0)$, and RL is $(1, 0, 1)$ in the unmerged form. The unmerged form is not bit-identical to what RL trained against, because the merged weights were rounded to bf16 once, with relative rounding error of at most $2^{-8} \approx 0.4\%$ per element. Before trusting either form, run the week-1 parity check on log-probs between the merged and unmerged RL model, to within about $10^{-2}$. Total memory is under 8 GB plus activations, which fits on the 4090 either way.

sections.heading: Interventions as experiments
sections.md:
Suppose ablating $\hat d$ at layer 18 drops the hacking rate on the report split from 30% to 12%. That is an observation, not yet a finding. Four questions stand between the two.

**Is it this direction, or would any direction do?** Build a null. Ablate $K$ random unit vectors at the same layer and position and measure the same rate each time. An isotropic random unit vector $u$ removes very little. For a stream with second-moment matrix $M = \mathbb{E}[h h^\top]$, using $\mathbb{E}[u u^\top] = I/d_{model}$,

$$\mathbb{E}_u\left[(h \cdot u)^2\right] = \frac{\mathrm{tr}(M)}{d_{model}} = \frac{\mathbb{E}\lVert h \rVert^2}{2048}$$

which is a tiny fraction of the energy. The difference-of-means direction usually removes much more, so an isotropic null is too easy to beat. A fair null removes a similar amount. Either sample $u \propto M^{1/2} z$ with Gaussian $z$ and normalize, which concentrates random directions where the stream has variance, or keep only random directions whose removed energy $\mathbb{E}[(h \cdot u)^2]$ falls within a band around that of $\hat d$. For steering, add random unit vectors with the same $\alpha$. Plot the null as a band.

The empirical p-value from $K$ null directions is

$$p = \frac{1 + \#\{\text{null effects} \ge \text{observed}\}}{K + 1}$$

so with $K = 50$ the smallest attainable p is $1/51 \approx 0.020$.

**Is the model just broken?** A damaged model hacks less because it does everything less. Under the identical intervention, measure the general-capability slice from week 1 and MBPP dev pass@1. Base dev pass@1 was 49.8% [43.9, 55.8] in the week-0 gate. A claim needs the target behavior to move while the paired CI on capability change stays close to zero. If capability drops 10 points too, report the result as damage.

**Is the effect bigger than sampling noise?** Use a paired design. Generate with and without the intervention on the same report prompts, with the same PRNG key per (prompt, sample). The two arms then share their random numbers, and their samples diverge only where the intervention changed the logits. These are common random numbers, and they tighten the paired CI considerably. Compute a per-prompt rate in each arm as a dict `{prompt_id: rate}` and pass the two dicts to `harness.stats.paired_bootstrap`, which resamples the shared prompt IDs. As an illustration, with 60 report prompts and 8 samples each, a per-prompt difference SD of 0.35 gives $SE = 0.35/\sqrt{60} = 4.5$ points, so a 95% CI of about $\pm 8.9$ points around an 18-point drop, which excludes 0. Protocol 3.2.3 also asks that the effect exceed twice the sampling-seed noise floor. The week-0 floor was 0.17 points on basic pass@1, but your behavior metric needs its own floor, measured over 3 sampling seeds.

**Did you pick the layer on the data you report?** With 28 layers, two positions and several strengths you are running far more than five comparisons, so protocol 3.2.7 applies. Holm's procedure sorts the $m$ p-values $p_{(1)} \le \dots \le p_{(m)}$ and rejects in order while $p_{(i)} \le 0.05/(m - i + 1)$. With $m = 28$ the first threshold is $0.05/28 = 0.0018$. Combined with the empirical null, $1/(K+1) \le 0.0018$ needs $K \ge 559$ random directions per layer. With 50 random directions, no single layer can pass Holm across 28 layers.

The cleaner design avoids the problem. Run the full layer sweep on the selection split, label those per-layer results exploratory, and pre-register the rule that picks one layer, one position and one strength from them. Then run exactly one confirmatory test on the report split. A single test needs no correction, and $K = 50$ to $100$ random directions is enough.

**Dose-response.** Sweep steering $\alpha = k\sigma_l$ from $k = 0$ up to about 4 times the typical projection magnitude. Write down the predicted shape before you look. The target behavior should rise roughly monotonically at small $k$, then saturate or turn erratic. Capability should stay flat at small $k$, then fall sharply once $h$ leaves its normal range, with degenerate outputs such as repetition or broken code fences. Report the whole curve with paired CIs and the random-direction band at each $k$, not a single hand-picked $k$. Choose any headline $k$ on the selection split by a rule written in the pre-registration, for example the largest $k$ whose capability drop on the selection split stays within twice the noise floor.

**What you may claim.** Ablation reducing the behavior is evidence of necessity: the model uses this direction for the behavior. Steering a checkpoint that rarely hacks (base or SFT) into hacking is evidence of sufficiency. Without the second result, say "ablating $\hat d$ reduces X", not "$\hat d$ is the X feature". Even with both, it is one direction at one layer among possibly many, measured by one behavior metric.

sections.heading: Where training changed the weights: LoRA delta norms
sections.md:
Activations tell you where a behavior is represented. The adapters tell you where training wrote. Both are cheap to compute, and together they make a stronger story.

In the shared notation, each adapted matrix gets

$$\Delta W = s\, B A, \qquad s = \frac{\text{alpha}}{r}, \qquad A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{in}}, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{out} \times r}$$

with $r = 16$ and $s = 2$ for this plan's adapters. qwix stores the transposes: `lora_a` has shape $[d_{in}, r]$ and `lora_b` has shape $[r, d_{out}]$, and computes `x @ lora_a @ lora_b * alpha / rank`. So $A$ = `lora_a`$^\top$ and $B$ = `lora_b`$^\top$.

**Frobenius norm without forming the product.** Start from $\lVert M \rVert_F^2 = \mathrm{tr}(M^\top M)$ and use the cyclic property of the trace:

$$\lVert BA \rVert_F^2 = \mathrm{tr}(A^\top B^\top B A) = \mathrm{tr}\left((B^\top B)(A A^\top)\right)$$

Both factors are $r \times r$ Gram matrices. For `down_proj` ($d_{out} = 2048$, $d_{in} = 6144$), $B^\top B$ costs $2048 \cdot 16^2 = 0.52$M multiply-adds and $AA^\top$ costs $6144 \cdot 16^2 = 1.57$M. Forming $BA$ costs $2048 \cdot 6144 \cdot 16 = 201$M and needs a 50 MB fp32 temporary. Over all $7 \times 28 = 196$ adapted modules the Gram form is trivial on the CPU.

**Comparing modules of different shapes.** Raw norms are not comparable. If a matrix has entries of RMS $\sigma$, then $\lVert W \rVert_F = \sigma\sqrt{d_{out} d_{in}}$, which is $2048\sigma$ for `q_proj` ($2048 \times 2048$) and $3547\sigma$ for `down_proj` ($2048 \times 6144$). At equal entry scale, `down_proj` looks 1.7x "more changed". Report the relative change $\lVert \Delta W \rVert_F / \lVert W \rVert_F$, and keep the absolute norm in a second panel.

**Is the change low-rank in practice?** The singular values of $\Delta W$ come from an $r \times r$ core. Take thin QR factorizations $B = Q_B R_B$ and $A^\top = Q_A R_A$, so $A = R_A^\top Q_A^\top$. Then

$$BA = Q_B (R_B R_A^\top) Q_A^\top$$

Because $Q_B$ and $Q_A$ have orthonormal columns, the singular values of $BA$ equal those of the $16 \times 16$ matrix $R_B R_A^\top$. A stable rank $\lVert \Delta W \rVert_F^2 / \sigma_1^2$ near 1 means training used about one direction of that module.

```python
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp

def lora_delta_stats(lora_a, lora_b, w, scale):
    """qwix layout: lora_a [d_in, r], lora_b [r, d_out], w [d_in, d_out]."""
    a = lora_a.astype(jnp.float32).T        # A  [r, d_in]
    b = lora_b.astype(jnp.float32).T        # B  [d_out, r]
    fro2 = jnp.trace((b.T @ b) @ (a @ a.T))
    fro = scale * jnp.sqrt(jnp.maximum(fro2, 0.0))
    _, rb = jnp.linalg.qr(b)
    _, ra = jnp.linalg.qr(a.T)
    sv = scale * jnp.linalg.svd(rb @ ra.T, compute_uv=False)
    w_fro = jnp.linalg.norm(w.astype(jnp.float32))
    return dict(abs=fro, rel=fro / w_fro, sv=sv, stable_rank=fro**2 / sv[0]**2)

def test_matches_explicit_product():
    k1, k2, k3 = jax.random.split(jax.random.key(0), 3)
    a, b = jax.random.normal(k1, (64, 4)), jax.random.normal(k2, (4, 48))
    w = jax.random.normal(k3, (64, 48))
    got, dw = lora_delta_stats(a, b, w, 2.0), 2.0 * (a @ b)
    assert jnp.allclose(got["abs"], jnp.linalg.norm(dw), rtol=1e-5)
    assert jnp.allclose(got["sv"], jnp.linalg.svd(dw, compute_uv=False)[:4], rtol=1e-4)
```

On this test module in the repo's env, the Gram form gave 237.0011 against 237.0011 for the explicit product, and the QR-core singular values matched a full SVD of $\Delta W$. With `lora_b` all zeros the norm is exactly 0.

**Reading the plot.** Plot relative norm per layer (x axis, 0 to 27) for each of the seven modules, one panel per adapter. Two details matter. First, $B$ starts at zero, so every nonzero norm is learned change, and a zero norm at init is a free sanity check on the loader. Second, the RL adapter sits on the merged-SFT base, so its plot shows change relative to SFT, not relative to base, and its denominator $\lVert W \rVert_F$ should come from the merged-SFT matrix. RL deltas are often much smaller than SFT deltas. Check whether yours are, and whether the layers RL changed most overlap the layers where your direction is most decodable. Such an overlap, if you find one, is a hypothesis for the capstone, not a result.

sections.heading: The headline figure and scorecard row 4
sections.md:
The deliverable is one figure that links an internal change to a training-caused behavior change. Design it so that a skeptical reviewer runs out of easy objections.

**Panel (a): checkpoints.** For each checkpoint (base, SFT, DPO, RL, every training seed), plot the mean projection $h_l \cdot \hat d$ at the chosen layer and position on the x axis, measured on identical teacher-forced report-split inputs. Put the behavior rate on the y axis, with bootstrap CIs on both. $\hat d$ is fit on the fit split, the layer is chosen on the selection split, and the points come from the report split, so the figure is not circular. On its own, a correlation across checkpoints and seeds is only suggestive.

**Panel (b): interventions.** Plot behavior rate and capability against $k$ (in units of $\sigma_l$) for ablation and steering, with paired CIs and the random-direction band. This panel carries the causal weight.

**Caption.** State what the figure does not show: one direction among possibly many, one layer, one behavior metric, a linear readout. Link the command, the config, the item-ID file and the per-item JSONL, as section 3.5 requires for every plot.

The alternative explanations a reviewer will raise, and the control that answers each:

- "It's length." Length-matched pairs and a length-only baseline.
- "It's tokens." Bag-of-tokens baseline and a layer-0 check.
- "Any big perturbation does this." Variance-matched random directions.
- "You broke the model." The capability curve under the same intervention.
- "You picked the best layer." The selection split and a single confirmatory test.
- "The models saw different text." Teacher-forced identical token IDs.

**Scorecard row 4.** Score interpretability on the seven criteria of section 7 of REVIEW.md, in the order Surprise, iteration speed, follow-up feasibility, enjoyment, relevance, JAX/TPU leverage and public signal. The weights are 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, which sum to 13, so a row is worth at most $13 \times 5 = 65$. Link evidence for every score, because an unlinked score counts as 1. Worked example: suppose you give Surprise 3 but forget the link, and score the others 4, 4, 3, 3, 2, 3. Then

$$3 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 4 + 2 \cdot 4 + 2 \cdot 3 + 2 \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 3 = 36$$

With the link, the Surprise term is $3 \cdot 3 = 9$ and the row is worth 42. Six points from one missing link is enough to reorder areas.

An area's weighted total is the sum of these row values over every row filled for it so far (scorecard weeks 2, 6, 8 and 10 by now). The top two areas by weighted total become the capstone finalists. If they end within 10% of each other, for example 42 and 39 ($39/42 = 0.93$), the week-10 choice does not change: both are still the finalists. The closeness only means that week 12 runs one pilot per finalist before the final pick, instead of piloting only the leader. In week 11 you draft a pre-registered capstone for each finalist. The week-13 decision also requires that the chosen area has a row with Surprise of at least 4 backed by your own data, so note now which finalist lacks one. If the interpretability figure surprised you, that figure is the evidence to link.

chapters.lab:
Suggested paths: put JAX code in your week-3 stack package (called `stack/` here; use whatever you named it), never in `harness/`, which stays JAX-free. Scripts go in `scripts/week10_*.py` and tests in `tests/test_interp.py`.

**Mon: reading and pre-registration (about 4 h)**
1. Read Hewitt and Liang (the sections on control tasks and selectivity) and Arditi et al. (difference of means, directional ablation, weight orthogonalization, activation addition).
2. Pick the behavior from the "behavior change worth probing" notes kept each week (section 3.5). Prefer the week-6 hacking signal if RL hacked, otherwise a format or length change that RL caused.
3. Commit `prereg/week10_interp.md` before running anything. It records the behavior and its checker, the capture positions, the fit/selection/report split sizes, the layer and strength selection rule, the null (K variance-matched random directions), the capability measures, the ablation variant (to zero or to the negative-class mean), and the compute plan (local, measured hours).

**Mon-Tue: the instrument**
4. Add `iv`, `cap_idx` and `resp_mask` arguments to your forward as in section 2, with a `make_iv` constructor that fixes every dtype. Add a capture-only path that skips `lm_head`.
5. Write `tests/test_interp.py`, starting on a tiny config (4 layers, d_model 32) so it runs on CPU in seconds:
   - two no-op specs with different directions give bit-identical outputs; the no-op matches the plain forward within 1e-5 in fp32
   - after warmup, 5 alphas x 3 layers x 2 modes add zero traces to the counter; run once with `jax.config.update("jax_log_compiles", True)` and keep the log
   - a deliberate Python-float-then-`jnp.float32` call does retrace (confirms the counter works)
   - all-layer ablation gives captured |h . d_hat| / ||h|| below 1e-4 in fp32
   - `lora_delta_stats` matches the explicit product and its SVD on a small module, and returns 0 when `lora_b` is zero
6. Write the memory prediction (3.76 GB for the full stream at B=32, L=512; 229 MB for 1,000 items at one position; 7.3 MB per batch leaving the device) in the notebook before the first capture run.

**Tue-Wed: data and directions**
7. `scripts/week10_contrast.py`: build pairs from your saved per-item JSONL (dev/train prompts only), match on prompt and length, drop `finish_reason=length`, assign the three splits by prompt ID, and save `data/week10_contrast.jsonl` with item IDs. Print the confound table: mean length per class, fence and think-block rates, and the length-only and bag-of-tokens baseline accuracies.
8. `scripts/week10_capture.py`: first run the merged vs unmerged RL log-prob parity check. Then teacher-force every pair through base, SFT, DPO and RL with one compiled forward and traced adapter scales. Save `[N_L, N, 2048]` arrays per position and model plus the ID list, and compare the file size with the prediction.
9. Fit `d_hat` per layer on the fit split. On the selection split, plot per-layer `||h_l||`, `sigma_l` and held-out separation.
10. Probes per layer: the real task, the per-prompt control (leak detector, should be about 50%), the per-token-type control (capacity), and the length-only and bag-of-tokens baselines. Plot held-out accuracy and selectivity per layer. Also run the random-label probe at N=400 and confirm train 100% and held-out near 50%.

**Wed evening: launch overnight sweeps**
11. On the selection split: ablation at each layer and at all layers, steering for k in {0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4} at a few layers, and 50 variance-matched random directions per setting. Use the same PRNG key per (prompt, sample) across arms, and score with the existing harness. Label every per-layer result exploratory.

**Thu: confirmatory run and capability**
12. Apply the pre-registered rule to pick one layer, position and k. On the report split, run the intervention, its 50-100 random-direction null, the general-capability slice and dev pass@1, all under the same intervention. Compute the paired bootstrap over prompt IDs with `harness.stats.paired_bootstrap` (dicts of per-prompt rates) and the empirical p from the null. Measure the behavior metric's noise floor over 3 sampling seeds.
13. Sufficiency test: add the direction to base or SFT and measure whether the behavior appears.

**Fri: weights, figure, scorecard**
14. `scripts/week10_delta_norms.py`: relative and absolute ||Delta W||_F per layer and module for the SFT, DPO and RL adapters (RL relative to the merged-SFT base), plus stable rank.
15. Make the headline figure (panel a: checkpoints; panel b: dose-response with null band and capability curve) and add it to the README results table with the command, config and JSONL paths. Write result rows with the 3.2.8 metadata.
16. Fill scorecard row 4 with links, compute weighted totals over all filled rows for every area, name the top two, and note whether they are within 10% and which one lacks a Surprise of at least 4.
takeaways: Make every intervention knob a jnp array with a fixed dtype inside one fixed function, so sweeps over direction, strength and layer reuse one compiled program, and prove it with a trace counter.
Reduce activations on device to one vector per item per layer: full fp32 streams cost 3.76 GB per batch at B=32, L=512, while 1,000 items at one position cost 229 MB.
Directional ablation h - (h . d_hat) d_hat leaves zero projection by construction, but later layers can write the direction back, so also ablate at every layer.
In a pre-norm model each block reads h/||h||, so a steering vector's effect scales as alpha/||h_l||; express alpha in per-layer units such as the std of the projection.

In 2048 dimensions, probe train accuracy and in-sample class separation mean nothing: 400 random-label points are perfectly separable, and pure noise gives a 3.7-sigma mean gap at 300 items per class.
Report held-out selectivity against a Hewitt-Liang control task with splits by prompt, and compare with length-only and bag-of-tokens baselines before reading a probe curve.
An intervention result needs variance-matched random directions, a capability measurement under the same intervention, paired CIs with shared sampling keys, and a layer chosen on a separate split.
LoRA deltas are cheap to analyze through r x r Gram and QR cores; compare modules by relative norm, and remember that the RL adapter's change is relative to the merged-SFT base.
